entries.english: He who has not seen you : does not count you in (when distributing food, things etc.).
The one who says that will do : prevents you from finishing the work properly.
He who does not realize that you are a man : gives you little pieces of (cooked) potatoes.
entries.meaning: To a man the host must give a whole good-sized potato. Underestimating one's dignity.

entries.luganda: Atakusonyiwa : naawe tomusonyiwa; ennyanja ekutta omira.
entries.english: One who does not forgive you : you don't forgive him either; the lake kills you, whilst you are drinking (its water in drowning).
The man who does not free your hand : makes you drop other people's things.
entries.meaning: One who pesters you continually, prevents you from doing your work.

entries.english: The one who does not like you : says you are used to the privations (hunger) of the town.
entries.meaning: He scorns you, saying: "Oh that hungry fellow, that needy wretch, he does not know any better".

entries.english: The one who does not like you : spreads every calumny he has heard about you.

entries.luganda: Ataakwalize ŋŋanda : akulaga kifo, nti "oyo agenze muganda wo".
entries.english: He that will not increase the number of your (well known) relations : is the one who points at the place (where a relation of yours, unknown to you, has been sitting, saying) "that person who just went away, is a relative of yours".
entries.meaning: If he had said that before, it would have meant establishing closer relations.

entries.luganda: Atali muzimbi : empagi bw'emukuba, tewaba musango.
entries.english: If a pole hits somebody who is not a builder : he cannot complain.
entries.meaning: He has nothing to do on the building-site.

entries.english: He who has not got strength : does not become mad.
entries.meaning: Mad people, as a rule have great strength and endurance.

entries.english: The man who has no daughter-in-law : grouses by himself.
entries.meaning: He has to look after himself in everything. M.101, Ssal.p.85. 0598 Atali nnannyini mbooli : asima aligguula. He who is not the owner of the potatoes : digs them up negligently. Carelessness in treating other people's property.

entries.english: The one who is not the owner (parent) of the child : is not ready to die for it.

entries.luganda: Atali nnyoko : 1) akulaba mu mutwe, eyakuzaala akulaba eri olubuto; 2) aku- wa nsigo ng'omwaka gugwako; 3) takugerera nnaku za bukulu.
entries.english: One who is not your mother : 1) looks at your head (outer looks), your mother looks at your belly (and worries whether you have enough food and has pity on your hunger); 2) gives you seeds, when the planting season is finished and when it is too late for planting (your mother would help in time); 3) cannot estimate your age (your mother knows it).
A tree does not fall on one who is not there.
entries.meaning: Used in proving an "alibi". No guilt.

entries.english: The one who was not there : kills the buffalo.
entries.meaning: He shows the others how they should have attacked it. Cheap advice. "Empty vessels make the greatest sound".

entries.english: He who need not travel himself : makes up a food-parcel for you with menvu (unsubstantial food, quickly perishable).
entries.meaning: An inconsiderate person will always underrate somebody else's needs.

entries.english: He who did not make the journey himself : reproaches the other (for coming back late).
One who has no personal experience of sorrow : pities you at the doorway only.
entries.meaning: He does not listen sympathetically. He does not let you in and explain in detail. Tamanyi kukusaasira.

entries.luganda: Atamanyi bifa ku mwoyo gwa munne : enkumbi afulumya bbiri.
entries.english: (A woman) who does not know what is going on in the mind of her co-wife : puts out two hoes.
entries.meaning: Perhaps she is sick. Lack of consideration!

entries.luganda: Atamanyi bikiinwa : bwe bamuyita okulya ng'asembera.
entries.english: One who does not understand a joke : sits down, if they invite him to the meal (although he sees that there is not enough food).

entries.luganda: Atamanyi busungu bwa muddugavu : amutikka entamu.
entries.english: He who does not know the anger of the black man : puts a cooking pot on his head.
entries.meaning: A cooking-pot is black with soot and makes him blacker than he is.

entries.luganda: Atamanyi liiso bwe liruma : anyiga mu ly'emmindi.
entries.english: The man who does not know how painful an eye can be : presses down tobacco in the opening (liiso) of the pipe.
entries.meaning: Play on words: liiso ly'omuntu - liiso ly'emmindi.

entries.luganda: Atamanyi mpewo y'emagombe : olusanja ajja na lumu.
entries.english: He who does not know how cold it is in the underworld : comes (to the burial) with one single dry banana leaf.
entries.meaning: He brings nothing for the dead. - Dry banana leaves were spread on the ground for the mourners to sleep on.

entries.luganda: Atamanyi nnaku : y'agamba nti "Baagenda kusevena", sso nga baagenda kutu- fiirira.
entries.english: He who does not know the hardships (of a soldier in war) : says "They went to play at soldiering", although they went to die for us.
entries.meaning: "He jests at scars that never felt a wound".

entries.english: The man who knows nothing : does not know that he knows nothing.
He who comes later than the other man (to the meal) : blames him for eating ravenously.
He that never gave him shelter before : praises him for gentle manners.
entries.meaning: He does not know him yet. "All that glistens is not gold".

entries.english: The man who is not the parent of the child : is the one who is fit to bring it up Old custom of the Baganda: "Omwana takulira wa kitaawe".
entries.meaning: Parents are often too soft and too indulgent.

entries.luganda: Atamwa omukwano omukadde : nga n'omuggya aligutammia.
entries.english: One who gets tired of an old friendship : will also get tired of a new one.
He who has not yet returned from his hunt unsuccessfully : don't call him a skinner of dogs.
entries.meaning: There is still a chance that he returns with-nnyama.

entries.english: One who is not dead yet : does not speak evil of his tribe.
entries.meaning: Otherwise he would deprive himself of the possibility of going "home". Rub.C. 1821. 0629a Atannafa : tiyeezika.. One who has not died yet : is not going to bury himself. It would be folly to squander one's property, as long as one has hopes of living. Cf. legend in Ap.Eng.56!

entries.english: One who has not bought anything yet : does not let one food parcel pass un- inspected.
entries.meaning: He wants to strike the best bargain.

entries.english: He who is not involved in a dispute : laughs (or: laughs at one who is involved).
One who has not yet finished his tour of inspection : does not praise everything.
entries.meaning: He might not be pleased with what he has not yet seen.

entries.english: One who has not yet left his own home : praises his mother for cooking well.
entries.meaning: He has no experience of how others cook. Small horizon.

entries.english: One who has not experienced sorrow yet : laughs at one in misery.
entries.meaning: "He jests at scars that never felt a wound" (Shakespeare).

entries.luganda: Atasaba taweebwa : enkoko oluba okunywa amazzi ng'eralamira waggulu.
entries.english: One who does not ask, does not receive : when the chicken is drinking water, it lifts its head to heaven.
entries.meaning: Even the chicken prays.

entries.english: One who wants to save a child from harm, when it plays with a knife : gives him a piece of wood.
entries.meaning: Averting one's attention from a dangerous thing.

entries.english: One who feels no pity on a poor man : talks evil of him.
entries.meaning: Expression used to encourage another to be charitable.

entries.luganda: Atasasula mabanja 1) amaaso aganaabira mu nsiko; 2) abanjirwa mu kikunta.
entries.english: One who does not pay his debts : 1) washes his face in the jungle (he does not dare to wash himself in the open, his creditor might see him); 2) is asked for payment, when still in bed (the creditor comes very early to find him at home).

entries.luganda: Atasenza bantu : bamuwa ddagala, alyoke asenze.
entries.english: (A master) who cannot (or does not want to) get settlers (on his land) : is influenced by means of charrris so that he should get (admit) settlers.
He who does not like settlers on his land : (says) "the edible rat does not eat the chief".
entries.meaning: He prefers to be alone and undisturbed. Rub.C.2153. 0643 Atatya musajja munne : tawangaala. One who does not respect his fellow-man : won't live long. He underrates his neighbour's strength and is overcome by him.

entries.english: Bw'otoya: 1106) He who does not want to leave a beautiful woman alone (or any enticing thing like money, nnyama etc.) : must defend himself (arguing) until death.
entries.meaning: All reasoning with him is of no avail.

entries.english: The man who never stops scratching off the meat (from the skin) : will cut the skin.
entries.meaning: Dutch "Wie het onderst uit de kan will hebben: krijgt het lid".

entries.luganda: Ataawone bwavu : 1) agula wa mutunda-bikadde; 2) asuubula magi.
entries.english: One who will never get rid of poverty : 1) buys from a secondhand dealer (what he buys there, won't last); 2) deals in eggs (they perish soon).
One who has not heard (anything evil about his neighbour) : does not go to court to accuse (him).
He who does not build for the king : where will he get a little chieftainship?
entries.meaning: "Muzinge" (pea-cock) is the king of the birds.

entries.luganda: Atazze mbwa ye kumpi : nti "eyange eyigga n'ekiro".
entries.english: The one who does not keep his dog near him : says "my dog hunts even at night".
entries.meaning: It will be eaten by the leopard. - Not taking care of one's property, especially of children; letting them roam about at night-time.

entries.english: One who puts out a trap to catch (enkwale etc.) does not neglect to inspect it.
The man who sets only one trap : won't have meat (with his matooke).
entries.meaning: Perseverance! "A home is not built on one pole". 6.34. 0656 Atengejja : ng'asaba oluwanga obulamu; nti ye oyo ekyamutta kyali kiki?

entries.english: He who puts up a net (for catching the animal) : walks carefully (without making a noise).

entries.luganda: Atudde entitibbwa : kabootongo z'atuula mu mumwa.
entries.english: He sits immovably : as syphilis sits on the lips (i.e.
entries.meaning: a long time, without healing up).

entries.luganda: Atudde katubidde : ng'embwa bw'etuula mu lumbe lwa nte.
entries.english: He is sitting and does not move away : as a dog sits where they have killed a cow.
entries.meaning: The dog won't budge, till he gets something.

entries.luganda: Atudde kitebe : enjala ky'etuula mu lubuto.
entries.english: He sits there firmly established, as hunger sits in the stomach.
entries.meaning: If you feed it at midday, in the evening it is still there.

entries.english: One who throws the marketplace into a panic : does not consider the lame.
entries.meaning: They cannot run away. - Used for orders impossible to fulfill.

entries.luganda: Atuli mu ttaano : ekkumi likwata mpaawo.
entries.english: He is on our five fingers (hand) : ten fingers get hold of a bowl (full of beer).
entries.meaning: One hand gets hold of a thief, two hands of something you should appreciate. Rule of politeness.

entries.english: A man who wants to ask an elderly person for a service : does not look round (for a long time).
entries.meaning: He goes directly to him, because he has confidence that he will be able to do it.

entries.english: A businessman who exhibits (his wares) : is likely to sell out.

entries.luganda: Atunda omutwe gw'ente : amala kunyiga ku gugwe.
entries.english: He who sells the head of a cow : should first feel his own head (feeling that there is no meat on it).
entries.meaning: He should not ask too high a price for mere bones.

entries.english: He looks in as if thinking "give me some of it so that I can eat it" : seeing that those in the ddiiro don't like it.
entries.meaning: Hungry eyes! 90.104, Ssal.p.88. Similar sayings might be found under "Otunula - - " or under "Okutunula - ".

entries.luganda: Atunula baakitujjula (= baakitijjula) : ng'emmanvu (= ng'engalabi) eyoza lu- monde.
entries.english: He looks ugly (ill-humoured, dejected) : like a little trough (or: an engalabi- drum) used for washing potatoes.
He looks disjointed (disappointed) : like a thief who has not brought anything (who was unsuccessful).
He looks malicious : like a dog warming itself at the fire.
He looks as if he could not move : like a bearded fellow who has the dribble of his saliva still in his beard (after the night's sleep).

entries.luganda: Atunula kirungube : 1) ng'embuzi eyali ekulabye; 2) ng'esswera ekkube.
entries.english: He looks and stares : 1) like a goat which has seen you; 2) like a big fly that has been hit.
(kyoto) He looks like one who says "give it more fire!" (cook quicker, I am frightfully hungry).
He looks with bleary eyes : like a puff-adder that is half-blind.

entries.luganda: Atunula na kimaka : ng'eggumba eggereke ku nkolo.
entries.english: He looks queer (out of place) : like a bone given as relish with a (cooked) banana-rootstock.
He looks with unwinking eyes (with a brazen face) : like an old man asking for a bride.
He who takes anything to his mother : never says that it is too heavy.
entries.meaning: For one's mother no sacrifice is too big. Lat. "Ubi amatur non laboratur; aut si laboratur, labor amatur".

entries.english: He who is afraid of the sun : does not become a chief.
entries.meaning: Formerly the official meetings were held in the open. Other meaning: He does not mind coming to the Lubiri often, waiting there in the sun, till he gets a post.

entries.luganda: Avaawo asigira : 1) ejjenje lisigira nnabbubi ; nti balintwala ogw'obulanzi, osiga- langa ku baana; 2) enkoko esigira wakasanke; 3) kabootongo asigira ennungu n'ebikaata.
entries.english: He who leaves his place (or: He who passes away), puts in his representative (heir) : 1) the cockroach puts in the spider, (saying) "When they will take me to my work as prophet, you will stay with my children"; 2) the hen puts in the kasanke (small red finch) (she bequeaths her feathers to the kasanke, who cannot take the big stiff feathers, but carries away the soft ones from under the wings for its nest); 3) syphilis puts in (is replaced by) cracks in the skin and rash (on palms and soles).

entries.luganda: Avaawo asigira : 1) omuliro gusigira evvu; 2) omwezi gusigira olumuli.
entries.english: One who leaves his place, puts in his representative : 1) fire leaves ashes; 2) the moon leaves the dry elephant grass stalks (used as torch when there is no moon).
He runs (drives) like (one who says) "I did not come with a child".
entries.meaning: Leaving all the others behind.

entries.english: Where a hammer beats repeatedly : there will be a crack.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Gutta cavat lapidem, non vi sed saepe cadendo". Germ. "Steter Tropfen halt den Stein".

entries.english: Where a person died : there is haunting.
entries.meaning: The muzimu hovers round.

entries.english: Wherever the snail goes : there also goes the shell.
entries.meaning: Said of two persons usually seen together.

entries.english: Where the hoe goes : there is no bad place.
entries.meaning: Farming is the backbone of the country.

entries.english: Where there are males together : there will also be females.
Where a big tree falls : there will always be little pieces (firewood).
entries.meaning: When a rich man dies, there is always hope of getting something.

entries.english: Where rain falls : falls no famine.
entries.meaning: A good "windfall" banishes poverty (want).

entries.english: Where rains fall : maize likes to be (thrives).

entries.luganda: Awakana nga muyala : nti egindi gengera; ko ye nti "nedda".
entries.english: He is questioning the truth of the statement (hoping that he is wrong), like a hungry man, to whom they say "In such and such a place the matooke are ripe"; he answers: Really?

entries.luganda: Awa kanyumiza : tewaala nkoko, waala mayiba.
entries.english: At the home of a good entertainer : chicken won't increase in number, but the pigeons.
entries.meaning: He has to give away too many chickens. "Mayiba" signifies here "visitors".

entries.english: Where strong things grow : it is not just one that grows.
entries.meaning: Said of great talents, powerful people etc. The one will followers. Lat. "Exempla trahunt".

entries.english: Where there is a messenger, there is always a message (to be given to him).
Where there is a leper present, one does not speak in proverbs.
entries.meaning: So many proverbs speak of lepers.

entries.luganda: Awali omulema : tewaweterwa (= tewafunyirwa) lunwe (or: tewagererwa lugero).
entries.english: Where there is a lame person, one does not point with the finger at him (or: one does not use proverbs).
entries.meaning: He would think that they are speaking about him.

entries.english: Where there is a story-teller, there is laughter (entertainment).

entries.luganda: Awalungi tewaba wannyu : Mujaguzo evuga n'okka e Bunyolo (= n'okkirira e Bunyolo).
entries.english: The pleasant places are not always your home (i.e.
entries.meaning: you cannot always enjoy your peace at home) : when the Mujaguzo (set of 25 royal drums) sounds, you might have to go down to Bunyoro (to fight).

entries.english: Where the distance is short : the big frog cannot jump.
entries.meaning: People living near to each other, often don't see each other for a long time.

entries.luganda: Awampi wazaayirwa : ennyama ku magumba ga nnannyiniyo.
entries.english: Where there is only a small distance (separation), there is (often) estrangement : (as it is with) the flesh on the bones of (old or sick) people.
entries.meaning: Sickness or other circumstances often estrange people living near to each other. With old people the flesh seems to hang loose on the bones.

entries.english: If one uses the pestle a long time (crushing maize etc.) the mortar breaks.
entries.meaning: The pestle lives longer than the mortar.

entries.english: The one who has put beer-bananas on the shelves (on the kibanyi for ripening them), should not criticise others for having inferior quality of beer.
entries.meaning: He has no guarantee yet, that he will produce a better quality. It is unwise to blame others for what can happen to ourselves.

entries.english: One who has married a bad woman ; is at least no (involuntary) bachelor any longer.
entries.meaning: "Half a loaf is better than no bread".

entries.english: (enda) If your mother is not there : your bowels ache whilst eating.
entries.meaning: The presence of the mother sweetens all food.

entries.luganda: Awatali waggale watiibwa : singa ensekere esula mu nnyindo.
entries.english: Where there are open doors one fears : otherwise the lice would live in the nose.
In the place of a (hospitable) home : comes a shrine for the lubaale.
entries.meaning: Said of the home of an inhospitable man, whose father (or predecessor) was known for kind hospitality.

entries.luganda: Awava munno : tewadda munno; awava okugulu, wadda muggo.
entries.english: Where an old friend has left you : no new one comes; where you have lost a leg, a stick (crutch) comes in its place.
Where the banana-rootstock is eaten with pleasure : there remains no banana-shoot.
entries.meaning: The farmer who sells his land, undermines his existence. The trader taking from his basic capital, works towards bankruptcy.

entries.english: He who calumniates a dead person : is completely self-possessed.
entries.meaning: Dead persons cannot defend their reputation.

entries.luganda: Awerekera ensangi : tagya nayo; kawawa akoma (= asigala) ku mulyango.
entries.english: One who accompanies a friend : does not go away with him; the cow-fly stops at the entrance (of the stable, whilst the cows enter).
entries.meaning: We accompany our brethren to the grave, but do not enter (into magombe) with them.

entries.luganda: "Awo we nnalabira (= bikoma)" : nga gwe babadde bageya atuuse.
entries.english: "That much I saw" : (so one ends his uncharitable talk) when the person that has been criticised turns up.
entries.meaning: "Awo we nnalabira" is the usual end of a story.

entries.english: One who pleads in court with lies : pleads stubbornly.
One who listens to a story-teller : gets dry teeth.
One who likes to be master : does not go about visiting.
entries.meaning: Because in other places he has not got the influence and power as at home.

entries.english: He who loves the child (umbilical cord) : loves also its mother (the strap in which the cord is wrapped up).
entries.meaning: The mulongo (umbilical cord) is wrapped up and hung up or worn on a strap. They are therefore inseparable, like mother and child.

entries.english: One who loves an unsightly person : (is the one who) makes him beautiful.

entries.luganda: Ayagala omwavu y'amunyiriza : kya misana ku lukokola.
entries.english: He who loves a poor man makes him tidy (helpfully removing some blemish on his body, dirt etc.) : as the midday-meal does to the elbow.
entries.meaning: Washing the hands one dries them on the arm and the elbow.

entries.luganda: Ayeefulukuta mu nsambu : y'aliyirira abaalyanga amakota.
entries.english: One who sneaks about in an overgrown bananary : pays for those who have stolen big bunches (of matooke).
entries.meaning: If he takes little bits left over, he is thought capable of stealing big things.

entries.english: A man who knows his own (bodily) weakness : does not kill an engabi (bush- buck).
entries.meaning: Hunting ngabi is strenuous work, not meant for weaklings.

entries.english: He is weak (despirited) like cocks that were fighting in the dewy grass.
entries.meaning: They are wet all over. Dampened spirits!

entries.english: One who sneers at a person who is lazy : 1) makes him (her) work in the garden; 2) makes him (her) furious.
He who is both bad and lazy : finds his lot with the dogs.
entries.meaning: His companions do not care about him and leave him to his fate.

entries.english: One who flatters a witchdoctor : encourages him to burn the maduudu-seeds (poisonous plant: Datura Stramonium).
entries.meaning: And finally the witchdoctor will be caught. But one who tells him the truth and warns him, to leave off his evil doings, might save him. Correptio fraterna!

entries.english: One who goes with a soothsayer (lubaale-man) : knows what he eats.
entries.meaning: The mmandwa eat many things which ordinary mortals do not eat.

entries.luganda: Ayitaayita : y'akubuulira kaseera; nti gindi njala nnyingi.
entries.english: He who travels about : can tell you where there is a shortage of food; namely in such and such a place there is great famine.

entries.luganda: Ayogera byantanantana : ng'ava ku mu mulwadde, nti "we nvudde oba taliiwo".
entries.english: He brings a doubtful message (bigambo) : as one who comes from a sick person and says: "perhaps he is no longer where I left him" (i.e.
He talks without restraint (i.e.
entries.meaning: loudly) like a hunter who has put up the net. Whilst putting up the net, the hunters work silently so as not to drive the animal away.

entries.luganda: Ayogera kaati : ng'ow'eggaali aloga; nti "nnenda kuwanga mayembe gange".
entries.english: He talks without restraint, like the owner of a bicycle trying to bewitch some-body; (because he talks quite openly about his sinister intentions, saying) "I am going to set my mayembe".
entries.meaning: Mayembe means charms or handlebars! Play on words! If they try to put some spell on a person, they never talk openly like that.

entries.english: He tells (us) what is evident : like one with sore eyes, when he brings a death-notice.
One who brings forth a child : is better off than one who kills a cow.
entries.meaning: The meat of the cow does not last long; but a child is the possession of a life-time.

entries.english: A woman who brings forth an ugly child : makes an offering (to the lubaale) on its behalf.
entries.meaning: To secure the protection of the lubaale.

entries.luganda: Azaala ekibi : alyowera (= ayiira, = ayirira) abasesi.
entries.english: (ekyana) A woman who brings forth an ugly child : brings forth for the benefit of the scoffers.
entries.meaning: The child will be an object of derision.

entries.luganda: Azaala omulalu y'amumanya : enseenene zigwa kwa kikome.
entries.english: The parent of a mad child knows how to handle him : the grass hoppers settle down in dull weather (cannot be caught when the sun shines).
She who brings forth a daughter : gets also a son (in-law).

entries.luganda: Azinira ku ntujjo : afuyibwa mpaawo ddu.
entries.english: He who dances at the feast of the twins : is given a full cup.
entries.meaning: The entertainer is worth his drink.

entries.english: He has committed the offence of Mantambuntambu.
entries.meaning: "Mantambuntambu" = bintu bya beene = other people's business; he has taken the law into his own hands, without taking the case to court.

entries.luganda: Babadde bawoza ogw'embwa : ng'endiga erinnya enju.
entries.english: They were dealing with the case of the dog (which had climbed the roof of the house) : when the sheep climbed it.
entries.meaning: For a dog to climb the roof, is a bad omen; but for a sheep to climb it, is worse. Used in recurrent bad luck. (cf. Job!) "It never rains but it pours".

entries.english: They have brought a death-notice to the lazy woman : that means that she need not work in the field.
entries.meaning: Convenient excuse from an unpleasant duty. M.123, Gram.258. 0771 Baboola mwavu. They "excommunicate" a poor man. A poor man is often not recognized as member of the clan, as relation, whilst the rich one has more relations than he wants.

entries.luganda: Babuulira omwana wa boowo : nga naawe omunaku owulira.
entries.english: They give advice to (warn) a child who has still his parents : but also you, an orphan, can hear it.
entries.meaning: Said to an adopted child. Rub .C.100, 0773 "Badereva ensimbi baziyoola mu makubo" : nti ggwe bakukwata omukono nga bayoola? (Jealous remark to the drivers) "Drivers pick up their money on the roads" : (answer of the driver) "Do they prevent you from doing the same?"

entries.english: (One who asks) "When they serve matooke, do they heap them up like plunder-ers?" : gives a hint to the server (i.e.
entries.meaning: that is enough for me). Otherwise there is nothing left for yourself.

entries.english: They like a fighting man : but not a quarrelsome one.
entries.meaning: Rather honest fight than a poisonous quarrel.

entries.english: (or: Abantu balamu baagala ayaze.) People like an important man.
entries.meaning: A rich (influential) person has many "friends" who hope to profit by him.

entries.english: People like a man who has built his own house.
entries.meaning: They are shy to visit one who lives with other people not well acquainted with them.

entries.luganda: Baganda baamirira alidde (= basanyukira alidde obwami).
entries.english: Brothers (relations) loudly congratulate one who has achieved a chieftainship (or any high position).
entries.meaning: They hope to profit thereby. Rub.C.2034. 0780 Baganda muliro : gusula mu nju, sso nga gugikyaye. Brothers (relations) are like fire : the fire lives in the house, although it hates the house. The fire often burns the house down.

entries.english: Let them take the goat away : and the litigants can then look at the (empty) stake, where the dispute goat was tied up.
entries.meaning: Removing the object of litigation.

entries.english: (He who complains) "They have cut up (divided) all the meat (each one grabbing what he could get)" : is left with a poor rib-piece.
entries.meaning: Said about unfair distribution.

entries.english: They regret the absence of one who is no longer there.
entries.meaning: "Absence makes the heart grow fonder".

entries.luganda: Bakaabira mubikire : naye abakutukidde mu ngalo!
entries.english: They mourn over one whose death has been reported (from afar) : but more over one who died in their hands.
entries.meaning: Distance diminishes the sorrow.

entries.english: They have sharpened the knife on the rough skin of the palm, to go on scratch-ing with it.
entries.meaning: Said of people arguing with an irritable fellow. He merely gets more stubborn and angry.

entries.english: "Let them talk" (says a man) : if they have been speaking to him about some-body he likes.
entries.meaning: He does not intend to let himself be influenced against him.

entries.english: (or: Abakama empisi - -) Those who milk a hyena : exert themselves.
entries.meaning: Difficult job! - Those who want to get something out of a miser, have to try hard.

entries.english: (kikazi) They despise the unsightly woman : and she brings forth a splendid little boy.
entries.meaning: They never expected that she could still produce a son and heir.

entries.luganda: Bakinaanise akyagala : nga mukk'omubbi azadde abalongo.
entries.english: They have put a bracelet on her that she likes : as the case of the wife of a thief bringing forth twins.
entries.meaning: 1) A thief's wife usually cooks and eats inside so as not to be seen; so when she brings forth twins, she has two reasons to be in privacy. - 2) Among the cere-monies to be performed at the birth of twins was also one of stealing matooke, which is just in keeping with a thief.

entries.english: They have dug the kibanja well with the hoe.
entries.meaning: So says the visitor who wants to relieve himself and sees no highgrass nearby, where he could hide himself. A polite way of asking for the latrine. Latrines were introduced only about 1910-20.

entries.english: "They have given it to somebody else" : is the expression of envy.
entries.meaning: Chieftainships, ebibanja, presents etc.

entries.luganda: Bakuba emyali : omubumbi n'aba mulamu (or: ne batatta mubumbi).
entries.english: They break the (unbaked) pots : but the potter must remain alive.
entries.meaning: Otherwise no more pots would be made. - Germ. "Man muss das Kind nicht mit dem Bade ausschfitten".

entries.english: It is better (fairer) to count the marriages and not the dead husbands (in order to prevent the impression that a woman, whose several husbands have died, is responsible for their death).
entries.meaning: Such a woman is generally feared. - Accentuate the positive!

entries.english: It is better to have debts than stolen goods.
entries.meaning: Theft involves injustice, but debts don't.

entries.english: They tell you about the banana-root-stock-eating season coming : and you make for yourself ladles for stirring!
entries.meaning: There won't be anything to stir, when famine comes!

entries.english: They tell you to walk to Mukoko and you grudgingly set out on the long journey.
entries.meaning: The king of Bunyoro formerly resided at Mukoko.

entries.english: They have knocked at the cluster of mpafu (Uganda-plum) : to see whether they are ripe.
entries.meaning: Used for "sounding" one's opinion.

entries.english: (One who says to you) "They tell you" : is in reality the one who wants to tell you.

entries.luganda: Bakugoba mu nju : nti "nnaasula mu mulyango".
entries.english: They send you out of the house : (and you say) "I'll sleep in the doorway".
entries.meaning: But that also belongs to the house. - Circumventing an order.

entries.english: "If they send you away (from home), you come to us" : (so he says; but when you come) he calls you a miserable hungry fellow, hanging round all doorsteps.

entries.luganda: Bakulagirira eddagala eritta engabi : oyokya binsambwe?
entries.english: If they advise a (superstitious) means of killing the bushbuck : do you burn the binsambwe (of whose bark nets are made)?
entries.meaning: Better trust the old proven means. - Do not burn the bridges, you might need them again.

entries.luganda: Bakulamulira, nti "ka banzite" : nti emagombe eriibwa obwami (= nti ogenda kumyuka kitaka)?
entries.english: They condemn you and you say: "Alright, let them kill me" : do you think that in the underworld chieftainships are given (or: do you think that you will be a mumyuka-chief there)?
entries.meaning: M.128, Duta 179. 0819 Bakuloze empyangira : kabootongo z'aloga omuluvu. (cf. Nnaakuloga empya-ngira: 3199) They have cured you of your self-assurance : as syphilis cures the glutton of it. Syphilis puts fat (pus) on his lips and he can't eat it.

entries.english: They have given you a lesson : as they gave the suspicious husband.
entries.meaning: The over-suspicious husband misinterprets any absence of his wife from the house, accusing her of infidelity, finally sending her away and making her commit infidelity thereby.

entries.english: They show off with the living.
entries.meaning: Name of King Mukaabya's mulongo. - After death one is soon forgotten.

entries.luganda: Bakunyaga n'ente : ne batakunyaga na mukazi-muggya.
entries.english: (It is better that the raiders) rob the cows only : and not your concubine as well.
entries.meaning: Because she might speak evil of you afterwards. The cows can't.

entries.english: (or: nti osinga kwagala ya bugo-ba?) You cough, when the beaters beat the game into your net : do you want only the little meat which the beaters get?
entries.meaning: The beaters shout whilst driving the game into the net. The hunters on the opposite side keep still and take care not even to cough. One who coughs is punished by giving him only a "beaters' portion". - Warning for one who is going to spoil his chances.

entries.english: "They are cheating you" : (so he says, but) he does not give you the thing on loan (which you wanted to buy from somebody else).
entries.meaning: Cheap advice of rich people to the poor. "Words are as easy as the wind". "Fine words butter no parsnips".

entries.luganda: Bakusinza nsumika : nti "ebijja bituutiira" (or: nti labs bwe bijja bituutiira).
entries.english: (Meeting) people who are better dressed than you : (makes you say) What comes here, is puffed up.
They have given you a chieftainship : and you use it for your own advantage only?
They call you with the nose (= give you a discreet hint) : and you give answer with the mouth?
entries.meaning: Giving away thereby the one who has warned you.

entries.english: They call you to the chief's place : but that does not (necessarily) mean affection for you.
entries.meaning: They might have accused you.

entries.english: They still put out my matooke.
entries.meaning: I have still a good appetite.

entries.english: (If) they hate your sister (brother) : will you ask for a barkcloth?
They are astonished at it : as when a married man eats with the slaves.
entries.meaning: He is supposed to eat with his family.

entries.english: They look at each other like dog and leopard.
They come to visit (have a look at) a mushroom that is full-grown.
entries.meaning: They try to make friends with a rich man, who is likely to die soon, in the hope of inheriting something.

entries.luganda: Balekera ddala : endwadde si ya kuwona.
entries.english: They have given up hope entirely : the sickness is beyond recovery.
"Boys, put the matooke into your claws!" (dive into the meal) : (one who says so) has little room where he could put more food.
entries.meaning: He has had enough and is afraid that they might not manage all the food.

entries.english: (One who says confidently) "They will make it a very strong house (for me)" : forgets perhaps the fire (which can destroy also a strong house).
entries.meaning: Said of one who is too self-confident about his material possessions.

entries.luganda: "Balikomya eyo ne bazza" : ye Munyolo agenda.
entries.english: "They might stop (me) there and bring (me) back" : says the Munyoro as he runs away from his master.
entries.meaning: One should try a good thing, although a failure is possible.

entries.luganda: "Balikuba ku nda eridde" : muk'omubbi talamula bba (= talabula).
entries.english: "They shall beat (for once) the bowels that have eaten (= they will beat the thief who has stolen)" : so thinks the wife of the thief and does not warn him.
entries.meaning: Because she herself likes to eat stolen meat.

entries.luganda: Balikuta nga : 1) kayamba kenkana mmale; 2) embuzi zibaaga ngo; 3) enjala zibaaga ngo.
entries.english: They will let you free : 1) when the "kayamba" (ejjamba = small fish) is as big as a "mmale" (mud-fish) (i.e.
entries.meaning: never); 2) when goats slaughter leopards (i.e. never); 3) when your nails can tear a leopard to pieces (i.e. never). Sarcastic promise of what will never happen. French "Tu seras intelligent, quand la poule aura des dents". Germ. "Wenn Neujahr in den Sommer Mt".

entries.english: (Although they might tell you) "They will kill him (the chief) tomorrow" : that does not prevent you from becoming his tenant.
entries.meaning: There is no personal danger for you.

entries.english: "They will speak of him" : (this expression is used) when they praise a hero (or any outstanding personality or event).
entries.meaning: Baligyogerako (enjala); balizoogerako (enzige); balimwogerako (musisi).

entries.english: "They will send me on my own errand" : (one saying so) does not get any-thing.
entries.meaning: A child has been sent to somebody with a basket (present) and the child asks somebody else to accompany him. But the latter refuses to go, hoping to be sent later alone and to receive a greater "bakshishi". Selfishness and its punish-ment.

entries.english: "Let them bring it (the army)" : (one who boasts like that) will not wait for it to fight (with it).
entries.meaning: He will run away. Courage of a braggart.

entries.luganda: "Balitta ku lingi" : asenga kwa Mukwenda okuli abangi.
entries.english: "They will kill a great number" : (one who says so) becomes a subject of chief Mukwenda (Ssingo), where there are many people living.
entries.meaning: Many consider it as an honour to be under him, even if they are in danger of being killed in the fight. "Kasita tulifa bangi".

entries.luganda: "Balo embogo yamutta" : ko Nnampulirazzibi, nti "bw'atyo bw'azifumita".
entries.english: (The hunters report to the wife) "Your husband has been killed by a buffalo" : the wife who has not listened properly, answers "Yes, he kills them just like that".
entries.meaning: Listen well to what you are told.

entries.english: They look at the nkunga (vegetable) - doubting whether they should eat it - : whilst the others who have bbugga (good vegetable), eat lustily.
entries.meaning: "Nkunga" (amaranth plant) is only eaten, when nothing else is to be had.

entries.luganda: Balubuuliza mbazzi : nga luli ku muddo lulya (= lugaaya).
entries.english: (olute) They ask for the axe to kill the miserable cow : and it goes on eating grass.
entries.meaning: A careless man does not heed a warning.

entries.english: How could they make such a narrow door?
entries.meaning: We can't get a thing through that door.

entries.english: They quarrel loudly (about an absent person) : like a man (going to the well) quarrelling with the waterpot (about things at home).

entries.luganda: Balunaayiza : ng'ow'embaliga ayita mu luwenda (= akulembera omusulo).
entries.english: They interfere unduly (in the quarrel = luyombo) : as one with outward turned feet (interferes with the grass) when passing along a track (= going first in dew-covered grass).

entries.luganda: Balusaggya : ng'omuwuulu agula enkulo; nti "onooziwa ani okuzifumba?" (cf.
entries.english: Oli balusagya: 3881) They do it thoughtlessly (hastily) (i.e.
entries.meaning: olugambo) : as a bachelor who buys scrapings of a hide; to whom will you give them for cooking? They need careful cooking which is beyond a bachelor.

entries.english: They have brought the sickness (death) upon themselves : like the money that buys cassava.
Those who eat from their own land : always look down upon others.
They got hold of each other firmly (in wrestling) like a kanzu encircling the body : and not like a suuka that flaps open.

entries.luganda: "Bampe ne nneeriira, balibuuza ani?" : afa tasasudde.
entries.english: "Let them give it (i.e.
entries.meaning: the goat) to me and I shall eat it (use it all up), whom can they ask for payment (when I am dead)?" : (the old man, saying so) dies without having paid the price. Dishonest mentality, methods of a "mulyazaamaanyi".

entries.english: (One who asks) "What do they accuse him of?" : makes the prisoner cry.
entries.meaning: The prisoner thinks that the man has pity on him, and starts protesting his innocence and asking for help.

entries.english: (One about whom they say) "They have killed him (in the war)" : deserves more praise than one who "died of sickness".

entries.luganda: Bamututte kya mwanisi wa taaba : ekibaaze.
entries.english: They took him away (quickly) as a tobacco-curer takes his tobacco out of the sun (when rain starts) : without delay.

entries.luganda: Bamwagala olusuusuuto : lwe baagala mulekwa mu lumbe.
entries.english: They love him in a flattering way : as they love an orphan (heir) during the mourning period (i.e.
entries.meaning: as long as they have hopes of inheriting something).

entries.luganda: "Baana ba muno beeyokyayokya nnyo" : nga y'amummyeko.
entries.english: "The children in this home fry lots (of gonja) for themselves" : (so the visitor remarks) if the owner of the house.has given him nothing to eat.
The children of Walumbe (children who have lost their parents) : disperse.
entries.meaning: As long as the parents are alive, they stay together.

entries.english: The young of Mr.Dog : disperse in all directions.
entries.meaning: They are given away or sold.

entries.luganda: "Banaabegabega ettaka" : nga muk'omubbi asindika bba okugenda okubba.
entries.english: "They will wipe out (their footprints) on the ground" : as the thief's wife tells her husband, when she sends him stealing.
They will come back : those we have sent will come back.
entries.meaning: Admonition for patience: Do nothing hastily in your impatience.

entries.english: They flatter you for your fine workmanship in beating out barkcloth : (and that makes you boast that) you can beat out even the bark of the lusambya trees (Markhamia platicalix).

entries.luganda: "Baana na baana" : ng'omu tannakuba munne lubale.
entries.english: "They are children amongst children" : (so one says, looking benignly on their pranks) as long as none of them has yet broken another's head.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Sunt pueri, pueri; pueri puerilia tractant".

entries.luganda: "Bandaba" : 1) afunda ku munaabo; 2) alinda kutoma; 3) alya kya luyovu.
entries.english: "They see me" (so says the man who would like to be invited to eat with others and thinks that they have noticed his presence, but) : 1) he has to satisfy himself with the water to wash his hands (he gets nothing to eat); 2) he has to expect disappointment (they don't seem to notice him at all); 3) he eats the scrapings (the miserable remnants).
(One who complains) "They have infested my plot with rats" : cultivates a small plot.
entries.meaning: If he had a big plot, he would hardly notice the rats.

entries.english: (abakazi) (One who says) "They love me" : desires (to be as healthy as the man who says) "They don't love me".
entries.meaning: The first one contracts sickness through various love-affairs and is worse off than the second one who remains healthy.

entries.english: "I have plenty of friends" : (so you say) but none who is trustworthy.

entries.luganda: "Bannange banjagala" (= bannange bangi) : 1) nga tonnagwa wabi; 2) bw'ofa wabula akukaabira.
entries.english: (You say) "My friends love me" (= are many) : (and I say) 1) "as long as you are not in trouble"; 2) "when you die, nobody will cry for you".
entries.meaning: Lat. "Donec felix eris, multos numerabis amicos : Tempora si fuerint nubila solus eris". "When poverty comes in at the door, love flies out of the window". "A rich man has many friends".

entries.luganda: Bannanze bwemage : bwe balanga enjobe mu lusa.
entries.english: They have accused me unjustly, as they accused the antelope in the marsh.
entries.meaning: It grazes there, doing no damage to the crops.

entries.english: (He who thinks) "Let them praise me" : forgets his inheritance.
entries.meaning: They do not want a proud heir. - Used about any proud fellow.

entries.luganda: Bantu mannyo ga mbizzi : gaseka kungulu, nga munda mulimu bussi.
entries.english: Humans are like the teeth of wild pigs : outside all smile, inside murder.

(A woman who complains saying) "They malign me" (by suggesting that she seems to steal her matooke, as her lusuku is so small and every day she is seen peeling them) : does not leave the peeling place (is always there).
What men eat, is not wasted.
entries.meaning: All that is done to develop strong healthy men, will benefit the country.

entries.luganda: Basajja mabale : gasannana; nga bw'oddira ejjinja n'okuba linnaalyo, n'eryatika.
entries.english: Men are like flint-stones : they hit each other; if you take a stone and hit it with another, it will break.

entries.luganda: Basajja nsolo : bw'omugobera mu nsiko, awaguza maanyi.
entries.english: Men are like wild animals : if you follow one in the wilds, he breaks (through the thicket) with great force.
entries.meaning: He does not give in without a fight.

entries.luganda: Basugumbira (= abasugumbira) e Mmengo : Kabaka alibookya.
entries.english: Those who risk going to Mmengo (the king's place) : the king will burn them to death.

entries.luganda: "Basujju bandidde" : abuulira Lubinga, nti anaasala atya okusinga mutabani we, Kasujju ?
entries.english: "The people of Busujju-ssaza are beyond me!" (so one says, who has been wronged and seeks justice) : he tells Lubinga (the old head-mutaka, a lenient old man), who will settle a case against one of his own children, a Kasujju?

"Land-owners drink beer at night" (says the man, going in search for beer) : (but where he wants to enter to get a drink, with people who do not like him) they beat him with an akasendwe (a short pole, supporting the inside-wall of a kisuwa-hut), pretending not to know him.
A grown-up duck (or: hen) : scratches itself.
entries.meaning: A grown-up person must fend for himself (herself).

entries.english: They make it known to one who was not suckled where he actually lives (i.e.
entries.meaning: a person who does not know his home because he or she was robbed and taken away as a slave). The very fact that they don't tell his or her home, indicates that he was taken slave somewhere. They don't want to lose the slave.

entries.english: They make a trestle for the kiryo (gourd plant) when it puts forth fruit.
entries.meaning: Men do not want to support others, when they see no hope of profit.

entries.english: "The tenants refuse to work" (says the small chief to his superior) : but in reality it is he that refuses to make them work.
entries.meaning: Blaming others for one's own insufficiency.

entries.english: (emikago) They make new blood-brotherhood-contracts (friendships) : and forget the old ones.
entries.meaning: No fidelity! Engl. "Old friends and old wine are best".

entries.english: "The robbers are breaking into our house" : (the coward whispering that to his sleeping partner) does not lift his head from the ground.
entries.meaning: He wants the other to get up.

entries.english: Those who have succeeded : forget those who have helped them to succeed.
entries.meaning: Ingratitude to parents, benefactors. 11.40, Ssal.p.17. 0924a Baatuma mugezi. They have sent a clever messenger. So they say, when he has delivered his message properly. Duta 1121. 0924b Batuusa ebbugga : beerabira embooge. (cf. Ssebatuusa: 4885) When "bbugga" (fine vegetable) is brought : "mbooge" (lesser vegetable) is forgotten. 10.36, Ssal.p.16. 0924c "Batusaze" : y'atiisa eggye. (He who tells his companions) "They have cut us off' : frightens the soldiers. Pessimism! Duta 560. 0924d "Baatutta baatumalawo" : akiina abaafa. (cf. Tufudde, tuweddewo: 5100) (One who says) "They have killed us and finished us off' : sneers at the dead. He counts himself among the deceased.

entries.luganda: "Batuvumye e mbuga amatulu" : nga ye y'alirina.
entries.english: "They have called us blind fellows at the chiefs place" : (one who talks like that) is himself a blind fellow.
entries.meaning: He speaks in the plural, although he is the only one who was reprimanded. He says "us", because he wants support.

entries.english: "They (the masters) have increased the number of porters" : (so he says, but) he still carries the load under his arm.
entries.meaning: It does not seem to make any difference to him.

entries.english: "How they have embellished the pole (in the house)" : (so the guests say) when they have eaten and had enough.
entries.meaning: Before that their interest was wholly concentrated on the food.

entries.english: They behave like braggarts (they wipe off the perspiration, as if they had been doing tiring work).
They go over the surface like a swimmer.
entries.meaning: They treat things superficially. A swimmer does not see what is below the surface.

entries.english: Parents give birth to the body of their children : but not (always) to their characters.
entries.meaning: Good parents may have bad children.

entries.english: They are parents of a rich man.
entries.meaning: Everyone who receives a present from him, calls him "mwana wange".

entries.luganda: Baze wange, onkyawanga : n'ompa enkumbi n'olubugo!
entries.english: Husband of mine, you despise me : give me at least a hoe and a lubugo (working garment) (that I can offer food to my relations, when they come to visit me).

entries.luganda: Baazibumbira kwatika : ne ziramira mu kyokero.
entries.english: They have manufactured them (entamu or ensuwa) only to be broken and, lo, they stand (the fire in) the oven.
entries.meaning: Weaklings are often strong characters.

entries.luganda: Bbwa ddene : ligambwako nnyiniryo; lumonde bw'alemwa omuggo, enkumbi eyamusimba y'emusima.
entries.english: A big dog (also bbwa ddumi) is mastered by his owner (who trained him); if the potato cannot be dug out with the stick, the hoe which put it in, will dig it out Difficult characters.

entries.luganda: Beesaanya we ndi : ng'ovuddewo nga bakugeya.
entries.english: They pretend to be friendly, whilst I am present : when you have gone they talk evil about you.
People show themselves pleased (exchange congratulations) if one has won a lawsuit (even those who wanted him to lose it).
The feet twist the grass (spread on the floor of the house) (put it in disorder).
entries.meaning: Many visitors disrupt family-life.

entries.english: The feet take their owner into trouble.
entries.meaning: Self-inflicted evil. Used about people who effect their own ruin.

entries.luganda: Bigere bya mbogo : obirinnyamu nga teriiwo (= obyegezaamu ng'evuddewo).
entries.english: The footprints of the buffalo : you step into them only when it is absent.
entries.meaning: No use facing a danger for which one is no match.

entries.english: "That will do" : (is what you say) when it is your man that has thrown (his opponent).
entries.meaning: You would not say so, if your friend has been thrown.

entries.english: The root-stock of the waterlily is famine food.
What even fills your cheeks : gives you something to chew.
entries.meaning: Planting food keeps you alive. Fruits of training and education.

entries.english: "Second-rate men" : that is what a very strong man thinks (or says) who thinks little of his fellow-men.
entries.meaning: Okujuula = to make weak beer, second infusion. Jjuule = washy beer.

entries.english: (They are) dry things that don't burn (ebitayaka) : like the stone in the fire place.
entries.meaning: It seems to be looking after itself.

entries.luganda: "Bikongo biwunya ttaka" : nga nnyoko y'abirimye (= nga mwannyoko abifu- mbye).
entries.english: "(These) yams smell of the soil" : (you can risk saying that) if your mother has planted them (or: if your sister has cooked them).
entries.meaning: Used in chaffing good-naturedly a person well-loved (mother, sister) who has cooked fresh produce from the garden.

entries.luganda: Bikubuze : ebyabula ab'e Mityana, okuyisa e Ttanda ewa Walumbe.
entries.english: You have forgotten the story of old : as the people of Mityana have forgotten it, about passing at Ttanda where Death lurks.
entries.meaning: An old legend warned people of a big hole at Ttanda (a village in Ssingo) where Death is supposed to have entered into the earth.

entries.english: If your property increases : (you are inclined to say) "it will not be lost to me".
entries.meaning: Nothing can harm me. "Mwoyo gwange ofunye ebirungi bingi - - wummula, olye, onywe, ogayagaane!" (Luk.12.19).

entries.english: "Thoughts are only known by one's own heart" : (so one says) if his friend does not know what he is thinking.
"Secrets are known in one's own heart" : as in the case of a boy who has eaten zebra-meat.
entries.meaning: The boy knows best himself, if it does him any good. Zebra-meat is not appre- ciated.

entries.english: "The things eaten are known by the stomach" : so the beggar says to himself and does not reveal what he has eaten already.
entries.meaning: Otherwise he might not receive anything.

entries.english: (ebigambo, ebikolwa) These words (or actions) put me to shame.
The advice went over his hair (did not enter his head).
entries.meaning: Said of one who does not want to be told.

entries.english: "I am caught by my own mouth (word)" : (so you have to say) if one of your own household has reported you.
"Those blessed teeth" : (they give that name to) a rich man who can kill many cows.

entries.luganda: "Bino byange na bino byange" : omukazi alimisa nsimo.
entries.english: "These are mine and those are mine" (says the rich man bragging) : but his wife has to use a worn-out hoe for digging.
entries.meaning: If he is so rich, why can't he give his wife a decent hoe to work with?

entries.english: "The stories (news) are brought to me here" : that is the (uncharitable) talk of the old people.
entries.meaning: The aged do not get about any longer and so they report from hear-say.

entries.luganda: Bintu bizibu okugaba : gw'owa enkoko atenda munnyu gwokka; ggwe eyagimu- wa takwogerako.
entries.english: It is difficult to give away things : he to whom you give a chicken praises only the salt, but does not speak about you who has given to him.
Accusations for which there is a witness against you : cannot be disproved.

entries.luganda: "Bita bisigale" : nga n'enkaaga alina ey'okubizzayo ku buko.
entries.english: "The beer-calabashes can remain here" : (so says the prospective husband, after having brought the beer and after having come to an agreement about the bride-price), if he has also the sixty rupees to be given to his buko.
(eby'okufuna) (To obtain good things) you have to go and look for them.
entries.meaning: "No pains, no gains". Germ. "Die gebratenen Tauben fliegen einem nicht ins Maul".

entries.english: Things that are not yet dry : are notAied up with fibres (in parcels).
entries.meaning: Applied to bad wishes which need not materialise at all.

entries.english: Things come out of houses : and go again into houses.
entries.meaning: The poor feed the rich; the bakopi feed the rulers.

entries.english: (ebintu, ebiseera) Things slip away quickly : as the ttimpa-vegetables (into which one puts his morsel of ttooke).
entries.meaning: Said about fleeting time or transitoriness of earthly things. "Time flies". Lat. "Sic transit mundi gloria".

entries.english: (obwato) Small boats sink when landing.
entries.meaning: Disaster might come at the end of the journey. "A narrow shave"; "just in the nick of time". "There's many a slip 'twixt the cup and the lip".

entries.luganda: Bugya dda : bukuyisa ku malaalo ng'olya (or: ng'oyimba).
entries.english: (The time of bereavement) having passed long ago : makes you walk past the old grave eating (or: singing).
entries.meaning: "Time heals all wounds".

entries.english: Age is wisdom : the old man does not tell what made him old (out of shyness and fear of being laughed at).

(obubuzi, obwana) The little goats are emaciated : 1) the owner finds them so (when they have died and he is shown the carcases; but if the keeper simply says that they have died, the owner does not believe it, because there is no proof); 2) but they grow up (they are at least alive).
The day breaks with worries coming.
entries.meaning: Rub.C.1058. 1009 "Bukya ngwota" : guggiira mu nju. (omunya) (cf. Bukya mbirya: 1007) Every morning I warm myself (on the warm smoke rising through the thatch) : (so says the lizard and) gets burned on the (burning) house. Neglecting a timely warning.

entries.english: Out of Bulemeezi there comes no simple "kid" : from there comes something full-grown..
entries.meaning: The Balemeezi are shrewd, renowned for talking and arguing.

entries.luganda: Buli gw'olaba n'akamyufu : ng'oyo yatabaalira Tororo.
entries.english: Not every soldier whom you see wearing the red patch, has fought at Tororo (big camp 1939-45).
It will come to an end for you : the standing of a woman through marriage is not the same as the standing of a princess.
entries.meaning: The latter remains princess all her life, whilst the former loses her standing at the death of her husband.

entries.luganda: Buli museveni muwangaazi : agidde awone mu bitter.
entries.english: Every soldier (7th army) is long lived : if only he escapes things that kill.
Every member of the mmamba-clan praises his own subclan (essiga), i.e.
entries.meaning: his own mmamba. Engl. "Every man thinks his own geese swans".

entries.luganda: Buli wanzina n'eyiye : Wajjenje azinya byoya, Wakikere mumiro.
entries.english: Each dancer dances with his own means : the cricket with its wings, the frog with its gullet.
Deceit is not a thing of yesterday only.
An ancestor's land is acquired by an active and cunning man.
entries.meaning: He has to fight for it, plead in court, defend his possessions.

entries.english: (That is showing) valour (buzira) : like the chicken that is buying a banana- bunch.
entries.meaning: A newly married wife goes home to her parents and, if the latter are pleased with the report about her husband, they give her a bunch of bananas, which she carries in an upright position (bulanga) on her head with a cock sitting on top of it, signifying that the man is capable of his tasks as a husband.

entries.english: Buffalo-dung : dries on the surface.
entries.meaning: You are in danger of slipping on it. Watch your steps! Treacherous friends!

entries.luganda: Busajja bwa nkuba : bw'agula omwenge, agula "Ka-bantende".
entries.english: (He shows the generosity of) a rain pool : when he treats men with beer(buying it from the owner of the house), he buys the name "Ka-bantende".
entries.meaning: The men, praising him for his generosity, make him spend all his money and even incur debts. - A pool, temporarily filled with rain water gives all its water away, till nothing is left. Therefore a spendthrift who has nothing left is given the name "Busajja bwa nkuba".

entries.english: Tenancy is like the (pointed) stick used for digging out potatoes : when it has become blunt, you point it again.
entries.meaning: When a squatter gets tired of his old place, he looks for a new one and is happy there.

entries.english: You offer congratulations to a hunter even when you have a right to partake in the feed.
entries.meaning: You give thanks even to one who has only done his duty.

entries.english: The home of the poor (beggars) : is fate.
entries.meaning: They have no real home; so they have to stay where they can. - The rich can select a place for their burial; the poor have no other place than that of their kika.

entries.english: (That is leaving) without saying good-bye : as famine does.
No work in the field brings forth famine.
Lack of experience : makes you enter into blood brotherhood with a quarrel-some fellow.

entries.luganda: Buuza ataakuldine : musumba wa mbuzi (= omuwa-butwa abuuza musumba wa mbuzi).
entries.english: Ask advice from one who will not ridicule you : the poisoner asks the goatherd (nti awafudde omuntu lull wa?).
entries.meaning: In olden times the corpses were taken into the wilds and there the musezi went at night, after having inquired from the goatherd (guileless person) about the place.

entries.english: If it is getting dark outside : it is not getting dark (dangerous) inside.
entries.meaning: In the house one feels safe.

entries.luganda: Bwa ddiba : buli afuluma (= bull muntu, = bull omu) asika wuwe.
entries.english: (bulenge) As with the edges of a skin (when they peg it out) : the man on either side pulls it his way.
entries.meaning: Arguing, haggling in trade etc.

entries.english: (One who says) "Daylight came whilst I was awake" : is speared on his bed.
entries.meaning: If enemies surround the village, they will find him unprepared.

entries.english: (One who says) "Daylight came whilst I was still awake" : (might get as answer) "Such a man is either a thief or a sorcerer".
entries.meaning: The musezi digs up the dead at night. Sarcastically misinterpreting above remark.

entries.english: Hastiness in giving : makes you give to a man who will refuse you (a gift).

entries.luganda: Bwangu na bwangu : ng'omutezi w'enkwale; ky'ajje atege ng'ategulula.
entries.english: Quickly, quickly (in quick succession) : as the trapper of partridges acts; he has hardly set the trap, he opens it again.
entries.meaning: Enkwale are easily caught with the kakunizo (string-trap).

entries.luganda: Bwe babuulirira omwana wa boowo : ng'ow'omunaku okutu akunkumula.
entries.english: If they teach a child who has still both parents (who is rich, free-born) : also the child of a poor man ought to prick up his ears.

entries.luganda: "Bwe bambuulira, saatuula" : nga lwali lwa mugagga.
entries.english: "When they told me (about the death of so and so), I did not remain sitting (I came at once)" : (if one says so) it was the death of a rich man.
entries.meaning: The speaker had hopes of inheriting something.

entries.english: When they call the beautiful ones : he answers (eagerly).
entries.meaning: Fondly imagining himself to be handsome.

entries.english: The weather in the morning : is (often) not the same as in the evening.
entries.meaning: "Don't praise the day before it is over". Lat. "Nescis quid serus vesper vehat" (Macrobius). Germ. "Man soll den Tag nicht vor dem Abend loben".

entries.luganda: Bwe bukya : si bwe buziba; enkoko ebuuza nnyina waayo omuziro.
entries.english: The weather in the morning : is not the same as in the evening; the little pullet asks the old hen their totem.
entries.meaning: Nti "tweddira ki?" Nti "ensogasoga". The little chick needs to ask that while the mother is still alive, and there is time to ask her.

entries.luganda: Bwe bukya : si bwe buziba; ensega yatta n'Omuyima omukago.
entries.english: The weather in the morning : is not the same as in the evening; the vulture made blood-brotherhood with the Muyima.
entries.meaning: The Muyima does not kill the vulture; since the vultures show the Mulaalo the carcase of any lost animal.

entries.english: (obulwadde) "My illness is still the same" (says the patient) : and makes you bring the sick-ness back.
entries.meaning: You, the doctor, think that the first medicine was not the right one and you give another, whilst the effect of the first one should have been waited for.

entries.english: (amannyo, amatama) As they (the teeth or the cheeks) travel together : so together they eat the food for the journey.
entries.meaning: "Equal work, equal pay".

entries.luganda: "Bwe gutyo yazaala bwe gutyo" : olukomera luzaala emituba.
entries.english: (A woman who abuses another woman, saying) "Oh, that miserable brat of yours (ogwana) brings forth also a miserable brat" : a hedge of mituba-sticks brings forth mituba-trees.
entries.meaning: The offensive woman might also have the misfortune of bearing an ugly child. "The pot calls the kettle black".

entries.english: Provided that the wild cat does not eat it : the chicken will lay eggs (will cackle).
entries.meaning: French "Petit poussin un jour pondra pourvu que chat lui laisse vie". "If nothing comes between - ". "Wind and weather permitting".

entries.luganda: Bwe mubanga mulya enswa : temuzitendanga kuwooma, nga temunnasaasira nkuyege ezaabumba ettaka.
entries.english: When you eat flying ants : don't talk about them being tasty without appreci-ating the hard work of the nkuyege (work-termites) that have built up the anthill.
entries.meaning: Honour to whom honour is due.

entries.english: "You see me like this, like this" : (one saying so, is so poor that) he has to sell his children.
When I die, they fold me up : a dead man does not bite.
entries.meaning: Song. Let us make merry as long as we are alive.

entries.english: (cf, Bwe bakubuulira: 1058) Whilst I tell you of my troubles : you are making signs with that stick of yours (pencil)?
entries.meaning: The speaker does not understand that his words are being written down.

entries.english: (One who says) "We are so many (so strong)" : says it to his would-be killers.
If you rely on your own counsel only : (your companion) will leave you in the forest.
entries.meaning: A wise man takes advice.

entries.english: If you cook for one who never gets enough : you don't plunder your whole bananary.
entries.meaning: You give him enough to prevent him becoming an enemy. (Omufumbira kafu, tafa mukago.) Duta 70.

entries.english: If you possess a young wife : you don't send away the old one.
entries.meaning: The old one is still good for working. Old things still can be handy.

entries.english: If you are poor (and without relations who would give you food) : a new mother will call you to eat.
entries.meaning: Others would not eat there, because she is unclean.

entries.luganda: Bw'ogoba musajja munno : embiro olekamu ezinadda.
entries.english: If you follow up your fellow-man in pursuit : you should think of your own chance of running back.
entries.meaning: He might turn round, get help from others and attack you. - Prepare for emer-gencies!

entries.english: When you fall into trouble : the one who was your friend forgets you.
entries.meaning: Germ. "Freunde in der Not gehen hundert auf ein Lot". Lat. "Donec eris felix multos numerabis amicos; tempora si fuerint nubila, solus eris" (Ovid).'

entries.english: If you sneer at an impudent person : you have to worry about what he (she) will answer.
entries.meaning: It will be even more offensive.

entries.english: If you beat something that does not cry : you will cry.
entries.meaning: You will hurt yourself, you tire yourself out.

entries.english: If you despise your companion : you increase your own trouble.
entries.meaning: Respect your friends! Lat. "Vae soli".

entries.english: If you see that somebody weeps with you : you weep more.
entries.meaning: And if somebody helps you at work, you yourself become more energetic.

entries.english: If you see a dog playing with a hide : it will eat it.
entries.meaning: Watch the signs of'danger.

entries.luganda: Bw'olaba omugenyi asookedde ku kyento : nga taagabe.
entries.english: If you see that a visitor starts sucking the top part of the sugar-cane : (you know) that he won't give anything of it away.
entries.meaning: The top-part is the least sweet. You cannot expect him to leave you the better part.

entries.luganda: Bw'olaba omuwuulu aliko entumbwe : ng'asula mwa jjajjaawe.
entries.english: If you see a bachelor with fat calves (on his legs) : (you know) that he lives with his grandfather (or grandmother).
entries.meaning: There he is well fed and treated as a favourite.

entries.english: When you have finished tasting the beer (which is being brewed), you cover it again.
entries.meaning: That means that the owner has given the visitor some of the beer.

entries.luganda: Bw'omala okusesema mu mwenge : nti "alinnyimba ndimutta".
entries.english: If you have been just vomiting at a beer-party (you frighten the others from 'talking about it, saying) "Whosoever tells tales about me, I shall kill him".
If you have thrown (in wrestling) a weaker man : need you also hurt him?
A lonely existence : cools down on one side.
entries.meaning: One who eats by himself lets the food get cold on the side where there is no-body eating.

entries.english: If you laugh at the bowl : you laugh at the potter (its maker).
If you pull something that does not want to come : after sometime you give it up.
entries.meaning: Said to somebody who has often been invited and does not come.

entries.english: If you don't eat in the chief's place : you won't get fat.
If you cannot leave (where you are dissatisfied) : you quarrel as you go along.

entries.luganda: Bw'ottottola ebya kyalo : bw'olwala w'abula akulumika.
entries.english: If you speak evil about things in the village : there will be nobody to bleed you, when you are sick.
entries.meaning: Dutch "Boontje komt om zijn loontje".

entries.english: If you send people and they don't come back : you also follow.
entries.meaning: The messengers who don't carry out your wishes worry you.

entries.english: If you carry a child on your back whom you have not brought forth yourself : you carry one who tries to slip out (is reluctant).
entries.meaning: Somebody else's children are difficult to manage.

entries.luganda: Bw'owulira oli ng'agarnba nti gobs embwa : nga mu kisenge eriyo ekyokulya.
entries.english: If you hear somebody ordering you to drive the dog away : (you know that) there is food in the kisenge.
"Those things of ours" : (if you remind somebody like that, it means that) a certain arrangement was made there.
(A tenant who complains about) conditions in the village (bya kuno), does not go away himself, but prevents other tenants from coming.
entries.meaning: Said about an habitual grumbler or about dissatisfied concubines.

entries.english: The property (which was stolen) from one who has run away : does not come back at all.
entries.meaning: He does not fight for it.

entries.english: Family affairs : are best known to the master of the house.

entries.luganda: Bya nswakaba : ng'emmese by'erya mu kifulukwa.
entries.english: Little trifles : as the rat eats them in a deserted home (no value).

entries.luganda: Bya nvumbo ebyo : bye biteesebwa mu kyama ababiri n'ababiri.
entries.english: Those are confidential things : things that are discussed between two and two.
What he has said : is said with the same intention as the poisoner had when he stood at the stake (to be burnt) (i.e.
entries.meaning: an open and full confession to plead for mercy). The poisoner mentioned the names of all he had killed.

entries.luganda: Bye bakubuulira by'otowonga (= Bye bamubuulira by'atawonga) : nti "lubaale anzita?" If they tell you what you should do and you refuse to sacrifice : (you say) "the lubaale is killing me?" (i.e.
entries.english: it is your fault that you are dying, because you don't take advice).
entries.meaning: Said of one who stubbornly refused to be advised by others.

entries.english: That is unrestrained (irresponsible) talk : as unrestrained as charms slipping over the head of one who had his ears cut off.
entries.meaning: If the ears were still there, the strings of the charms would get stuck on them.

entries.english: (ebifi) "The two pieces are the same" : so says one who has already eaten the bigger piece (of meat or other food).
entries.meaning: It cannot be checked any longer. "Destroying evidence".

entries.english: When you have no food : your eyes don't despise the singed banana-leaf (in which food is being cooked).
entries.meaning: What is cooked in that, is a treat!

entries.english: "Your conversation does not tire me" : says the host, when the guest has only just arrived.
entries.meaning: But he has not listened yet!

entries.luganda: "Ddamu mpulire" : ng'anoonya bya kutwala (or: alinda bya kutwala).
entries.english: "Say it again, that I may hear" : (one who talks like that) tries to make sure, what he wants to tell others.
(ebbwa) (A sore causes) anxiety in the soul : if it breaks out again on a scar.
entries.meaning: It might not heal a second time.

entries.english: A skin : (means) exertion for the curriers (who beat the leather soft).
entries.meaning: Unless they work hard , the skin will remain stiff. It should get as soft and pliable as cloth. - "No pains, no gains". Lat. "Per aspera ad astra".

entries.english: A debt does not simply perish.
entries.meaning: It does not cease by itself; it must be paid or at least condoned.

entries.english: It is useless work to cut firewood (for ripening the mabidde).
entries.meaning: They will ripen in the lusuku, if you have the patience to wait.

entries.english: The king does not simply visit : he fights.
entries.meaning: Even going for a hunt or a visit was called an "expedition". The king gets the same honour and is feared in the same way, as if he went to war.

entries.english: If the flying things travel without coordination : they beat each other's wings.
entries.meaning: Concerted action only leads to success.

entries.english: What follows is not the same as what precedes : old thatch is not enough for the house (if put on again).
entries.meaning: Said of father and son, testator and heir, king and crown-prince, etc.

entries.luganda: Ebifiiramu bye bigunyuza : omugenyi tabuuza mutwe gwa nkoko.
entries.english: The words that are not spoken (but only hummed) in a game (muzannyo) make it interesting (appealing) : the visitor does not ask for the head of the chicken (because he has the rest of the chicken inside him).
News (rumours, scandals etc.) spread quicker and farther than the sound of drums.

entries.luganda: Ebigambo bingi : empapula ntono ; nga tabimalewo.
entries.english: I should have many things (to say or to write) : but the paper is too small; (so one says) if he has no time, if he is in a hurry.
Words pass on.
entries.meaning: Walls have ears! One must be careful in talking.

entries.luganda: "Ebigambo bya kuno bingi" : ng'omwami y'asuza ababbi.
entries.english: "There are plenty of wrongs here" (so the people say among themselves) : if the chief himself gives shelter to thieves.

entries.luganda: "Ebigambo bya kuno nga tibyekweka" : nga bamugambye gw'ayagala.
entries.english: "The news of this place cannot be kept secret" : (so says a man) if they have been talking about somebody he likes.
entries.meaning: He likes the conversation, because it means honour and glory for him.

entries.english: Words are easy : but real friendship is difficult.
A message is no load.
entries.meaning: It is easier to find a man for conveying a message than to get a porter for carrying a load.

entries.english: "My feet have misled me" : (one who says so) is just disgusted (because, in the place he came to he received nothing to eat).

entries.luganda: Ebigwamu bye bitwala embwa mu katale.
entries.english: The remnants (of food that fall to the ground) take the dog to the market.
entries.meaning: Said of the selfish purpose that people have in their actions.

entries.luganda: Ebigwawo tebiraga : Wandiga atambula n'omwana we.
entries.english: Evils come unannounced : (therefore) the mother-sheep takes the lamb along wherever she goes.
entries.meaning: Left alone, the lamb might be harmed.

entries.luganda: Ebijjula mu mwoyo : akarnwa bye koogera.
entries.english: What the heart is full of : the mouth speaks of.
entries.meaning: Germ. "Wes das Herz voll ist, des geht der Mund fiber".

entries.english: Mangled feet that go to the chief's place : don't come back with nothing.
entries.meaning: Admonition for the chiefs to help the poor and crippled.

entries.luganda: Ebikwatibwa n'omusibe tibitonda : tibibalibwa mu kuliwa.
entries.english: The things that are found in the hands of a prisoner are not considered as his property (even if they should be) : they are not counted (given back), when he has to pay damages.

entries.luganda: Ebinene n'ebinene tebisibagana : ttimba singa asiba enjovu.
entries.english: Big things do not come to grips with big things : otherwise the python would take the elephant into its coils.
Things in a heap get mouldy.
Things are owned by the living.
entries.meaning: The dead have forfeited the right to property.

entries.luganda: Ebintu bwe bigwamu obuzito : ekikere n'emmese benkanya embiro.
entries.english: When things fall heavily (danger from falling walls, fire etc.) : the frog and the rat run equally fast (away).
entries.meaning: Fear gives speed even to the crippled.

entries.luganda: Ebintu tebifaanana abifuna : singa emmese eyitira mu nveera.
entries.english: Things don't look like their owners : otherwise the rat would walk about with its booty.
entries.meaning: The rat gathers a lot but eats everything. And a rich man might have collected possessions which he might lose again. - Germ. "Der Schein triigt". "Sente tizimufaanana".

entries.english: Things are not (always) judged as they are seen.

entries.luganda: Ebiriko akuluma : tiweegaana; ng'akuloopye wa mu nju.
entries.english: Statements (accusations) for which a witness (accuser) can be had : cannot be disavowed, if the one who has given you away is of your own household (wife, children, etc.).

entries.luganda: Ebirungi birekwa ku kibuga : oleka omujaguzo evuga ng'oserengeta mu kyalo.
entries.english: Good (enjoyable) things are left behind in the king's place : you leave the beating of the royal drums and go to your village.
Good things are far away.
Things of the past are soon forgotten : otherwise the dead would be exhumed.
entries.meaning: "Out of sight, out of mind". "What the eye does not see any longer, the heart does not grieve about".

entries.luganda: Ebiriibwa mu ttoggo : byogerwa mu ddumbi.
entries.english: What they eat during the heavy rains (March-May) : they talk about during the lesser rains (autumn).
entries.meaning: Pleasures reveived from good food (and other amenities) are remembered a long time.

entries.luganda: Ebisula byefuula : omutabaazi yeefuula omwayi (= omunyazi).
entries.english: What is kept over night changes (deteriorates) : the warrior becomes a maraud-er.
Troublesome things : get hold of a pipe of tobacco (soothing influence of a "smoke").
Books are like mushrooms : the bad ones kill.
entries.meaning: Munno 1919 p. 118. 1193a Ebitajudde tebinjiikira. What is not filling the vessel : does not get poured over me. I can take a few handfuls without being noticed.

entries.luganda: Ebitali bigabane : bwe babyanuka (= babinyaga) biba by'omu.
entries.english: Things which are not divided up (which are common property of many) : become (suddenly) the property of one, when they are stolen (e.g.
entries.meaning: a piece of land, undivided, belonging to three children, changes over to one creditor).

entries.luganda: Ebitali byetegeke : embwa bwe bagikuba, omukalo edduka.
entries.english: Things for which one is not prepared : (are comparable to) a dog that runs away from a piece of dry meat, when he is suddenly beaten.
entries.meaning: An unexpected question perplexes a person.

entries.english: Many nets : are the death of the animal.

entries.luganda: "Ebitooke bindaaluseeko" : "kwata kimu n'okissa mu nvuba, bisooke bijee-mulukuke".
entries.english: "My banana-trees have become tall" (so says the woman and they answer her jestingly) : "get hold of one and put it into the stocks, that they start getting sense again".
entries.meaning: The woman means "bindaaluseeko" (they have grown tall) and the others purposely misunderstand her as saying "bindaluseeko" (they have become mad).
