entries.meaning: A clever father begets a clever child. - Hereditary qualities!

entries.luganda: Mwasa-ngabo : bw'ogiteekawo agifumita n'agyasa n'akwasa ekifuba.
entries.english: (He is) a shield-shatterer : if you put up your shield, he pierces it, splits it and splits also your chest.
A poor man appears in public, provoking people.
A poor man brings robbing of food.
entries.meaning: If nobody gives him food, he takes it without asking.

entries.english: One who asks "What did you quarrel about?" : renews the quarrel of yester-day.
You have said "mwebale" to people with a goitre.
entries.meaning: You get no answer for your kindness. - People who have a goitre, do not like to talk.

entries.english: One who speaks harshly : will have to carry his gun himself.
entries.meaning: Nobody is inclined to help him.

entries.luganda: Mwogeza-bboggo : ng'ayita na mbwa; nti eridde ki ndiwe (= okuliwa)?
entries.english: (He is) a harsh fellow : like one who passes by with a dog (which is beaten by somebody and angrily asks) what has it eaten (stolen from you), what I should have to pay for?
Where you don't live : don't (try to) deal out the plates.
entries.meaning: You don't know which belongs to whom. - Do not interfere in the private affairs of others.

entries.english: Also for the mabidde (beer bananas) which will perish (which will prove unfit for brewing beer) : grass is cut.
entries.meaning: The brewers use lusenke grass for the treading of the brew. - One has to take risks. Germ. "Wer nicht wagt, gewinnt nicht". - One does many things which finally prove futile.

entries.luganda: "Nammwe mutuulanga bubi" : gw'ayagala ye all ku ludda oluliko ekitono.
entries.english: "But you are sitting quite in disorder" : (so the host says) when the one whom he likes sits on the side where there is the smaller piece.

entries.luganda: N'asirika amanya : ekikere bakibikira kwa kyeya ne kikaaba ku nkuba.
entries.english: Also the silent man can have knowledge : the frog is proclaimed dead in the dry season, and still it croaks again in the rainy season.

entries.luganda: N'asirikirira amanya : ekikere bwe bakibikira okw'ekyanda, olumbe kwa ttoggo kwe kyabiza.
entries.english: Also the silent man can have knowledge : if they proclaim the frog dead in the dry season, it puts an end to the funeral rites in the wet season.

entries.luganda: Na tte eryawuumanga : bw'erimala okugwa wansi, nga n'abaana abato bagituula mu mayembe.
entries.english: It is so, even with a cow that was fierce before : when it has fallen down (when it is dead), even the small children sit between its horns.
entries.meaning: A dead enemy can't do harm any longer.

entries.english: "The finishing of the funeral rites (kwabya olumbe) can also take place here" (says the one who is responsible for it) : if it is for a poor person.
entries.meaning: If it had been a rich man, he would be particular about the place.

entries.english: (One who - when warned that he is in danger of being killed - says) Oh, I see (and neglects the warning) : he is the one they will kill.
I see that you throw me away without any compunction.
entries.meaning: I see that you care little about me (you don't speak to me, don't apologize etc.).

entries.english: "I see that you are neglecting me" : (so you say to one) who despises you without telling you so.
entries.meaning: Despising in acts, not in words.

entries.english: I see from the way you are greeting me (that you don't like me).
"Whatever shall I be asking?" : he who asks such a question, should ask for a "kooterezo".
entries.meaning: A "kooterezo" is a small tent-like arrangement, built up with sticks, elephant-grass stalks and covered with barkcloth, under which a slow fire is smouldering from chips of mugavu-wood. - Don't always rely on yourself; work together with others!

entries.english: I shall eat them (eby'okulya n'okunywa) and they will go through me.
entries.meaning: Expression for looking forward to a great feast!

entries.english: "I shall die with my strength" : (says) the old man, breaking a stalk of the castor-oil-plant (fondly imagining that the feat required strength).
"Shall I get nothing at all (no meat at all)?" : (one who says so) snatches the knee of a cow (better that than nothing).

entries.luganda: "Ndifiira (= nnanfiira) ku kinene" : 1) ensanafu ku ggere ssajja (= ku kigere eki-sajja); 2) ensanafu ku ntumbwe.
entries.english: "I shall die on something big" : 1) (says) the safari-ant, biting the big toe; 2) (says) the safari-ant, biting the calf.
entries.meaning: "You may as well be hung for a sheep as for a lamb". "In for a penny, in for a pound".

entries.luganda: "Ndifiira mu bakazi bannange" : bamuyisa mu musiri gwa ntungo.
entries.english: "I shall die amongst my women-friends" : (she says) when they lead her through a semsem field.
entries.meaning: Semsem has pods which are called mabeere (breasts).

entries.luganda: "Ndifiira mu bangi" : bamuyisa ku musiri gwa ntungo (or: afiira mu lukangaga Iwa ntungo).
entries.english: "I shall die among many" : (he says) when they lead him through a semsem-field (or: he dries on the frame for semsem-drying).
entries.meaning: The pods contain many seeds.

entries.luganda: "Ndifiira mu basajja bannange" : bamuyisa mu musiri gwa kasooli.
entries.english: "I shall die among my men-friends" : (he says) when they lead him through a maize-field.
entries.meaning: All the maize plants have "beards" (silk).

entries.luganda: "Ndifiira mu ppanda zange" : nga n'akamwa kalungi (= ng'ayogera bulungi).
entries.english: "I shall die among my relations" (he says) : (but that will happen only) if he does not offend them.
"Let me die, where it is warm" : says the cockroach on the banana-shelf (underneath is the fire place).

entries.luganda: "Ndifiira waggale" : bamuyisa ku kifulukwa (= ku kifulukwa ayitako kkutwe).
entries.english: (or: Ndifiira ndirwanira - - ) "I shall die where there are closed doors" : they lead him past a deserted house (or: but a deserted house he passes in a hurry).
entries.meaning: He predicts more than he can keep.

entries.english: A sheep (ram) does not show its anger beforehand (like a dog etc.) : it simply attacks.
entries.meaning: Said of people whose anger comes suddenly (instead of threatening first).

entries.english: "In walking I am hampered, by my fatness" : (one saying so) does not find anybody to carry a load (mugugu) for him (her).
entries.meaning: He overfed his body, giving nothing to others; therefore: no help in his difficul- ties.

entries.english: "I shall buy something precious" (he says) : and then he buys a wrapped-up enkejje (small fish).
entries.meaning: To buy "a pig in a poke". Germ. "Die Katze im Sack kaufen". - Said of a disappointed marriage partner.

entries.luganda: "Ndikibuulira ani?" : nga taliiko mukwano gwe yeesiga.
entries.english: "Whom could I tell it to?" : (says the man who) has no friend of his whom he can trust.
"I shall confide (the secret) to a trustworthy person" : (so you say), but if you tell one, it will go through the whole village.
"I shall eat it to-morrow" (says the thief) : then they catch him with it and make him carry it (to the chief).
"I shall eat it with salt" (says the poor man, when he gets a piece of meat; but before he can get ash-salt) : he will eat it with water.
entries.meaning: To produce salt from the ashes of a certain kind of grass takes time.

entries.english: (One who assures you) I shall get you there : (very often) does not get you there.

entries.luganda: Ndi mufu muggya : simanyi bifa magombe.
entries.english: I am a newcomer amongst the dead : I don't know what happens in the under-world.
entries.meaning: Expression for ignorance. A "new man" needs counsel.

entries.english: "I am wise" : (that statement is true only) if I agree to be advised.
entries.meaning: "Wise is the man who listens to advice" (Prov.12.15).

entries.english: I am a saleable woman : (says the female slave) I am tying up my garment firmly (for the journey to another master).

entries.luganda: Ndi mutuba mulami : n'omuto atema ensimbo.
entries.english: I am a barkcloth-tree of good quality : even a child cuts branches from me.
entries.meaning: I am generous, I have an open hand.

entries.luganda: "Ndi nnanti nkalu" : ye azimba ku nnanti embisi.
entries.english: "I am a dry being" : (one saying so) builds on a green (alive) being.
entries.meaning: I myself am destitute, but I rely on rich relations. - Comparison taken from horns growing on the heads of animals, or nails growing on fingers.

entries.english: "I shall take you there" : an ugly woman can take you to a beautiful one.
entries.meaning: Planting potatoes prepares the ground for bitooke. With humble means one can achieve great things.

entries.luganda: "Ndirwanira mu bakulu bannange" : omukadde bamuyisa mu jjobyo.
entries.english: (The old man exclaims in his old fighting spirit) "I shall fight together with my old leaders" : (therefore) they lead him through (a plot of) jjobyo (penta-phylla plant).
entries.meaning: The white flowers of jjobyo symbolize grey hair (old age). - There the old man is amongst his comrades.

entries.english: Ndifiira waggale: 3043) Pilk.No.86.
"Where shall I go now?" : let the sickness kill me and let me go to rest.
entries.meaning: So one says who has tried all medicines and gives up hope.

entries.english: "I want to take a big thing (to my future parents-in-law)" : (a suitor who talks like this) will die, before he ever reaches at his parents-in-law.
entries.meaning: He who aims too high, misses the target.

entries.luganda: "Ndiwulira" : bamufumbira mu kasooli (or: banuulira mu kasooli).
entries.english: (One who says) I shall listen (obey) : will be cooked with the maize cobs (or: they break (him) off with the maize cobs).
entries.meaning: Said of a stubborn fellow, taking no warning and finally coming to grief. -"Ndiwulira" is the name of a grub feeding on maize cobs (under the bracts). - Engl. "The pitcher goes so often to the well, that it is broken at last".

entries.english: I shall sing in the camp at Rubaga (residence of king Muteesa I.).
entries.meaning: Expression signifying the intention of applying for a chieftainship from the king.

entries.luganda: "Ndudde okwewagira" : 1) enkolo azirya n'ekiro; 2) muwogo alya na miti.
entries.english: (One who says) "It's a long time, since I ate well" : 1) eats banana stumps at night (in day-time he is ashamed to do so, because formerly he laughed at the poor people eating the stumps); 2) eats the cassava together with the woody part (in the tuber).

entries.luganda: Ndya kya bukaba : ng'emmese ey'omu ggwanika.
entries.english: I am eating in a shameful way : like the rat in the cupboard.
entries.meaning: To take the food from under one's very nose. Anyaga bunyazi.

entries.english: "I eat for two" : like the stomach of a lubaale-priest.
entries.meaning: He asks for food or drink whilst being in a trance, and later again for himself. The first is for the lubaale; the second for himself.

entries.luganda: "Npende ogw'enswa : ninende ogw'ennyama?" (omulimu) "Shall I go for the flying ants : or shall I go for meat?" Both are good things; but only the one or the other is to be had at the same time.
entries.english: The choice is difficult.
(One who tells his wife) "I shall say weebale, when I have my food" : does not train her, if she is lazy.
entries.meaning: Not only the success should be praised but also the effort. He should encourage her, when she is at work.

entries.english: Although it has not rained (yet) : at least we have seen the rain clouds.
entries.meaning: Although you have given little, you have not refused (to give). Although you have not yet given anything, still you have given a promise.

entries.english: Also those which crow : were once eggs.
entries.meaning: Even the proud cocks were once only little chicks. - All big things have small beginnings. Lat. "Juventus spes patriae". Germ. "Jeder Meister, denk daran, fing einmal als Lehrbub an".

entries.english: "I urge them (the cocks) on, when they fight" : says the kasanke (small fire-finch) at the death of the cock.
entries.meaning: The kasanke wants to get feathers for its nest. Lat. "Duobus certantibus tertius gaudet".

entries.luganda: Ngabo nzira : ogirabira (= ogimanya) ku biwundu.
entries.english: A courageous shield (used by a courageous man) : is recognized by the scars (received in the battle).
A shield does not go visiting (it goes robbing and plundering).
"I see it" (the water for washing the hands) : (one saying so) waits for the luwombo (containing a special dish, meat, fish, chicken etc.).
entries.meaning: Before washing he wants to see, whether it is worthwhile washing.

entries.english: Empty hands are pleasant for their owner (and nobody else).
entries.meaning: They have not to carry anything. - A guest who comes with nothing, is not appreciated.

entries.english: I refuse (to carry) heavy things : and you want to put butter (or clay) on my head?
"My relations are many" : (you might be correct), but you have no trustworthy one.
entries.meaning: He who is too communicative, won't possess a real friend. - Dutch "Vrienden in den nood, duizend in een lood".

entries.english: A hornbill is not spoken to in a whisper.
entries.meaning: Its voice is also loud.

entries.english: "Will you be able to eat that?" : (so one remarks) if they have given (a big piece) to one he does not like.
(If one says to you) "I am going my way" (without answering your question where?) : when he gets into trouble (musango), he tells you (afterwards).

entries.luganda: "Nnende nfumbire omusajja" : bwe ligwa mu vvu, y'asooka okulya.
entries.english: "Let me go and cook for my husband" (so says the woman) : but when a piece of ttooke falls into the ashes, she starts eating (before her husband gets any-thing).
entries.meaning: The wife is supposed to eat after her husband.

entries.luganda: Ngo tebuukira walungi : buli lw'ebuuka, nti "ebadde endidde".
entries.english: The leopard does not prowl about, where it is safe : whenever it is prowling (you say) : "It was going to attack me (eat me)".
As great poverty dishes up the matooke : so it eats it.
entries.meaning: "Ngujuuba" = atalina mwana: she has not to dish up for anybody else.

entries.english: He keeps his claws hidden in their sheaths.
Hunger : 1) causes stupidity (can make one mad raving); 2) is painful (raises up the gases in the throat); 3) makes one look furious.
entries.meaning: "A hungry man an angry man". 65.4. 3116a Njala : evumbula. Hunger finds out. If one is in hiding, he will have to come out for food.

entries.english: (He is) a madman : like one possessed by a lubaale, who beats with sticks.
entries.meaning: A violent fellow is here compared with a "medium", possessed by a spirit.

entries.english: The dispersion comes from the well.
entries.meaning: All come together there and take water and go home again in different direc-tions. - Now-a-days applied to the church.

entries.luganda: Njogera bye ndaba : nti "emmese tenywa mwenge"; nti mu kita ebadde enoo-nyemu ki?
entries.english: I speak what I see : "a rat does not drink beer"; but what was it looking for in the calabash?

entries.luganda: Njogera bye ndaba : nti "Gatuulemu" wuuyo ajja.
entries.english: I speak what I know (says who insists on being believed, whatever he says) : (and they say about him) "Hush!
entries.meaning: There comes Gatuulemu (amagambo)". A dogmatic fellow is not pleasant company.

entries.english: "What am I bringing up?" : (one who asks such a question) is bringing up a "kagubi" (mischievous bird).
entries.meaning: No respect, gratitude towards parents.

entries.english: The sun has brought the news.
entries.meaning: Every day brings fresh news.

entries.luganda: Nkaabira mubikire : naye ankutukidde mu ngalo!
entries.english: I bewail the death of one, whose death notice came from far : but what shall I do, when somebody dies in my arms!
entries.meaning: I help people in distress who live in far-off lands; what shall I do, when distress is near?

entries.english: (That is) something permanent (unchangeable) : like the amulet (on the neck) of the grasshopper (permanent growth).
Tough meat is better than no meat at all; where you pull off the meat, you eat.
entries.meaning: "Half a loaf is better than no bread".

entries.english: "Let me eat and feel that I have eaten it" : (one who says so) spends the night without sleep.
entries.meaning: Overeating or overdrinking results in a bad night.

entries.english: A dead enkejje (small fish) : travels further than a live one.
entries.meaning: A live one stays in the water; a dead one is transported far inland. A poor man has to walk more for his food than a rich one.

entries.luganda: Nkerettanyi : bw'ogitega (or: bagitega) amenvu, erya bibombo.
entries.english: (He is like) an "enkerettanyi" (cute animal) : if you try to catch it with (a bait of) menu (ripe bananas), it eats bibombo (creepers) only.
entries.meaning: Alluding to shrewd and cunning people.

entries.english: (= "Nkizzizzawo" : akira "kinku- tuseeko".) (One who can say) "I have repaired it again" : deserves better praise than (one who says) "it broke in my hands".
entries.meaning: Repairing is better than throwing away.

entries.english: A strangled chicken : is not eaten by Muslims.
entries.meaning: They are only allowed to eat it when it has had its neck cut by a Muslim.

entries.luganda: Nkoko tekuba A hen does not belch.
entries.english: If it belches, it is dying.
entries.meaning: - Said of somebody who acquires possessions and squanders them all.

entries.luganda: Nkoko teyota : bw'olaba eyota nga bagiwujja.
entries.english: A hen does not warm itself at the fire : if you see it warming itself, they fan it (i.e.
entries.meaning: they roast it over the fire).

entries.luganda: "Nkoko yange eyo yeeyambula bbombo" : nnannyiniyo we yeeyambula aba- longo.
entries.english: "That chicken of mine sheds its first down" : (then probably you) its owner, discard also the umbilical cords (of the twins).
entries.meaning: At the birth of twins people used to garland themselves with bbombo (creeper plant with yellowish green fruits which are covered with a soft growth).

entries.english: "Let me get busy and make it tasty" : (said) Nnalunga, when she mashed the arum-lily tubers (instead of simply boiling them).
entries.meaning: Nnalunga of the nvuma-totem was one of the wives of King Jjuuko and of out-standing beauty. - Going too far with good intentions.

entries.english: The cough of a man : drives the leopard away.
entries.meaning: A woman's cough does not frighten it. - Effect of a commanding behaviour.

entries.english: The banana-rootstock cannot be moulded (between the fingers like matooke).

entries.luganda: Nkonge ya muvule : nnantagwira kyeya kimu.
entries.english: The stump of a muvule tree : does not fall in one hot season.
I am warning you, as the door made of kibo-palm branches does.
entries.meaning: That kind of door creaks very much. - Warning of a thief, trying to enter. Kibo = raffia palm.

entries.luganda: Nkubye mu kisaka ejjinja : kuwulira bivaamu (= okulaba ekinaabuukamu).
entries.english: I have thrown a stone into the thicket : to hear what is going on in there.
entries.meaning: Poking into a secret of somebody.

entries.luganda: Nku1agirira okutega : bw'olitta olimpa (= n'oleeta omwange)?
entries.english: I show you how to set a trap : if you will kill (an animal), will you give me (meat) (or: bring meat to my home)?
entries.meaning: He who has led you to success, ought to get his due from you.

entries.english: "I know your evil inclination" : (one who says so) does not give you a chance to defend yourself.
entries.meaning: M.590, 17.38, Ssal.p.39. 3154a Nkusalidde ga nkolwa. (amagezi) (cf. Onsalidde: 4519) Duta 381. 3154b "Nkusuulidde mwoyo" :. nga nnakyeyombekedde akufumbira embaala. "I like you" (says the) woman-house-owner who cooks flying ants (mbaala) for you. If she does that: it is a sign that you are her "darling". Mbaala-termites are a rare treat. Dict.800. 3154c "Nkutabadde" : omunafu atabaala omulima. "I am attacking you" : the lazy fellow attacks the tiller. He comes to him early in the day to get food from him. Duta 856. 3154d "Nkutaddeko abiri" : ow'ettulu g'ateeka ku basengezzi. "I am looking at you attentively (with both my eyes)" : (says) a one- eyed fellow, looking at those who filter the beer into the calabashes. He should speak in the singular, as he has only one eye. Duta 519. 3154e Nkutuse buyiso : sikyadda mu ssasa. (cf. Tukutuse bwa mpiso: 5107) I am broken like a needle : I am not going back to the smithy. I am beyond mending, have no hope any longer. Kag.163. 3154f "Nkuwawaabidde" : takuviirako awo. (One who says to you) "I accuse you" : does not give you peace (till you give him compensation). 41.52. 3154g "Nkuwe nkuwadde) ekyanya" : ow'amalibu ky'awa ennoga (= akiwa ennoga). "Let me give you room" : as the toothless fellow gives room to the morsel (he throws into his wide-open mouth). M.591. 3154h "Nkuyita okulaba" : nga ow'amalibu asanze bafumba ebikongo. (cf. Okuyita okulaba: 3819) Rub.C.1169. 3154i "Nkuyigiriza okutega - " (cf. Nkulagirira okutega: 3153) Rub.C.1198. 3154j Nkuyiire nkuwe akanyama akabisi owuute otuzzi. Let me be good to you and give you a little fresh meat, so that you can suck the juice! Special sign of friendship; from fresh meat one can get more than from smoked meat. Rub.C.1397. 3154k "Nkwane ono nkwane : talema kugwa mu kabi. "Let me be friend to this one and that one" : (one who is careless like that in choosing his friend), won't fail to get into trouble. Ssal.p.7. 3154l Nkwatanyekwatanye : Kalambi ne Bbira. Intimately connected : like Kalambi and Bbira (two villages in Busiro with no natural boundaries). 86.36. 3154m "Nkwatiraako" : si bumbowa (= tafuuka mumbowa). "Give me a helping hand" (to make such a request) does not mean that one is asked to be an executioner. One who asks somebody to hold a thief for him, does not ask him to punish him. - One should not ask too much assistance from one's neighbour. Duta 1327. 3154n "Nkwegaanyi" : omuggo akwekwesa. (cf. Ssebayita mbwa: 4887) "I shall do you no harm" (he says) : but he hides the stick from your sight. Treacherous promises!

entries.english: "I keep away from you" : (says) the little finger to the ngalabi drum.
entries.meaning: The drummer does not touch it with his little fingers.

entries.english: "I reckon on you" : as the lazy woman reckons on her mother-in-law.
entries.meaning: Reliance on others without personal effort.

entries.english: "Let me kill you" : as the glue kills the fly.
I am still sitting (busy) dishing up the food for my husband.
entries.meaning: A married woman was supposed to leave all other work alone, as long as the husband was eating.

entries.english: I shall count (the cents) on the string : those which are not strung up get lost.
entries.meaning: For that purpose the cents have a hole in the middle.

entries.english: A mother of many children : has no ggobe (leaves of beans) left.
entries.meaning: Each child comes and asks for vegetables. A mother gives everything for her children.

entries.english: The "nnabe" (termite eating red ant) makes the anthills (i.e.
entries.meaning: the termites) migrate. Also used as an abuse.

entries.luganda: Nnabe zzisa : ng'ekiti ky'embazzi ekizisa ginnaakyo.
entries.english: A ruthless destroyer : like the handle of an axe that destroys its fellow trees.
entries.meaning: The nnabe-ant destroys the termites.

entries.english: "I shall change round (the information for my purposes)" (says the double- dealer to himself) : like a favourite (who tries to get information from his friends) and uses it against them (before authorities).
(He is one) who meddles in a conversation which he has misunderstood : like the chief of Ssambwe (Bulerneezi) (whose title is "Nnabugwamu").
A person doing jobs for herself (which should be done for her by others) : like the chief-woman (of the king or an other big man), attending to somebody else.

entries.luganda: Nnabyejeeguula ng'enswa : tennaba kutuuka gy'egenda, ng'embugo esuula.
entries.english: A thoughtlessly spending person is like a flying ant : it has not yet reached its destination and throws away the clothes (wings).
A spendthrift : like a bachelor squandering his money.
entries.meaning: Doing so, he will not be able to acquire a wife.

entries.english: A pretentious person : like a lamb that grazes amongst the cows.
entries.meaning: I want to be among the great.

entries.luganda: Nnagenda ne kye bannambye (=-- bakuwammye) : ng'enuneeme etodde.
entries.english: I went with what they told me : the heart being full with it.
A twister (double-dealer) : (is a man) who invites you to a meal and talks about your voracity afterwards.
"I shall drink (beer) there and sleep there" : (one who says so) has a friend there, where he drinks.
I have made blood-brotherhood (with him) : and he will betray me (by causing others to do me harm).

entries.luganda: "Nnajja kulaba nnyabo" : bw'atambula (= atuuka) abuna ekyalo.
entries.english: "I came to see my mother" (says he) : but when he comes, he roams about in the village.
"I came with my own property" : like the spotted goat suckling her young in the chief's place.
entries.meaning: The goat has been confiscated by the chief for an unpaid debt, whilst being with young. After weaning the debtor claims the young.

entries.english: "I came with my own property" : and that has embellished the chief's place.
entries.meaning: He claims praise for the improvement in the place.

entries.english: "I come to finish (the job)" : but he never finishes quickly.
entries.meaning: Referring to the bridge over the river Kkoba near Katende, which defeated the builders. - Business-men's promises!

entries.luganda: "Nnajjukiranga ne nseka" : nga si ggwe bakigambye.
entries.english: "I thought of it and I laughed" : (so you say) if they have not been talking about you.
entries.meaning: Criticism does not hurt, if it is about somebody else's faults. Trouble does not hurt, if it has befallen somebody else.

entries.english: A favourite girl is not to be trusted.
entries.meaning: A tree may look straight and nice; but the wood might be useless. Appearances are deceptive. "The proof of the pudding is in the eating".

entries.english: "With whom shall I share this little piece?" : (one saying so) satisfies nobody.
entries.meaning: The thing is too small to be divided.

entries.english: An idle talker : like a man who speaks evil of his companion.
entries.meaning: He will not find another friend among whom he has talked.

entries.luganda: Nnakamwa ntette : ye yabuulira nnyini ttooke, nti ettooke ly'emmanju lyenge-dde.
entries.english: An idle talker : tells the owner of the banana bunch: the bunch behind the house is ripe.
entries.meaning: The owner surely knows that better than an outsider. - Also said of "kasooli".

entries.english: A person who beats children badly : does not bring up the only child of a woman.
entries.meaning: She won't entrust it to him (her).

entries.english: A woman clad only with a loincloth : is like a female slave who avoids her marriage relations.
A pretentious person (one who holds her neck erect) : like a woman dreaming that the war-drums are sounding.
entries.meaning: She expects that her husband will go to war and bring home booty (meat, female slaves to help her etc.).

entries.english: A woman in childbirth trembles : if she sees somebody helping her.
entries.meaning: If nobody is there, she does not tremble and helps herself. - Exaggerating one's trouble, sickness etc.

entries.luganda: Nnakawuka : we kagwa mu nvubo amansula.
entries.english: If a "kawuka" (harmful insect) falls into the nvubo (hole dug in front of the anthill to gather the flying termites) : a person also called "Nnakawuka" throws it out.
(One who says) I hit my old hag (wife) : does not give the real cause.
entries.meaning: He is just bragging (yeetendereza). He does not give the reason for the beating.

entries.luganda: Nnakubyejuula : ng'omusanvu gw'oku nju; ne nnyinimu gumukuba.
entries.english: A bullying person : is like the twigs that are put at the side of the house (to prevent trespassing); they might easily get the owner of the house also into trouble.
entries.meaning: Another explanation: A scandal-monger is like those twigs; they help to keep the privacy or to prevent the hens from scratching the soil on the veranda; but they are also an obstacle to the inmates. - A scandal-monger (ow'omu nju) does not only talk about outsiders, but also to outsiders about the owner of the house.

entries.luganda: "Nnakuddamu ntya, jjo?" : bw'akukwata takuta (or: akusiba; akunyweza).
entries.english: (A man who asks you) "What answer did I give you yesterday (to your ex- cuses)?" : will not let you go (unpunished) (or: ties you up).
I shall fix you with a spear : like the old man who fixes his door (from inside) with the (slanting) stick.
entries.meaning: I shall pin you to the wall.

entries.english: I have grown up without stealing.
entries.meaning: He who says so, is either a liar or he has grown up in a poor man's house, where there was nothing to steal.

entries.english: "I shall become very fat (I shall eat my fill)" : (says one who sees) a big heap of banana-peelings.

entries.luganda: Nnaakumala amamiima : nnabanfuddu ge yamala nnabbubi.
entries.english: I'll get you into my crushing grip : as the nnabanfuddu got the spider.
entries.meaning: Nnabanfuddu is an insect which kills spiders. - Completely overpowering.

entries.english: "I knew you from olden times" (therefore you may pass over my ground) : but when the one who knew you goes away, the path is closed.
entries.meaning: Friendship and long acquaintance give many a right.

entries.luganda: "Nnaakussa ekkande" : nti kasooli wa kuno tayera awunda awo, ng'ogwa nna- kande kusaawa.
entries.english: "I shall cultivate diligently that overgrown banana plantation" (so one says who has been told) : in this soil maize does not just grow well, it flourishes, and he throws himself into clearing the plantation.
(That is the) misfortune of children (inferiors) : also one who is not a parent beats them (chiefs, schoolmasters etc.).
An independent being : like the thumb.
entries.meaning: It goes its own way, different from the other fingers.

entries.english: I shall examine it : as one examines a parcel of mpande (peanuts).
entries.meaning: To know what is in, one shakes it.

entries.english: A person wandering about aimlessly : like the spirit of a dead person who had no children.
entries.meaning: One who has had children is supposed to visit them.

entries.english: The beer which the (unmarried) woman-householder brews : brings her the kicks (blows) of the drunkards.

entries.luganda: "Nnali nkirabye" : enseenene eva ku mumwa gwa nsawo.
entries.english: "I have seen it before" : (says) the grasshopper, trying to escape from the opening of the bag.

entries.luganda: Nnaalinnya : omukazi talinnya nnyumba n'egwa munyale.
entries.english: The title "Nnaalinnya" does not indicate that the woman climbs on a roof and the soot falls down.
entries.meaning: A woman does not climb the roof (for building, thatching). Therefore if a man sins with a married woman and he is caught, he will be killed and his house will perish. His wife will not repair it.

entries.english: A sensitive person : like the ears of a sick man (every noise is pain).
entries.meaning: Or: A person keen to hear news : like the ears of a sick man (he has to rely on information from his visitors).

entries.english: A fierce (difficult) character : is like a hero.
entries.meaning: One keeps out of his way, to escape harm.

entries.luganda: Nnalukoola : all mu kibira; amayu gaggya.
entries.english: A solitary settler : is (like one) who lives in a forest; when the fire comes, the huts burn down.
entries.meaning: Nobody is there to help him.

entries.english: (The one who says) "I knew the kind of death that would kill me" and (he who says) "I did not know it" (both have to die once) : we all are going the same way.
entries.meaning: Engl. "We are in the same boat".

entries.english: He who says "I am late", but comes with a parcel (a gift) : is more welcome than (one who says) "I came in a hurry" and brings nothing.

entries.luganda: Nnalwanjo : alya mu basenze abaggya, ng'emmere bajja nayo mu migugu.
entries.english: A shameless parasite : one who goes to eat with new tenants who came with the food in their bundles.
entries.meaning: They have not planted any food yet.

entries.english: (One who says) "I shall stay a little longer" : is like a smith who warms himself at somebody else's fire.
entries.meaning: He could warm himself at his own forge.

entries.english: "I want to get two pieces (bifi)" : (one demanding that) causes a quarrel over the meat.
He who has two homesteads : is likely to die from hunger.
entries.meaning: Each of his two women thinks: "the husband will not come" and does not prepare any food for him. - "To fall between two stools".

entries.english: One who has two homesteads : does not give the chief his dues.
entries.meaning: Every time the chief comes, the man is in the other place.

entries.english: A woman with shrunken breasts (virago) : drinks beer like a man.
A useless person : (as useless) as the collar of a dog.
An irresolute person (a sit-on-the-fence) : is like a boundary stone.
entries.meaning: Said of persons who do not take sides, are neutral, undecided etc. Also of those who are wavering, double-dealing. - Germ. "Auf beiden Schultern Wasser tragen".

entries.luganda: Nnampa-we-ngwa : ng'envubu; ab'oku ttale bagibuuza omusolo, nti ndi wa nnyanja.
entries.english: A "sit-on-the-fence" : like a hippopotamus; the shore people demand the tax (and the hippo says) I belong to the lake.
A "sit-on-the-fence" : like a catholic wearing no medal (rosary).
entries.meaning: He does not dare to show himself as a catholic.

entries.english: An unwelcome visitor makes a welcome one suffer hunger.
entries.meaning: The unwelcome one is not offered food and the other has to wait till he goes.

entries.english: A huge banana-plantation : (is like) the teats of a dog (reaching from the thigh to the chest).
entries.meaning: Both give much nourishment.

entries.english: A lucky person (cook) : who manages to take the myungu (vegetable marrow) out of the cooking pot, with the fruit-stalks still on (and dishes them up like that).
entries.meaning: The stalks fall off easily from the soft myungu. - Congratulations on the successful accomplishment of a tricky job.

entries.english: A great number (of guests) does not cook (the food) : it burns it.
entries.meaning: With slow and thorough cooking they would become impatient.

entries.luganda: Nnamunnoona : ebbala erimu terimubuusa na nnyange.
entries.english: One white patch does not make the (white-shouldered) crow fly with the egrets.
entries.meaning: One should not place oneself above one's standing.

entries.luganda: Nnamunkanga tadduka buko : kubanga bw'osimba effumu n'ajja n'agwako.
entries.english: A dragon-fly does not avoid its relations-in-law : because if you stick your spear into the ground, it comes and sits down on its top.

entries.luganda: Nnamunye tamala kubala nnyumba : buli ezimbwa ng'agirinnyako.
entries.english: The wagtail is not particular about houses : it flies down on any house that is built.

entries.luganda: Nnamunyi w'atubira : 1) enkofu teyitawo; 2) pnaali tatengejja (= ayisa mu lyato).
entries.english: Where the wagtail sinks : 1) the guinea-fowl won't pass; 2) the crested crane won't float (= passes by boat).
entries.meaning: Where wise men fail, fools should not dare to attempt.

entries.luganda: Nnamusava w'olumu : 1) takusisa lunnyo; 2) takusuuza ntula.
entries.english: A big fat cow that is going to be eaten (by many people) in one day : 1) does not make you erect a frame (for drying the meat, because all the meat is going to be cooked and eaten the same day); 2) does not make you throw away the ntula (vegetables) (because tomorrow you will have no meat).
entries.meaning: Do not do useless things! - "Lay a penny by for a rainy day!"

entries.english: A presenter (introducer) : like the nsawo of the Bagwe.
entries.meaning: The Bagwe, a Bantu-tribe near Busia (near the Kenyan border) have a custom of presenting a pregnant woman or young mother with all sorts of medicine and advice, especially, if the woman is of another tribe. The whole lot (of medicine, advice, instruction) is called "nsawo".

entries.luganda: "Nnaamwatulira" : abulako munywanyi we (= abulwako munne, = tabaako munne).
entries.english: (One who says) "I shall tell him openly" (a person who reproaches one public- ly) : has no friend.
entries.meaning: Nobody likes to be put to shame.

entries.english: A person with one white hand (from syphilis) : like one who has one clean hand and shares out with two.
entries.meaning: The other seems not to be washed. - "Nnangalongya" is an old form for "na-ngalo-mpya".

entries.english: A double-dealer : like the Munyoro on the language-boundary.
The owner of the little bowl (who has broken it accidentally) : does not smash it altogether, but lovingly holds the broken pieces together.
entries.meaning: If another had broken it, he would have been angry.

entries.luganda: Nnannyini kasooli : y'amuwa abaayi; bw'aba azikiriza, nti atuuse ekiryabaayi.
entries.english: The owner of the (growing) maize : gives it to the marauders when it is half-ripe, (saying) it has reached the state of "ekirya-baayi" (= ekiryabatabaazi).
The owner of the big mushroom eats his fill, whilst it is fresh.
entries.meaning: He need not collect and dry small quantities till he has a meal.

entries.english: The owner of the household spoils his home (through bad example or negli-gence).
entries.meaning: He is responsible for the evil caused thereby.

entries.luganda: Nnannyini mmere ayomba : nga ne nnannyini mbuzi ayomba?
entries.english: If the owner of the (food) garden quarrels : should the owner of the goat (which trespassed into it) also quarrel?

entries.luganda: Nnannyinimu ayomba : nti newakubadde ewunya, nze empoomedde.
entries.english: The master of the house (and not the guest) has a right to complain about the food (or to reprimand the personnel) : although the food tastes badly, the guest must say: it is sweet to me (I like it, it tastes nice).
The owner of the dead person (nearest relation) gets hold of the stinking corpse.

entries.luganda: Nnannyini mulimo : takeera kwota One who has work to do : does not sit near the fire in the early morning.
entries.english: The work will make him warm.

entries.luganda: Nnannyini ndwadde, nkugamba nti siisulewo; nti leka kundwaza mwoyo.
entries.english: The sick person (says) I tell you, I am not going to live to-morrow; (reply) stop worrying me!
I have plucked tobacco leaves : but I have no trough (to pound the leaves).
entries.meaning: Applied to a poor man, who, when he has finally collected the "bintu", cannot get a wife.

entries.luganda: Nnantabwaza (= nnantabweyaliza) : akuba mu ly'enkejje obusomyo (okunyu- nyunta eggumba lyayo).
entries.english: A poor man sucks the marrow out of the bone of an enkejje (small fish).
entries.meaning: He cannot afford better bones. - The enkejje-bones contain very little marrow (only in some joints).

entries.english: He who does not listen to a concubine of his father : will listen to his real mother.
entries.meaning: "Muka-sse" is a word used in the Lake district of Buganda and on the islands.

entries.luganda: Nnantagambwa kabi : ng'ekkubo erigenda mu ffumbiro (= ng'ekkubo ly'omu kiyungu).
entries.english: One about whom nobody speaks evil : is like the path leading to the kitchen (i.e.
entries.meaning: all good things come from there).

entries.english: A useless person : like a lazy woman who is barren.
entries.meaning: She does no work and cannot produce any children. Si mwana, si lubimbi!

entries.luganda: Nnantaggwa buto : ng'akafuba k'ennyonyi; ak'enkulu n'ak'ento babubaaza bumuli.
entries.english: (He or she) never stopped being a child : like the breast of a bird; the breast of an old bird and that of a young one are both carved with a reed.
entries.meaning: They both remain soft.

entries.luganda: Nnantaggwa buto : ng'ekifuba ky'ennyonyi; baagizaala ku Myanga na kaakati bakibaagisa kamuli.
entries.english: (He or she) never stopped being a child : like the breast of a bird; it was born in the reign of Mwanga and now they carve it with a little reed.
entries.meaning: Often applied to persons in "second childhood".

entries.english: One who does not omit to pay regular visits : is like a friend of the bananary.
entries.meaning: The bananary thrives, if the owner visits it often. The friendship thrives if the friends meet often.

entries.luganda: Nnantakiika : nti embuga egabula baganzi (or: eby'embuga biriibwa baganzi).
entries.english: One who does not present himself at the lukiiko : (complains) "the good things of the chief's place are given only to the favourites".
entries.meaning: Expression of envy: By staying at home he will not change such sentiments.

entries.english: (You are) never to be seen (a rare treat) : like the flower of endaggu (kind of yam).
entries.meaning: Endaggu hardly ever flowers.

entries.english: One who does not tell you where he is going : cannot be looked for.
entries.meaning: In case of an emergency it is difficult to find him.

entries.english: You are a fine fellow : like a river in which there are (plenty of) nsonzi (small fish).

entries.luganda: Nnasajja : ng'omugomo (= omuya) ogutta emmamba (= ensonzi).
entries.english: You are a fine fellow : like a wicker-trap for mmamba (lungfish) (or ensonzi (small fish)).
entries.meaning: Expression of praise, gratitude. - Omusajja asanyuka n'omukazi asanyuka; omusajja alya mmamba, omukazi alya obuyamba (small fish).

entries.english: I have cut shoes (for my feet) : (says the parent) to save myself from treading on thorns.
entries.meaning: Meaning: I have brought forth children, whom I can send instead of going my-self.

entries.english: (The one who says) "I slept whilst the sickness was gnawing me" : laughs at the one (who says) "I walk about with it".
entries.meaning: Exchanging experiences about each other's sickness.

entries.english: The chameleon is not killed with one blow.
entries.meaning: Nobody should be condemned on account of one mistake. - One failure should not hinder from trying again. - Engl. "A cat has nine lives".

entries.english: "I shall go over the mountains" : (says the man) who has disowned his relations (i.e.
entries.meaning: "I shall not come back").

entries.english: I shall keep company with those who sell beer : (because) the brewers them- selves are (often) without it (between the brewings).
entries.meaning: Desire to have a supply always.

entries.english: (A woman who can say) "I have brought forth one child" : is free from the reproach of barrenness.
Now he revolts against the king : whilst he is building (his house) in Bunyoro.
entries.meaning: There the king's arm does not reach him; and he does not intend to return to Buganda.

entries.english: (An unannounced visitor, who says) "I have come to eat" : goes away hungry.
entries.meaning: Perhaps he arrives after the meal; or nothing is prepared. No cook there etc.

entries.english: "I am going my way" : (a person saying so goes away in anger and) when he (she) dies (by hanging himself) you will be held responsible, because you might have been the reason why he hanged himself.

entries.luganda: Nneekutte ku mugongo gw'enjovu : sigenda kufa nnyanja.
entries.english: I hold on to the back of an elephant : (therefore) I shall not be drowned in the lake.
entries.meaning: If I make friends with rich (powerful) people, I'm safe.

entries.english: I am swinging from place to place like the tongue of a bell.

entries.luganda: Nneesittadde ku jjinja : ngudde ku lwayi.
entries.english: I stumbled over a stone : (and) fell on a long piece of banana-fibre (= into a trap).
entries.meaning: Banana-fibre is used in setting certain traps. - French "Tomber de Charybde en Scylla". Germ. "Vom Regen in die Traufe kommen".

entries.english: (To say) "I am gnawing my own bone" : is meanness.
entries.meaning: One who hears that, understands that he will not be given any meat from that bone.

entries.english: A young bull does not develop (prosper) as well as a young heifer.
entries.meaning: Also applied to boys and girls.

entries.luganda: "Nnyama ntono" : okaayana eri mu ngalo (or: mu nkwawa)?
entries.english: (You say) "That is little meat" : are you complaining about the piece you have received already (which is in your hands, under your arm)?
entries.meaning: Take your piece and go away!

entries.english: The owner of the (killing) spear : is not cheated out of his meat.
entries.meaning: All hunters partake; but the killer (or the one who first spears it) gets the best part. - If one gets the loan of a thing, that leads him to prosperity, he should also help his helper, when he gets the means.

entries.english: If the owner of the bracelet (who has loaned it to you) wants it back, you hold out your hand (for him to take it).

entries.luganda: Nnyinimu akugoba : nti nnaasula mu bisegguusi?
entries.english: If the owner of the house drives you out : (you ask) have I to spend the night under the porch?
The master (mistress) of the house has authority.

entries.luganda: Nnyini mwana akubuulira : ko ggwe Bambuulira.
entries.english: The owner of the child tells you : and you say: They tell me (= I hear).
entries.meaning: The former certainly should be considered as trustworthy.

entries.luganda: Nnyoko abanga Omunyolo : n'akuzaala mu kika.
entries.english: If your mother is a Munyoro : you are born in the clan (of the father).
entries.meaning: The child follows the nationality of the father. - It is better that you are born of a non-Muganda mother and a Muganda father than vice-versa.

entries.english: "I am looking for a nice stick" : (one who says so) comes out (of the forest) without it.
entries.meaning: Fable of the heron. - One who is too particular and never satisfied, achieves nothing.

entries.english: I am as immovable as the rock Nnalubaale (hillock in Mawogola).
(effumu) "You come and fail" : (says the attacked person), if the spear has missed him.
(ente) Even he who owns only one cow : fumigates it (to keep the flies away).
entries.meaning: Even the poor man protects his little property.

entries.english: An old field : makes you eat your meal without nva (vegetables, additional dishes).

entries.luganda: Nsambu y'ewala : ekuliisa kiro (= lwa ggulo).
entries.english: A field (garden) that is far away : postpones your meal till late at night (till evening).
entries.meaning: Distance and transport of food delay the cooking.

entries.english: A field that is far away : does not still the hunger.
entries.meaning: One carries only little food on account of the distance. M.618. 3327 Nsawo tebba : bwe kibula, nga muntu y'akibbye. The bag does not steal : if a thing is missing, it is a person who has stolen it.

entries.english: A bag does not steal : the property of its master.

entries.luganda: Nsawo y'omukulu : tebula zziika (= tebulamu zziika).
entries.english: The master's bag : always contains treasures.

entries.luganda: Nsekedde mu kikonde : ng'omuwuulu asikidde abataano.
entries.english: I laughed up my sleeve (lit.
entries.meaning: in my fists) : like an unmarried fellow who inherited five wives.

entries.english: "I am an enseenene (edible grasshopper) : I come from a long journey.
entries.meaning: Expression used, when a visitor comes from far.

entries.english: (One who answers to your question: What are you doing there) "I am tying up my things" : finishes off the banana fibre in his garden.
entries.meaning: He does not want to let others know what he is tying up and uses therefore lots of byayi. - Application also to personal secrets of one who wants to settle his difficulties without anybody else's advice or help.

entries.english: Bad tying up : depreciates the dried bananas.
entries.meaning: Nobody will buy them on the market, if they are wrapped up badly. Neat things are attractive.

entries.english: Bad tying up : makes you fight with the forest.
entries.meaning: A crisscross bundle of firewood makes the passage through the forest difficult. - Application as the previous one.

entries.english: The uncultivated land does not quarrel (with you) (i.e.
entries.meaning: about treatment, goats, hens, children coming into it). Even if you burn it in the hot season, it will give you fresh grass and medicine herbs again.

entries.english: One cowry-shell : is not enough to hit a bird.

entries.luganda: Nsimbi emu : tennyombya; nga wa luganda y'agitutte.
entries.english: One cowry-shell (cent) : does not make me quarrel; (so one says) if the one who has taken it is a relation of his.
entries.meaning: But he would quarrel, if it had been an outsider.

entries.english: A bad cowryshell looks quite respectable in a string of hundred.
entries.meaning: An otherwise bad character gains in good company.

entries.english: Money is not counted well for you by somebody else.
entries.meaning: You had best do it yourself.

entries.english: (One who says) "Money does not help itself" : traps it with one trap only.
entries.meaning: Money by itself is not productive; one must try to increase it. - A trapper who puts out only one trap, has not much chance.

entries.english: Let the money be sweet (to him)!
entries.meaning: Sarcastic remark about being too much attached to riches. Envy? "Sour grapes"!

entries.english: I have planted bwanda (a portulaca-plant which forms thick carpets on the ground and which cannot be rooted out easily).
entries.meaning: I have created something that will last.

entries.luganda: Nsirikirirwa nfiirwa : bannyinaze babiri, enkoko emu!
entries.english: I am speechless and cheated : two sisters and one hen!
entries.meaning: So says the brother of the two sisters who are married to the same man. He was on a visit there and received only one hen as kagenyi.

entries.luganda: Nsolo imenyi : bw'esula ku kyalo timwebaka.
entries.english: When a stray wild animal is in the village : you won't sleep.
entries.meaning: The habits of a local wild animal you know. - Unknown danger!

entries.english: The plantain-shoot grows next to the old stump.
entries.meaning: Formerly they cut the old banana stem about half its height and let the stump stand (now forbidden). - The place of the child is near its mother.

entries.english: "I (eat and) sleep at home" : a bachelor wrestles (i.e.
entries.meaning: I am a married man). A bachelor is always ready to share pot-luck; but a married man must often refuse an invitation, as his wife is supposed to have cooked for him.

entries.english: Enswaswa: 1743) Rowl.Guide No.23.
(A man who says) "ntadde" (I give it up, I am going) : (is like) a tree that sheds its leaves.
entries.meaning: They never go back on the tree. Expression of disappointment with frustrated efforts.

entries.english: Something insufficient : like matooke that are cooked in a small cooking pot.
entries.meaning: "Kkobe" or "kikuta ky'ekkobe" stands for a very small ntamu (cooking pot).

entries.luganda: Ntaama ngevvu : bw'ogirabako omukira nga ya mugagga.
entries.english: If you see on a fat sheep the (whole) tail : (you know that) it belongs to a rich man.
entries.meaning: A poor man sometimes cuts off a piece of the fat tail (up to three times) and lets it heal up; a rich man can afford to kill the whole sheep. - The rich live from their surplus, the poor from hand to mouth.

entries.luganda: Ntambaazi ya kinyomo : erinnya omuti nga yeetisse.
entries.english: The impossible (large black) ant : climbs the tree carrying a load.
entries.meaning: It will fall with the load. - Foolishness in attempting the impossible.

entries.english: I walk as a man walks with a child (i.e.

entries.luganda: Ntasumika bagitonda wabiri : olubugo nga balututte.
entries.english: A man who walks naked has to answer for two things : if they have robbed him of his barkcloth (i.e.
entries.meaning: 1) for walking naked; 2) for the circumstances in which he lost his cloth). He might have been caught in a crime (stealing, adultery).

entries.english: "I see it now" (that I have been too hasty) : says the aggressive husband (after sending his wife away) seeing that he has no wife any longer.
(One who says) "I understand" : (does not really understand) but is asking.
entries.meaning: Acting differently from what one says.

entries.english: "I add to the lubimbi (one day's cultivation) of yesterday" : (a woman saying so) does not only swallow (gobble down) the food greedily, but gets tired of it.
entries.meaning: A lazy woman has a tremendous appetite. She does less in two days than a laborious in one.

entries.english: (One who acts on the principle) "Let me get rich quickly" : cheats his own bloodbrother.
entries.meaning: His greed kills other better feelings.

entries.english: A messenger (ambassador) does not die in the place he was sent to.
entries.meaning: Immunity! Ntumwa is also a proper name.

entries.luganda: Ntuuse mu lyaffe eddemeezi : abula w'alya ekyemisana.
entries.english: I have arrived on our Bulemeezi-road (says the Mulemeezi-traveller) and has no place where he can eat at midday.
entries.meaning: He is still far from home; but now he hopes to reach a Mulemeezi chief who will give him supper.

entries.english: "Poor fellow" : that is how a dog consoles its mate.

entries.luganda: "Ntwalanga ku nkumbi ya nnyabo" : asula tiyeebisse.
entries.english: "I am longing for the hoe of my mother" : (a girl saying so) does not sleep well.
entries.meaning: Thinking of the work she wants to do, having the same laborious mind as her mother. - Other version: kubanga akkuse nnyo!

entries.english: "Let me move away from the fireplace" : (says one who has finished roasting (maize cob, gonja etc.).
entries.meaning: "Nkoto" is really the place behind the masiga (hearth-stones). - Germ. "Sein Schalchen im Trockenen haben".

entries.luganda: Nva za munyaga : ziriibwa wa mwoyo.
entries.english: The vegetables of a dirty cook : can only be eaten by a courageous person.
entries.meaning: One with a weak stomach had better leave them alone.

entries.english: One female slave does not like the other.
The mother of an ugly child : does not take it from her back.
entries.meaning: She is shy of showing it to the people.

entries.luganda: "Nze embaga zantama" : nga ne ky'ayambala "I got tired of these feasts" (says one) who has nothing to dress up in.
entries.english: Being ashamed of his poverty.

entries.luganda: "Nze ndi kkubo lya mulimba" : likala mmanju.
entries.english: "I am the path of the liar" : that path gets trodden out at the back of the house.
entries.meaning: Those who are after evil things, do not want to be seen. Saying of the sorcerer (witchdoctor) when leaving the house of the patient.

entries.english: "I grew up without play" (I am not used to dancing) : says one who is dressed in an old barkcloth.
entries.meaning: Disguising his poverty. Sour grapes!

entries.luganda: "Nziddemu nziddiddemu) mu bisolo byange" : nga mulimu n'ez'embuga.
entries.english: "I have put them (the cows of the chief) amongst my own" : (says one herds-man to the other), if the chief's cows are amongst them.
entries.meaning: A practice not approved of by the cattle owners.

entries.english: "I do not want any noise (quarrel)" (says the brewer) : still he brews beer (which causes rows).
Relieve me of the bother of one who comes for fire (and says: I'll come back to eat).
entries.meaning: Are those to whom you take the fire not cooking?

entries.english: As long as you have not fallen yet : you don't know what has thrown you down.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Experientia docet". Germ. "Durch Schaden wird man klug".

entries.english: If you were a weaverbird : you would build a nest right on my mouth.
entries.meaning: You are a garrulous person. - Weaverbirds chatter incessantly.

entries.luganda: Obikka ku maddu : nti "malako ennyama, ompe eggumba".
entries.english: You are disguising your desire : (saying) "finish the meat and give me the bone".
entries.meaning: You really mean to say: Are you going to finish all the meat on that bone?

entries.english: You have seen trouble : well, the one who sees, finds.
entries.meaning: Sarcastic play upon words: obonyeebonye = olabye.

entries.english: The respect for a (former) chief does not come to an end as does that for a former trader.
"I have finished with stealing" (says the husband who has been stealing) : if they have taken his wife (as a hostage) to the chief's place (till he gives himself up).
entries.meaning: He has been running away, but had to come back to ransom his wife.

entries.luganda: Obubuiwa : bukuliisa (ettooke) eriri mu maaso ga mumw.
entries.english: (= Obubulwa buku-tooza - - ) Having no food in front of you : makes you take the ttooke from your neigh-bour's helping.

entries.luganda: Obubulwa ggye : busembeza emmandwa ku lubu.
entries.english: The absence of an army : brings the lubaale priest to the front rank.
entries.meaning: The king (chief) not having sufficient soldiers calls the mmandwa with his charms to the front. Otherwise the mmandwa are despised.

entries.luganda: Obudde butuukira mu muti ne bukya.
entries.english: (other form: Ennyonyi etuukira - - ) Dawn comes upon the tree and the day starts.
entries.meaning: The birds in the trees greet the morning with their song. Also used of a new settler who lives for the time being with a relation of his and looks slowly for a kibanja.

entries.luganda: Obudde bwe buziba : ennyonyi yeeyuna omuti.
entries.english: When the day comes to a close : the bird takes shelter in a tree.

entries.luganda: Obudde tibuleka nnyinibwo : nnannyini lugendo y'abulekawo.
entries.english: Darkness does not force one who wants to wander to remain at home.
entries.meaning: It is the wanderer who leaves the darkness to itself. Said also of bad weather.

entries.luganda: Obufuzi bw'emmese : bulabika ng'omaze okuzimba enju.
entries.english: The fact you are put in charge of rats, is seen as soon as you have built your house.
entries.meaning: They feed in your house as if they were children.

entries.luganda: Obugagga ntuuyo : zittulukuka ng'ogenda, bw'owummula nga zikuggwako.
entries.english: Wealth is like perspiration : it abounds when you are active, but comes to an end when you rest (on your laurels).
Favouritism is passionately struggled for.
Laziness begets weakness (physical and moral).
entries.meaning: Dict.702, L.86. 3421 Obugenyi buwombeeka (= bugonza) : nga musulo guwombeeka essubi. Presents appease (soften) the heart : as the dew softens the grass.

entries.english: Trying repeatedly for the bait in the trap killed the ssessolye (little birds eating menvu).
entries.meaning: Engl. "The pitcher goes so often to the well, that it is broken at last". Dutch "De kruik gaat zo lang to water tot zij breekt". Germ. "Der Krug geht zum Brunnen, bis er bricht".

entries.english: To be of olden times : makes the muvule wither.

entries.luganda: Obugulu obutono : sibumegga nnyinibwo; singa nnamunye atambula agwa.
entries.english: Short legs do not throw down their owner; otherwise the wagtail would fall whilst walking.
Immorality is eating your eyes, and you give as reason for it: "The lubaale Wamala has rubbed ashes into my eyes".
entries.meaning: False excuses. Ap.Emp.211. 3427 Obuukabuuka ng'emmese emulise mu maaso ekiro. You are hopping about like a rat whose eyes gleam at night. Said of a person who has no fixed home and turns up everywhere, like a vagabond.

entries.english: Old age is like food put aside : it is eaten by the one who remembers (that it has been put aside).
entries.meaning: Old people are often put aside and forgotten. Ssal.p.81. 3431 Obukadde ŋŋoma. Old age is like a drum. A drum makes a noise when it is moved about on account of certain articles which were put inside by the maker; an old person groans when getting up and down.

entries.luganda: Obukadde obusinda amaluma : bwetisse mukene all ku mutwe.
entries.english: Old age which complains of plain food : is carrying a headload of mukene (small lake fish - "excellent nva").
entries.meaning: Silver hair is here compared with the glittering little fish; but they are "nva" he can't eat!

entries.english: You are jumping over ground, where a heap of grass has been burnt, like a man who does not eat bbugga (vegetable).
entries.meaning: Bbugga is often planted (and grows well) on such ground.

entries.english: He who wants to put old thatch on the roof again : does so early in the morning.
entries.meaning: During the day it raises dust and soot. - The courageous tackle things without hesitation. Engl. "Faint heart never won fair lady".

entries.luganda: Obukojja bwa munno si bukojja bwo.
entries.english: The marriage relations of your friend (or your marriage partner) : are not yours.

entries.luganda: Obukya buziba : omwana alwa ddaaki n'ayisa amuzaala.
entries.english: After the morning comes the evening : the child finally overtakes the parent.
One who is going to be tired of being principal wife, gives her powers away to one of the concubines (e.g.
entries.meaning: looking after the lusuku, the kitchen etc.). She intends to leave that husband.

entries.english: (One who says) "Life is long living" : makes fun of the people of the mush-room clan.
entries.meaning: "Kiwango" has a double meaning: 1) life everlasting, 2) place name in Bukee-rere (butaka bwa Baabutiko); but even the bakulu of the mushroom clan (Musitwa, Mberenge) have died.

entries.english: Life is like ttooke : it goes (perishes) when the cultivator goes.
Lameness does not come (only) in later life (like old age) (it is possible also in childhood).
A lie is a child's way of escaping (punishment).
The finding of just one ear of corn does not keep hunger away.
entries.meaning: Engl. "A drop in the ocean!" 65.2, Ssal.p.72.

entries.english: "The millet corn was not mine : it belonged to the elephant".
entries.meaning: A ruse, adopted by Wakayima (the hare) in the fable, to get compensation. See Apollo, Engero, p.29: "Wakayima ne Ggulu-ddene"!

entries.english: Beauty is better than riches.
entries.meaning: Even in old age one shows former beauty. Also said of a good name. French "Bonne renommee vaut mieux que ceinture doree".

entries.luganda: Obulungi bw'enswa : atalya mutima gwa mbuzi, aguliira mu nswa.
entries.english: The beauty (taste) of flying ants : one who does not eat the heart of a goat, eats it in a flying ant (it is not butchered).
The beauty of hills you admire : when you see them from afar.
entries.meaning: Nearby you see the barrenness, the stones, hard climbing. Engl. "Distance lends enchantment".

entries.luganda: "Obulwa bukula musaayi" : nga si ggwe bafumise oba nga tebafumise wuwo.
entries.english: "A fight gets lively, when blood is drawn" : (so one says) only if it is not you who has been speared, or if they have not speared your own relation (son, father, brother).

entries.luganda: Obulwa dda : 1) blikaza ekkubo ku lwazi; 2) bukutula empalaata.
entries.english: Walking on a rock for a long time : 1) makes a visible path on it.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Gutta cavat lapidem, non vi sed saepe cadendo" (Ovid). Germ. "Steter Tropfen halt den Stein". Long life : 2) gives a bald head (baldness). Dying young saves you from getting it. 84.4, Duta 889. 3457 Obumanyi bukira obuzibu (obuzira). (cf. Bukira obuzibu: 1001) Acquaintance is better than courage. If one is hunted by his enemies, he can hide himself at his friend's home; if he has no friends, he might be caught and be killed in spite of his courage. 61.2. 3458 Obumpi bw'ensuwa : bugiyisa nsumbi. The smallness (shortness) of a waterpot : causes it to be called "nsumbi" (water jar). A "small" man may be a "big" one. "Appearances are deceiving". Germ. "Schein triigt". Rub.C.2007. 3459 Obumyufu bw'amaaso si buzira : singa endegeya mu kasooli bagigobesamu ma-fumu na ngabo. (cf. Okumyuka amaaso: 3766) Red eyes do not necessarily mean courage : otherwise one would have to drive away the weaverbird from the maize with spear and shield.

entries.english: The strong qualities surpass each other.
entries.meaning: Each in a way is more important than the other.

entries.english: You fly high, but not far : like the pigeon.
entries.meaning: You aim high, but will soon come down.

entries.english: Serfdom kills the lazy man.
entries.meaning: If he does not work, he will be sent away soon.

entries.luganda: Obusenze bwe bubula : enswa entunda ezimba ku mpawu.
entries.english: If the "entunda"-termite does not want to work on its own anthill, it builds on the hill of the "mpawu"-termite.
entries.meaning: One who is too lazy to build his own house, is a parasite on somebody else.

entries.english: To be a representative does not go well together with urging on people impor-tunely.
entries.meaning: The musigire of the chief will lose the case when the chief comes back.

entries.luganda: Obusiro tebutuukirwako : ajja okulya, atuukira ku ndagala.
entries.english: Busiro (the king's place) is not reached at once : one who is going to eat, reaches first the banana leaves (spread out as table cloth).
entries.meaning: One who wants to become Prime Minister, has to start from the bottom: Mutongole - Muluka Ggombolola etc.

entries.luganda: Obusiru obwakukutte bwa nkoko : bugizaalisa mu kyalo.
entries.english: The madness that got hold of you is that of a hen : it makes her lay eggs in the village (away from home).
(One who says) "The animals of this place do not die" : sets only one trap.
entries.meaning: The hunter who is more persevering and lays traps all over the place, will get more. - One man's advice is not sufficient.

entries.luganda: Obusungu mugenyi : 1) akyala n'addayo; 2) amala kuboonoonyesanga yeege-nderera.
entries.english: Anger is like a visitor : 1) he comes and goes; 2) first it causes you to do evil and then it goes away.

entries.luganda: Obusungu obungi tebukkutibwa (= tibukkutwa) : Nnamunkanga eyabukkuta ekifuba kabanika.
entries.english: Great anger is never satisfied : the dragon-fly that got its fill, got a distended chest.
entries.meaning: It looks like an angry animal. - Used as a warning for angry people.

entries.luganda: Obutajja kundaba nnasiba embwa ku lumbugu n'egaana okululya?
entries.english: Is the reason that you never came to see me : because I have tied the dog to the lumbugu (grass) and it refused to eat it?
entries.meaning: What have I done, that you shun my company?

entries.english: Eating not only one (caster-oil-berry) : killed the pigeon.
entries.meaning: Those berries high up are safe enough, but.those further down lead to disaster, because there is the trap.

entries.luganda: Obutamanya bya mwaka : ng'emmese esula omw'omulima.
entries.english: Not knowing the time of the year (season) : means being like a rat that lives in the house of a farmer.
entries.meaning: The farmer has always food in his house. The rat need not worry, therefore, about the seasons.

entries.english: Not knowing the misery (that awaits you at home) : makes you run back to the place where they have sold you.
entries.meaning: The slave girl is badly treated by the new master and tries to run home. But she does not think that she probably will not find much love there, because they preferred money to her. - Engl. "Out of the frying pan into the fire".

entries.english: Lack of experience : makes you contract blood-brotherhood with a quarrel-some person.

entries.luganda: Obutamera kirevu ; njuba ya kikome, ekuliisa lwa ggulo.
entries.english: Beardlessness is like a cloudy day (overcast sky) : which makes you take your supper early.
entries.meaning: When the sun is not visible, you can't tell the time. If a person has no beard, you might be mistaken in guessing his age.

entries.english: When it is not yet evening : do not complain that there are no "vegetables" (meat, fish, greens, termites etc.).
entries.meaning: They might easily come yet.

entries.english: Taking without asking they considered as befitting a dog only (not man).
Without mutual bargaining in trading (buguzi) : there will be no sale.
entries.meaning: If both stubbornly insist on their price, there will be no exchange. Rub.C.1826. 3488 Obutasingwa mpaka : butta omukwano. (cf. Omukwano kyayi kya mpiso: 4218) If an argument is not settled : it kills the friendship.

entries.english: Pains (bulumi) which show no visible signs (swellings) are only understood by the patient himself.
entries.meaning: It is easy to minimize somebody else's inner trouble. M.641, 12.12. 3491 Obuteebaliza ku munno : bwe buggya. Not to say "Weebale", when your neighbour has received something, is envy.

entries.luganda: Obutekkaanya : bukutindiza balugu (ng'enva ze balya zirandira wansi).
entries.english: Thoughtlessness makes you lead up the balugu-plant (yam) (because what is eaten of that plant, is not above, but below ground).
(= Obuteemanya - - ) Not to shout "ku lwa Kabaka" (when spearing an animal) : means enmity.
entries.meaning: The king is supposed to be the lord of all. "Lese-majesty".

entries.english: Obuteemanya - - ) Not knowing one's own failings : makes you blame one who is better than yourself.
entries.meaning: Lack of self-knowledge causes you to underestimate another who surpasses you. - Compare Matt.7.3: "n'otolaba kisiki mu liiso lyo". - Engl. "The pot calling the kettle black!"

entries.english: Not answering quickly to the tuning-efforts causes a harp (i.e.
entries.meaning: its pegs) to be twisted frequently. Disobedience causes punishment.

entries.english: Not building its own house : has killed the wild pig.
entries.meaning: It lives in hollows (caves) made by others. If the owner comes, he can easily kill it.

entries.english: Unripe matooke ought to be offered with enva (vegetables).
entries.meaning: Without relish they are not eatable.

entries.english: If the (tough) porridge breaks the stick (used for stirring) : do you bring a papyrus-stalk (to stir with)?
entries.meaning: If strong measures did not bring success, will weaker ones do?

entries.english: To give is not to share.
entries.meaning: Giving is not the same as sharing. Giving something to one does not cause mis-givings; but in distributing things to many, one has to beware of favouritism.

entries.english: Forced obedience puts the collar round the dog's neck.

entries.luganda: Obuyisi bw'omu : nsega y'ebika (= bulangwa nsega).
entries.english: The passing away of the lonely traveller is made known by the vultures (circling over the body).
entries.meaning: He has nobody else to announce his death. Applied to persons who are alone or single-handed.

entries.luganda: Obuzadde bulima : obusuutira we babwagala (= okwenyumiikiriza we bakwaga-la).
entries.english: Parenthood is like tilling the land : they (the parents) like to be praised for it.
Bringing forth saves the "mbooge" (vegetables) from being killed (plucked).
entries.meaning: When the mbooge-plant goes to seed, it is unsuitable for cooking and is no longer plucked ("embooge ey'obwana").

entries.english: The place where one is born is not the place where one grows old.

entries.luganda: Obuuza nga Munyolo : akulaba n'ensuwa, nti ogenda iziba?
entries.english: You are greeting like a Munyoro : when he sees you with a waterpot, he says: are you going to the well?
entries.meaning: Lunyoro "iziba" corresponds to Luganda "emugga".

entries.english: Where they like the rags : they spread out the mat for them.
entries.meaning: A beloved person, even in rags, finds a warm welcome.

entries.luganda: Obwami ddiba lya mbogo : terizingwa omu.
entries.english: Chieftainship is like a buffalo-skin : it cannot be rolled up by one man.
entries.meaning: The chief requires the cooperation of many.

entries.luganda: Obwami kyambalo kyazike : nnannyinikyo bw'akikuggyako togaana.
entries.english: Chieftainship is like a borrowed garment : if its owner takes it away from you, you cannot object.
A small chieftainship makes you question the one you have sent (with a mes-sage).
entries.meaning: The messenger does not care to report at once, as he would, if a big chief had sent him.

entries.english: Being quick in giving : makes you give things to one who won't give you any-thing in return.
Poverty makes you eat your mother.
entries.meaning: If one has no money to buy meat, he says: "0, nnyabo! Singa nnina nsimbi, nnandiguze".

entries.english: Poverty is not (as bad) as having debts.
entries.meaning: What he has, is his, and nobody troubles him.

entries.english: Poverty does not make one thin.
entries.meaning: In olden times everybody had his food, although he had no money.

entries.english: Poverty does not let you know whom you might love (who might love you).
entries.meaning: Having nothing, you have no chance to show your love.

entries.english: What is poured out, cannot be gathered again.
entries.meaning: "No use crying over spilt milk". - Slander, suspicions. - The dead do not come back. - Lat. "Et semel emissum volat irreparabile verbum" (Horace). - What is done; is done.

entries.english: (obulwadde) Sickness from a spear-wound and from witchcraft are not (to be treated) alike.

entries.luganda: Obwemage bwe balanga : enjobe mu lusa.
entries.english: (A person whom they accuse) without reason : is like an antelope in the marsh (accused of having damaged the crop).
entries.meaning: A marsh-antelope causes no harm to potatoes or other crops.

entries.english: Great forgetfulness makes you ask something from a person, to whom you have (in the past) refused a request.
entries.meaning: You probably won't get anything either.

entries.english: Trust (safety) is found on the lake.
entries.meaning: Escaping with the canoe saves the fisherman from attack on the land (the water is his element).

entries.english: Hypocrisy kills the sorcerer.
entries.meaning: He tells the people: "such and such a thing may not be eaten, as it is for the lubaale"; but then, he eats it himself and offends the lubaale who will kill him.

entries.english: To be tied up all round ,: is like a banana "in the jacket", fighting in the cooking pot.
(obu1wadde) Illness of the belly : brings along illness of the head.
entries.meaning: When the body is not fed, the will to work is hbt there either.

entries.english: Porridge served to one man gets cold on one side (the one he is not eating from).
entries.meaning: Or: An old man (obukadde) sleeping on his bed, gets cold on the side he is not sleeping on, because he has not enough body heat. A big job needs- more than one man to manage it.

entries.english: The time which a liar mentions (in his narrations) is not disputed.
entries.meaning: You cannot disprove his statement that it was 6 hr. or 9 hr. (he is always right).

entries.luganda: Obw'omutambuze tibuziba : enjuba egudde ng'agamba: npenda emisana.
entries.english: For a traveller it does not get dark : although the sun is down, he says: 0, it is still light!
The sickness "obwosi" (of children who are deprived of breast-feeding) hurts more those children born before (by the same father).
entries.meaning: Those of a different mother (although by the same father) feel more indifferent. Engl. "Blood is thicker than water".

entries.luganda: Odaagana (= otaagana) : ng'olwatta Mpoobe e Kibiri.
entries.english: You make vain attempts (to escape your fate) : like Mpoobe (who was killed by Walumbe) at Kibiri.
entries.meaning: Being worried into telling a secret killed Mpoobe.

entries.luganda: Oduula nga musibe : nti tunaalaba okusula nga tutunula.
entries.english: You speak sarcastically like a blind man : (saying) we shall find a place for sleeping, while we still "see" (whilst it is still day-light).
Die and don't come back (be courageous and don't fear death) : like a man who fights for a woman (in the battle).
entries.meaning: So a father encourages his warrior-son.

entries.luganda: Ofubye ng'akagobera embuga : nti bwe kanaalya omwana wa beene.
entries.english: You are solicitous like one who drives a wild animal away from the chief's place : (fearing) it might eat somebody's child (the chief's).
entries.meaning: A mukopi is supposed to work for the chief's interest.

entries.luganda: Ofudde lwa nnabamba : kawumpuli lwatta omuwazi.
entries.english: You died of a contagious sickness : plague killed the tanner.
entries.meaning: The man who scraped off the fat and the meat from the inside of the cow's skin (the enkulo), did not know that the animal had perished of rinderpest. He died after eating the enkulo.

entries.english: You prefer an "ekkubi" (big bird of prey which sucks only the blood of the animal killed) to the big grey eagle, which takes the booty along.
entries.meaning: "Eddiirawamu" robs you also of the meat, whilst the "ekkubi" leaves you the carcass. - Of the two evils one chooses the lesser.

entries.english: You prefer to be with one who says "I shall sell you", rather than with one who says "I shall kill you".
entries.meaning: Being sold is the lesser evil. Life is more than freedom.

entries.english: You have become like the edible-rat of Kanyanya : once gone (escaped) it did not come back.
entries.meaning: Comparing a living person with the dead. - Kanyanya is a mutala in Busiro. -The dead do not come back.

entries.english: You are going to Mbaale to your Baganda-brethren.
entries.meaning: Mawokota is considered to be the cradle-land of the Baganda and Mbaale is its principal place.

entries.luganda: Oggye ku mutwe : otadde ku kibegabega.
entries.english: You have taken (the load) from the head and put it on the shoulder (i.e.
entries.meaning: you have made it easier; you have helped me).

entries.english: (The order) "kill it" (the cow or the goat) can only come rightly from the mouth of the owner.
You have driven the lizard into the grass (the thatch of the house).
entries.meaning: The grass is the element of the lizard. - Said of a man who has been asked about a matter in which he is well versed.

entries.english: Friendship that is lacking in mutual interests (consideration), does not last (is not solid).
(If) you become mad : (that means) you get rid of debts.
entries.meaning: There are people who feign madness to escape their debts.

entries.english: Beer that is mixed again with ferment : makes the brew tasty.
Friendship that comes to an end, no longer knows the one who started it.
entries.meaning: All the good of former days is forgotten.

entries.english: You are disputing something (muttering to yourself) : like one with sick (bleary) eyes, kindling a fire.
Fire that has a poker (stirrer), does not go out.
entries.meaning: Undertakings that have an active promoter, will develop.

entries.english: The expectation of the mubisi being tasty (pleasant to drink), encourages you to brew.

entries.luganda: Ogunaanyula : tegubuulirwa muwemba, ne bw'ossaako omungi.
entries.english: Unfermented banana-juice (mubisi) that is going to be good beer : is not influenced by muwemba (millet, added for fermentation) even if you add much of it.

entries.luganda: Ogusula gwe gukuwa empoza : nga mulungi.
entries.english: A case which is postponed (for another day) gives you a chance of defence : if it is in your favour.
entries.meaning: A hopeless case does not give you any chance, even if it is postponed. - Dutch "Nacht brengt raad".

entries.english: Work for which no payment is asked : goes with "thank you".
Work which is not a command : does not make one angry (or: is not irksome).
