Since the mubisi (banana juice) has not yet oozed out : this (fact) causes you to refrain from beating the child (if he takes and sucks a lyenvu).
entries.meaning: You don't consider it a loss.

entries.english: Friendship that prospers : can come to an end.
entries.meaning: Munno 1920 p.30. 3577 Oguzzanga ku busenze : n'otoguzza ku butaka. (omusango) You might risk committing an offence, if you are a tenant : but not if you are on your own land. A tenant can always find another place.

entries.luganda: "Ogwa gonja (= olwa gonja) teguggwe?" : nga y'alidde eky'engabo.
entries.english: "Will the affair with the gonja not come to an end?" : (says the one) who has already eaten the best part of it (ekiwango ky'engabo).
entries.meaning: The others grumble, that they have received only the smaller parts (eby'ensubi). - No consideration for others!

entries.english: A body that is clothed : does not walk naked.
entries.meaning: What is the use of worrying? You have got what is necessary.

entries.english: Old friendship : does not make you take one barkcloth (for the burial).
entries.meaning: If the friendship has died, you consider yourself free from obligations. Faith-lessness!

entries.english: Work for the chief : kills the man who refused to go.
entries.meaning: The chief will not let him live on his land.

entries.luganda: Ogw'embuga : 1) gutta ogw'obuko (ng'abakazi alina babiri); 2) tigulekeka.
entries.english: The work for the chief (communal work) : 1) comes before the work for the father-in-law (if one has two wives); 2) cannot be left alone.
The chief's beer is not drunk by him who remains at home.
entries.meaning: He must come to the mbuga; he cannot send for it.

entries.english: One who accuses another of a crime committed in the dark (without witnesses) : talks about little clouds (i.e.
Gluttony throws the rat into the beer-calabash.
entries.meaning: "Curiosity killed the cat".

entries.english: The trial of a liar never comes to an end (in arguing).
entries.meaning: He changes his statements continually.

entries.luganda: Ojaganya ng'eyakimeza okw'enjala : nti obutiko bugenda kukuloga enjala?
entries.english: You are rejoicing like one who has watched a mushroom grow in famine-time : are mushrooms going to appease your hunger?
entries.meaning: Mushrooms do not nourish. - Taking pleasure in worthless things.

entries.english: You are rejoicing, like a toothless fellow, who has found a tooth.
entries.meaning: That tooth is of no use, as he cannot fix it into his jaws.

entries.luganda: Ojjanga kwa nkuba : omusana guleeta enjala.
entries.english: Come during the rainy season!
entries.meaning: : the hot season brings famine. Come at a favourable time!

entries.english: "Come and have food with me" (he says) : and then he calls you a "miserable hungry fellow, hanging round all doorsteps".
You think of covering yourself (to go to sleep) : when the dawn is breaking.
entries.meaning: Starting work when it is too late. - Sowing when the rainy season is over.

entries.luganda: Okaabidde mu lwabya : wakasanke mu lwa mpungu.
entries.english: You wail at the mourning-rites : like the kasanke (small red finch) at the mourning for the eagle.
You become old in your body : but you are still young in your mind.
entries.meaning: Praise for an old man, who - in spite of his age - is still generous. Ssal.p.30. 3600 Okaladde : ng'akayonsa obusatu. You are furious like a little goat that suckles three young ones. She cannot suckle them fairly, because she has only two teats.

entries.english: You are (unreasonably) angry : as it is unreasonable of one who is not sick to clamour for porridge (buugi).
entries.meaning: That is food for sick people. Ssal.p.36. 3602 Okalya dda : kadda dda.

entries.english: You are a sour fellow : like freshly peeled mbidde (beer-bananas).
entries.meaning: They contain a lot of bitter sap. - Said of an unlikable character.

entries.english: You are the limit : you cook (for your husband) only a tiny bit in the evening!
(ebiriba) You are difficult (crooked, stubborn) : like cow-hides on which tobacco is dried (in the sun).
entries.meaning: They turn up at the edges.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'afumba ekiro : nti ssebo tunaaliira mulyango.
entries.english: You are talking (nonsense) like a woman cooking late in the evening : (saying) ssebo we can eat in the doorway (in the moonlight).
entries.meaning: The husband purposely misunderstands "mulya-ngo" (leopard) and asks: and in daytime you eat "lion" (mulya-mpologoma).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'afumba obutooke obuto : nti ewaffe tulya ga bisiisa.
entries.english: You are talking (nonsense) like one cooking unripe bananas : (saying) at home we eat caterpillars.
entries.meaning: "Bisiisa" has two meanings: "unripe bananas" and "caterpillars". Therefore she gets the answer: "Ffe tulya ga ssekesa" (we eat centipedes).

entries.luganda: Okekkera nga agula endiga (= ente), nti yaswala amagulu.
entries.english: You are talking like a man who buys a sheep (cow) and complains about its ugly legs.
entries.meaning: We might ask: Is the animal meant for stamping budongo (mortar) or for treading mwenge?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'agula nnandere : nti taliimu maaso; k'oli nti ogula wa kukuuma waka?
entries.english: You talk nonsense like one who buys a "nnandere" (small fish in Lake Kyoga), saying: but it has no eyes!
entries.meaning: ; (reply) do you buy it for watching your house (in your absence)? If these fish are kept for long, nnyenje or rats might eat their eyes; a sign that they are not fresh.

entries.luganda: Okekkera nga muk'omugoma; nti ow'omwange leero agireese n'amayembe gaayo?
entries.english: Are you joking like a drummaker's wife, who says: Oh today my husband has brought his fare with the horns on?
entries.meaning: When cattle were killed in the lubiri (king's enclosure), the drummers were given the heads and the women greeted their husbands with this joke.

entries.luganda: Okekkera nga nnakawere omuli w'omunnyo : nti nnawonyezza "kigongo".
entries.english: You are talking like a mother whose newly born child has died, because the mother has taken salt during her pregnancy, saying: I have saved my kigongo (my life).
entries.meaning: The others hearing her, interpret "kigongo" as "fillet" (piece from the cow's back) and say: Give us to eat of that piece!

entries.luganda: Okekkera nga nnakyeyombekedde asima kandi : nti kuliko nsajjalala; nti ekiku-suza wekka mu nju, ng'abasajja ball mu ttaka kiki?
entries.english: You are talking like a spinster digging up kandi (kind of yam) and saying: there are tasteless ones among them; (sarcasm) why do you live alone in your house, if there are men in your soil?
entries.meaning: "Lusajjalala" has two meanings: 1) tasteless, inedible yam; 2) manikin, miserable specimen of a man.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ava eri omulwadde, nti twasuze ku bugubi.
entries.english: You are exaggerating like one who comes from visiting a sick person, saying: we have stayed with him till the cry of the quails (early morning).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'eyeekubye ekigere : nti simanyi kye kinanviiramu.
entries.english: You are talking nonsense like one who has hurt his toe and says: I do not know what will come out of it (i.e.
entries.meaning: what harm will come of it). The other interprets "kinanviiramu" as "what profit shall I get out of it" and says therefore: will 5 cents be enough for you?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omufumite : nti omusaayi gupnenze munda; bulijjo gubeera wa?
entries.english: You are talking like one who has been speared : (saying) my blood is flowing into my body; (answer) where is it otherwise?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omugemuzi agamba, nti enkukunyi zampaatidde ku kibuga.
entries.english: You stretch a point like one who has taken victuals to the bbooma and says: the fleas have attacked me in the chief's place.
entries.meaning: Reply: but the katikkiro who is always there probably will be eaten by them in the skin (empogola). Play of words: "okuwaata" means either "to attack" or "to peel bananas".

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omukazi agamba, nti emmanga eyo tekyayita kambe.
entries.english: You are talking like a woman, saying: down there (in the lusuku) a knife cuts no more (matooke) (i.e.
entries.meaning: there is no ttooke left). Reply: perhaps an axe might serve! (insinuating her laziness in cleaning her lusuku).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omukazi omuzadde : omwana bw'akaaba, nti bwandu bwe bumu-kaabya.
entries.english: You are talking like a mother, whose son is crying (saying) : it is stomach-ache that makes him cry.
entries.meaning: Sarcastic answer: the king has also a big mwandu (harem), does he cry all day? - Mwandu means "stomach-ache" or "harem".

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omulimi w'empindi agamba, nti empindi zange zali ziri matuba, ennyonyi zizirya.
entries.english: You are exaggerating like a planter of beans, saying: my beans over there are as big as figs and the birds feed on them.
entries.meaning: Reply: and your maize-plants are probably like muvule trees!

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omukunku eyeekoonye : nti ekigere nkimazeewo; nti kyakume-zeeko ggulo?
entries.english: You are talking like one without toes who has stumbled : (and says) I have ruined my toe!; (sarcastic answer) has it (the toe) just grown this evening?
entries.meaning: (formerly you had no toes).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omulwadde agamba, nti kasookedde ndwala siryanga "ka mu ntamu" wabula obusera bwe nnawuseeko eggulo bwokka.
entries.english: You are exaggerating like a sick person (complaining) : since I have been sick, I have not eaten anything cooked in a cooking pot; I have sipped only a little porridge in the evening.
entries.meaning: Answer: was that cooked in a snail's shell?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omulwadde anywa taba : nti kasooka ndwala siriimu mukka.
entries.english: You talk (nonsense) like a sick man who is smoking : (saying) since I fell sick, I have no breath.
entries.meaning: Reply: but what is that you are puffing out of your pipe? - Play of words: "mukka" means "breath" or "smoke".

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omulwadde nti lulinzita nga lummazeemu amaanyi.
entries.english: You are talking like a sick person who says: the sickness will kill me as my strength is finished.
entries.meaning: Reply: What do you want strength for in the underworld? Do you expect to build down there?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omulwadde nti olumbe lwanzimba munda.
entries.english: You are talking (nonsense) like a sick person : (saying) the sickness caused a swelling inside my body.
entries.meaning: Question: Has the sickness gone cutting poles and elephant-grass-stalks? - Mis-interpreting the word "kuzimba": "to swell up" and "to build" (tonal difference only!).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'Omunaawa : nti Kabaka yandeka nga ndi Mugongo; nti kaakano oli muluusi?
entries.english: You are talking like a certain Munaawa (Muganda of Mawokota) saying: When the king died, I was at Mugongo (place on the Masaka road); (the other under-stands: I was a mugongo (female animal bearing), and asks) and now you are a muluusi (animal not yet bearing)?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'Omunnabuyaga : nti leero Kajeerero ali Nkira, nti edda ggwe wamukiranga?
entries.english: You are talking (nonsense) like a man from Buyaga (county) saying: Today the Kajeerero (chief) lives at Nkira (place); (reply) have you formerly surpassed him?
entries.meaning: Misunderstanding the expression: "ali Nkira" (he lives at Nkira), and inter-preting it as "alinkira" (he will surpass me).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'Omunyolo : nti okulya enkolo, ndya lumonde; nti enkolo, nga lumonde gw'olabye?
entries.english: You talk like a Munyoro (Muyima) who says: I should prefer to eat potatoes, rather than banana-stumps; (reply) where you eat banana-stumps do you find any potatoes?
entries.meaning: Banana-stumps are only famine food; therefore where you see people eating them, you can be sure potatoes are no longer there. Engl. "Castles in the air".

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'Omunyolo y'afa : nti mwoyo gundi ku mbuga.
entries.english: You are talking (speaking bad Luganda) like a Munyoro who is dying and complains : my heart is in the chief's place.
entries.meaning: He wants to say: "mwoyo gumbuga" = my heart is oppressed.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'Omuyima (= Omulaalo) : nti nnalidde enjuba; nti eyiyo eri munda?
entries.english: You are talking like a Muyima (herdsman) saying: I have eaten the "njuba"; (reply) oh!
entries.meaning: your sun then is inside the body! In Luganda "njuba" means "sun"; in Luyima it means "blood cooked from the lancing of a cow".

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'Omuzungu : ndiyo; nti wabuna nsi?
entries.english: You talk nonsense like a White man, constantly saying "ndiyo"; are you all over the place?
entries.meaning: "Ndiyo" means "yes" in Kiswahili, but "I am there" in Luganda.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'omwavu gwe bakwatira ku kibuga : nti singa bantadde ndaba omugagga mu kyalo, mmugwako.
entries.english: You are talking like a poor man they have caught in the town (without musolo-ticket) : (saying) if they would let me free, I would go and see a rich man in the village and beseech him to help me.
entries.meaning: Reply: Are there no rich men here in the kibuga? e.g. the Prime Minister?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ebbango, nti bwe nnatuuka, nnagwa bugazi.
entries.english: You are talking like a hunchback, saying: when I arrived, I fell on my back.
entries.meaning: He could not very well remain lying on his hump!

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ebikaata ava embuga : nti tukutte mu gabuguma.
entries.english: You are talking like one with syphilitic hands, coming from the chief's place and saying: we got hold of some hot things (hot meat).
entries.meaning: Answer: Evidently! your hands prove it!

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ejjanga abika, nti gundi yafa : nti naffe tulabye bw'okaaba.
entries.english: You are talking like one with inflamed eyes, bringing a death notice, So and so died : (reply) we also see how you are weeping.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ekirevu akuma omuliro : nti bampeeyo essubi nkume omuliro; nti eryo lyonna erikuli ku mumwa?
entries.english: You are talking like a bearded fellow lighting a fire and saying: let them give me some dry grass, that I may light the fire!
entries.meaning: ; (reply) what about all that growth round your mouth?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ekiwalaata abika : nti olumbe lwanjera (= lwatwera) ekyenyi; nti naffe tulaba bwe kikutte e Bule ne Bweya.
entries.english: (kyenyi) You are talking like a man with a bald head, bringing a death notice, (saying) this bereavement has swept off all my hair; (reply) we also see that your fore-head extends from Bule to Bweya (two places in Butambala, very distant from each other).

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ekiwalaata akka (= akkirira) ekibira : nti munterekera ku butta; nti tunaabuseera wa omaze okugenda n'olubengo?
entries.english: You are talking like a bald fellow who goes down to the forest and says: keep some porridge for me!
entries.meaning: ; (answer) how shall we grind the flour, if you take the grinding stone (the bald head) with you?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ekiwalaata alabye engo, nti bwe ndabye ensolo, enviiri ne zinva ku mutwe.
entries.english: You are talking like one with a bald head who saw a leopard and says: when I saw the animal all the hair came off my head.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ekiwalaata : nti ekimmalako abaana sikimanyi; nti kyo ekya-kumalako enviiri wakiraba?
entries.english: You are talking like one with a bald head, saying: I don't know what finished off all my children!
entries.meaning: ; (reply) did you ever see what finished off the hair (on your head)?

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'ennungu eyalya obwa-Mukwenda : nti obuyinja bunnyiga (= bunkosa); nti va mu Mityana (= bwa-Mukwenda), ogende (= olye) Buyinja.
entries.english: You are complaining without reason, like the man with syphilitic cracks on his feet, who became Mukwenda (big chief of Ssingo) and said: the pebbles (on the road) hurt me; (reply) leave Mityana (capital of Ssingo) and go to Buyinja (mutala in Ssingo).
entries.meaning: Deliberate misunderstanding "buyinja" and talking about the place Buyinja. Being chief of Buyinja he will have power over the "buyinja".

entries.english: You are talking like one with a skin-disease in Kyaggwe (i.e.
entries.meaning: scratching your-self). In Kyaggwe there is the embwa-fly which bites severely.

entries.luganda: Okekkera ng'ow'oluwumu ayombera embuga, nti tuva kusasambuka n'omwami.
entries.english: You are talking (in a double sense) like one with ringworm quarreling in the chief's place, saying: we are coming from a quarrel with the chief.
entries.meaning: "Kusasambuka" means "quarreling" or "peeling off" (in the ringworm the skin scales off).

entries.luganda: Okekkera, nti amannyo galiko emmere; nti gatema mmuli?
entries.english: You are talking (nonsense) like one who says: there is food on your teeth (they are not clean); (retort) what are the teeth for?
entries.meaning: perhaps for cutting reeds?

entries.english: You have grown thin : like one who is too stingy to eat his own produce.
You are walking with a protruding chest (stuck out) like an ensejjere termite, when it enters a head-pad (lying on the ground).
You are fooling like a night-wizard who argues, saying: my calabash ought to be full (i.e.
entries.meaning: give me more beer). Reply: Do you not trample down the bitooke during your night dances? And you expect us to give you more beer?

entries.english: Leave the kibanja there and do not uselessly covet (what you did not plant).
entries.meaning: Admonition to go on cultivating, even if you intend to leave your place. You might not leave, after all, and then you would have nothing to eat.

entries.english: You are mistaken : a peasant does not eat ttooke mbidde in Kabula (ssaza).
entries.meaning: During the persecution under Mwanga the Christians fled to Kabula, where ma-tooke were a rare treat (for chiefs only). "Okirimbire" then became a name "Kirimbire" for Yozefu Nsingisira, a former Ssaza-chief of Buvuma, later a chief in Buddu (Katabalwa), from whom the above expression originally came.

entries.english: You are tired of the past times : now you pray whilst lying down.
entries.meaning: You have ceased practising Christian religion and practise traditional worship.

entries.luganda: Okembye mu kya kkobe : eky'ettungulu kiwoomerera.
entries.english: (kikuta) You have licked at the peel of the kkobe-fruit : the skin of the forest-onion is therefore sweet to your taste.
entries.meaning: You won't be able to do it (= oteganira bwereere).

entries.english: You plucked off the jjobyo-plant (vegetable) which are plucked already.
entries.meaning: You try to do a job that is done already.

entries.english: You have hit the wooden trough (lying outside the house) : that means alarm for the bat.
entries.meaning: I am warned, I know what your intention is.

entries.luganda: Okoosekoose mu ga lumonde : anti tegamalako maviivi.
entries.english: You walk stooping in the potato leaves (field) : they don't reach even to your knees.
entries.meaning: You try in vain to hide yourself. Your excuses are of no use.

entries.luganda: Okuba kalakya : omwavu akakuba ku mmamba.
entries.english: You attempt the impossible : like the poor man trying to buy a lungfish.
Are you playing about without ever finishing?
entries.meaning: Said to one who works leisurely and never comes to an end.

entries.english: To be as easy (it is as easy) as it is for a sickness to kill a one-eyed person.
entries.meaning: It need only destroy the other eye, as one is dead already. - Said of a thing which presents no difficulty.

entries.luganda: Okubeera ku lusozi : ne weeyama olusozi.
entries.english: (That is like) living on a hill, whilst you decry the hill.
entries.meaning: To declare one's dislike for something and still like it.

entries.luganda: Okubuga : ng'omugenyi atakkuse; nti n'abakadde ab'enunanga nnaabasiibula.
entries.english: To be importunate like a visitor who did not get enough to eat; he says: I have to say good-bye also to the old people down there.
entries.meaning: He hopes to find them eating and be invited to partake.

entries.english: Stammering like a he-goat.

entries.luganda: Okubula obuwolezo : butta abaana ba wamusu.
entries.english: To have no defence kills the young of the (edible) rat.
entries.meaning: These animals are tracked by the young shoots they have nibbled off and are killed; but nobody defends them. - Applied to people who are without witnesses for their innocence.

entries.english: To be without child : means to help oneself.
entries.meaning: Such a woman has to do her work without being helped by children.

entries.english: A question is not an accusation.

entries.luganda: Okubwesooka si kubulya : 1 ) singa empampagama y'etta enswa; 2) ebigere ebi-sooka ku buliri biba mirannamiro.
entries.english: To be first as tenant does not mean necessarily that one gets a chieftainship (obwassabaddu) (another might come after him and get it) : 1) otherwise the natural cavity in an anthill would gather the flying ants (and not the nvubo which was made later); 2) (because), although the feet are first put down on the bed (and not the head), their place is at the foot of the bed.
You have beaten on it with too small a stick (i.e.
entries.meaning: you try in vain) : like one who has only stumps instead of fingers, trying to get hold of an "empomero" (calabash without neck for storing butter).

entries.english: To clean one's lips : like one who pronounces (shouts) the word "baffe" (peculiar movement of the lips).

entries.luganda: Okuddinnanibwako si kwagalana : singa essanja tiribabula lulagala.
entries.english: To follow each other (in age) does not necessarily mean to love each other : otherwise the dry banana-leaf would not singe the green one (the dry banana leaf is older than the green one).
(That is like) giving to the "kaneene" (otterlike animal) nsonzi (small fish) (something that looks like magnanimity).

entries.luganda: Okuddiza guba mwoyo : 1) omukazi omunafu asala ku lusuku lwe n'addiza ensiko; 2) emigga giddiza ennyanja; 3) n'owuwo akumma.
entries.english: To give something without being asked (a gift, food, drink) is a sign of appre-ciation (love, sacrifice, noble spirit, generosity) : 1) the lazy woman cuts off a part of her bananary and gives it back to the wilderness (sarcasm!); 2) the rivers give their water to the lake (although there is plenty of it there); 3) and your own relation refuses (outsiders are often more generous than one's own kin).
To run away (unconcerned about anybody else) like a wild animal that has no young.

entries.luganda: Okufa si ppombo : nti eridiba (= nti eridiba mangu).
entries.english: Dying is not just a fashion (about which you might say) it soon will fall into disuse.
entries.meaning: "It is appointed unto all men to die" (Hebr.9.27). Germ. "Gegen den Tod ist kein Krautlein gewachsen".

entries.english: To lose both the spittle and the sneeze.
entries.meaning: To add a second evil to the first; to make matters worse.

entries.english: To be generous is not easy : generosity reveals a noble mind.
To give is to lay up for oneself.
To take a rest like freshly cut firewood.
entries.meaning: Such wood is cut whilst still green; then it is left lying till it is dry; finally it is broken up and taken home.

entries.english: To rush off in a panic : as a person does who has laid out tobacco to dry (when rain starts suddenly).
To disappear unnoticed like hunger (famine).
entries.meaning: Hunger and famine disappear without much ado.

entries.luganda: Okuggya si kuzzaayo : kitaawo bw'afa tozzawo mulala.
entries.english: Taking away is not putting back again : if your father dies, you can't put an-other one in his place.

entries.luganda: Okuggwa enkuuka : ng'omusezi ly'aggwa mu lutabaalo.
entries.english: To come to a definite (complete) end : as the night-wizard comes to in the battle.
entries.meaning: When he is killed, nothing can be inherited.

entries.luganda: Okugwa ettente : ng'omukulu omukwate ku kutu.
entries.english: To lose one's dignity : like an old man (person of standing) whose ear is grasped.
entries.meaning: To get hold of somebody's ear is considered as very familiar - an impossible act with a person of respect. Therefore the expression "munkwatire ku ntanyenya" (= mundabire) can only be used for two very intimate persons.

entries.english: To breathe painfully : like a consumptive person who has not had enough potatoes.
entries.meaning: He can hardly say the full word "lumonde", when he asks for more.

entries.english: Loud wailing does not restore to life.
entries.meaning: "It is no use crying over spilt milk".

entries.english: To be doubled up (walking stoopingly) : like one who carries unbaked pots (from place to place).
entries.meaning: He holds them carefully in front of him, stooping, whilst he walks.

entries.luganda: Okukizza munda : ng'akaabira eddiba ly'enjobe; nti eddiba lyange litobye ebi-renge ; nti anti mu mazzi mw'ekulidde.
entries.english: To draw in the breath (as sign of astonishment or disappointment) like one who complains about the skin of the marsh-antelope (his garment), saying: the fringes of my antelope skin got wet; (answer) but that skin has grown in the water (when it was on the antelope!).

entries.luganda: Okukuba akalali ak'engalabi eseka n'enti mu mubiri.
entries.english: To burst out laughing : like the engalabi drum that laughs with the pegs in its body.

entries.luganda: Okukuba embukutiro : 1) omwavu z'akuba omugagga; 2) omukadde z'akuba omuyaiyu, nti gulya kabi ki?
entries.english: To pay attention (or to look forward eagerly to) : 1) as the poor man does to the rich man; 2) as an old man does to the (meat of a) wild cat, (saying) what bad things does it eat?

entries.luganda: Okukuba engulegule : omusezi z'akuba ku ndeku; nti waseranga mu bya nkago, ebya mbidde bye walekanga!
entries.english: To examine tentatively (by striking the knuckles of the finger on an empty vessel or feeling with the palm of the hand over something covered) : as the night-wizard does on the beer calabash (asking: is there no beer left?); (reply) when you were dancing at night among the food-bananas, did you leave the beer-bananas unharmed?
entries.meaning: You have destroyed the bananas and now you want beer from us!

entries.english: To beat a child : is not to hate it.
entries.meaning: Engl. "Spare the rod and spoil the child". "A father who spares the rod hates his son" (Prov.13.24).

entries.luganda: Okukubiira ensingo (= essingo) : ng'ow'ettulu alamusa abangi (= abasatu).
entries.english: To turn the head constantly : like a one-eyed man greeting many (or: three persons).

entries.luganda: Okukulabako : ndabye ku muzi gwa jjinja.
entries.english: Seeing you is (like) seeing the root of a stone.
entries.meaning: A stone has no roots; I never have the pleasure of seeing you.

entries.english: To roll saliva round the mouth (to talk nonsense, to jabber) : like the termite in the hot season.

entries.luganda: Okukuma ekkungu : omubootongo ly'akuma mu luggi.
entries.english: To heap up (swell) one's importance : as the syphilitic appears to do, when sitting in the doorway.
entries.meaning: Everybody tries to avoid him.

entries.english: To guard the barkcloth-curtain : when the spirit is away.
entries.meaning: The spirit was supposed to be hidden behind the curtain. - To wait for nothing.

entries.english: To get hold of the wrist of the father (to prevent him from doing what he intends to do).
Fortune-telling leads to practising witchcraft (and murder).
To greet in a friendly manner at your friend's home is no special sign of kind-ness.
entries.meaning: Everybody does that. "N'abakafiiri si bwe bakola?" (Matt.5.47).

entries.english: To act in the manner of a rhinoceros (namely to attack straightforwardly) : the buffalo goes treacherously round about.
entries.meaning: Honest anger - cunning revenge; open attack - treacherous ambush.

entries.english: To rattle off a message : like one who brings the death-notice of somebody who is not his relation.
You are strutting : like a hunchback with a load of calabashes.
entries.meaning: You are "putting on airs".

entries.english: To make the shield break its teeth, make it unfit for the fight.
entries.meaning: Expression used for "kugaana" (to refuse to obey).

entries.english: You are circumspect : like a rat gnawing at a food parcel (of entungo, binyee-bwa etc.).
You are very careful (not bumping against anybody) : like a warrior who has been stealing eggs.
You are moulding your lump of matooke : as if your teeth were not able to split it.
To stay a long time in Buddu : means contracting malaria.
entries.meaning: Used as an excuse for hurrying up - I can't stay longer.

entries.english: To stay long with your relations in law : means getting pigeons (instead of chickens).
entries.meaning: Because you have finished off the latter.

entries.luganda: Okulwa ku kyalo : 1) si kukimanya; 2) kukumanyisa enkuba gy'efuluma.
entries.english: To live long in a village : 1) does not always mean knowing it; 2) teaches you where the rain comes from.

entries.luganda: Okulwa ku luggya : kukulabisa entumbwe za ssezaala wo bwe zaaswala.
entries.english: To linger in the compound of your in-laws makes you see the calves of your father-in-law in a way that embarrasses him.
entries.meaning: One sees too much. - Too great familiarity etc.

entries.english: If one has not been in the war for a long time : he starts building grass huts with a special (complicated) roof (not bending the "mikwero" towards the middle).
entries.meaning: Such is useless trouble as the warriors might have to leave to-morrow.

entries.english: If the marriage has lasted for a long time : it makes you ask your wife for a (roasted) banana.
entries.meaning: In the beginning you were given it without asking. - Love cooled down.

entries.english: Waiting a long time : makes the swelling ripen (a syphilitic swelling on the wrist).
To tear one's good name to pieces : as the vulture does with the dead body.
To pocket the ransom and the object of the ransom.
entries.meaning: To take the money for the upkeep of a child and then claiming the child. - To take the price from the buyer and the purchased article.

entries.luganda: Okulya ennyingi si kugejja : singa enkoko yenkana nte.
entries.english: To eat much does not mean to get fat : otherwise the hen would look as big as a cow (because it eats all day long).
To eat much meat : does not end desire.
entries.meaning: Lust comes back undiminished. Otherwise an old man would have had enough sleep in his long life. Goethe: "Von Begierde taumle ich zum Genuss; Und im Genuss verschmacht' ich vor Begierde".

entries.english: To eat much : does not make the shin of the hen fatter.
You can come to eat : (but after that) please go!
entries.meaning: Said to a visitor who might upset the household, daughters etc.

entries.english: You can keep a male dog from trouble : but not a bitch.
entries.meaning: It is easier to keep a boy from harm than a girl. If the girl misbehaves, she might come home pregnant.

entries.english: To bite your beard : do you call that food?
entries.meaning: They call the old man to come for food; but he is silent and refuses to come.

entries.english: To keep an eye on him : as the squinter does on one who is hidden.
entries.meaning: The hidden person does not know, whether the squinter looks on him or in another direction.

entries.luganda: Okumyuka amaaso : si buzira; omukazi endegeya agobya ffunfugu.
entries.english: Red eyes are not a sign of courage : because even a woman can drive away weaver birds with a lump of soil.
entries.meaning: Weaver birds have red eyes. French "L'apparence trompe".

entries.english: Returning, you speak admiringly (or enviously) about the things you have seen on your visit : but you don't do so whilst going there.

entries.luganda: Okunguyidde ng'ey'omuluvu : w'alaba akalengejja n'akakutulako n'alya.
entries.english: You are deprived of all relations : like a chunk (bone) of meat in the hands of a glutton; where a little piece (of meat) still hangs on, he bites it off and eats it.
You don't reach (fit) at all : like a pipe held (in the hands) together with a spear (on either side too short).
entries.meaning: You are dressed very badly.

entries.english: To make vain excuses : like one who does not want to make blood-brother-hood.
entries.meaning: To avoid the ceremony, he says: "I have eaten", because they used to eat only after the ceremony.

entries.luganda: Okuusakuusa nga anaakwokya : nti siigawo evvu.
entries.english: You are hypocritical : like a musawo who is going to burn you with an awl (hot iron), ordering you: smear ashes on (to deaden the pain).

entries.luganda: Okusekera mu bikonde : nga asikidde omugagga.
entries.english: To laugh into one's fists : as one laughs who has become heir to a rich man.
entries.meaning: One who becomes heir upon the death of a rich man, may not laugh openly; so he has to cover his mouth, when he is tempted to laugh. - Germ. "Sich ins Fdustchen lachen".

entries.luganda: Okusigalawo kuzirinda : ng'omwana w'omufu y'asabye lubugo.
entries.english: To be kept waiting (for what has been asked) : like the child of the dead father, when it asks for a barkcloth.
entries.meaning: It is given grudgingly, because there was no real friendship with the father.

entries.english: To sprinkle flour on water (to do something useless).
entries.meaning: It all flows away. M.711. 3782 Okusooba si kubba. (cf. Okusoonooka: 3783) To walk stealthily does not mean to steal.

entries.luganda: Okusoonooka si kubba : singa nnawolovu amaze ebintu (= amazeeko abakazi enkumbi).
entries.english: To walk stealthily does not mean to steal : otherwise the chameleon would have finished off everything (or: would have stolen all the hoes from the women).
To walk without purpose : (means that) anyone who meets you abuses you (makes fun of you).
To teach an idiot : you first open his ears.
entries.meaning: To be successful in an undertaking you first remove the obstacles.

entries.luganda: Okutengejja : ng'asaba oluwanga obulamu; nti oyo teyafa lumbe?
entries.english: To do a useless thing : like one who asks life (health) from a skull (jaw-bone); did he (to whom the jaw-bone belonged) not die himself (and prove thereby to be helpless against death)?
entries.meaning: Skulls and jaw-bones of ancestors were decorated and invoked.

entries.english: To use strength : like one who throttles a madman.
To kill all en masse : as the dog eats eggs.
entries.meaning: He cannot bite off pieces, but destroys the whole egg, breaking it in his mouth. - Used for wholesale destruction of an army, of families etc.

entries.english: You have the guinea-fowl in your hands : (and now) you grumble about the (little) pigeon?
entries.meaning: You are never satisfied.

entries.english: To sit waiting for a long time : like the one who mourned over Nnamumwa (a legendary person, who remained unburied for many days).

entries.luganda: Okutuula ekisajja ekikulu : embwa ky'etuula mu lumbe lw'ente.
entries.english: To sit there with the air of an important old man : as the dog sits at the slaugh-tering of a cow.
To glitter : like pearls (found on the road).

entries.luganda: Okutya okusekwa : omwana tayambala lugoye lwa kitaawe.
entries.english: For fear of being laughed at : the child does not put on the garment of his father.
entries.meaning: Behave as befits your age and position!

entries.english: To argue with a lubaale-man : does not blister your lips.
entries.meaning: By arguing you make him confirm his statements.

entries.english: In the long run the ensejjere-termite (flying ant, remaining long in the same anthill) buys a slave.
entries.meaning: As the people take torches to catch the ensejjere, flying after midnight, it looks, as if men had to provide light for their swarming.

entries.luganda: Okuwera enkolokooto ey'omuvumbuzi w'amawolu : ky'ajje avumbule, ng'akuba mu ngalo; nti abanaagalya banaakuba mpina?
entries.english: To show eagerness as one does who has dug out matooke, put into the hot ashes the previous night : hardly has he dug them out than he claps his hands (beating off the ashes from his fingers); (therefore they ask him) will those who are going to eat them, start dancing to your beating?

entries.luganda: Okuwonga okungi : si kuzza lubaale (= si kuwuliza lubaale).
entries.english: Many offerings : do not propitiate the deity.
entries.meaning: The sick person dies all the same.

entries.english: To plead (to defend oneself) does not chip off the teeth.
entries.meaning: Everybody has a right to defend himself. - Lat. "Audiatur et altera pars".

entries.english: Resting is not attaining.
entries.meaning: Engl. "No pains, no gains" Germ. "Rast' ich, rose ich".

entries.english: To answer "wangi" : is not slavery.
entries.meaning: Respectful obedience is good manners also towards those who are not our superiors. Rowl.Guide 90 explains: "does not always mean readiness to obey".

entries.english: To pass on top (to be superficial) : like a swimmer.
Passing just to see (not to eat) : like the toothless person who found them having (eating) yams.
entries.meaning: They are too tough for him.

entries.english: To quarrel with great anger : as one quarrels with a man with whom friendship has died (dried up).
Letting the cow calve is better than killing it.
entries.meaning: It is more profitable to till the land than to sell it. - "You can't eat the cake and have it".

entries.english: To bring forth children is good : if you see them about you.
entries.meaning: If they remain alive; but if they die, one after the other, it means sorrows.

entries.english: To cause dissatisfaction : as the parent does who deals out sprats.
entries.meaning: He gives one child a big one, the other a small one, appearing to be partial.

entries.english: Love eats the understanding.
entries.meaning: Engl. "Love is blind". "Love is a furnace, but it won't cook the stew".

entries.luganda: Okwambala bulungi si kuwasa bawala : singa akasanke kamaze abawala mu nsi.
entries.english: Dressing well does not mean marrying girls : otherwise the little red finch would have finished all the girls on earth.

entries.luganda: Okwasaamirira si kumira : singa eŋŋaaŋa emira bugobo.
entries.english: Keeping the mouth open does not mean swallowing : otherwise the horn-bill would swallow food unchewed.
To sneeze : like one who takes snuff.

entries.luganda: Okwebaka kufa : ye asiba oluggi (= y'akomeka oluggi).
entries.english: Sleep is death (to the outer world) : therefore he locks the door.
entries.meaning: He does not want to be disturbed.

entries.luganda: Okwefetta ng'omukazi omunafu : nti "baze bw'alinvuma, ka ne nzita emiko-no" ; sooka otte enjoka ezirya amatooke.
entries.english: To talk nonsense like a lazy woman : (saying) "If my husband is going to abuse me, I shall stop working (in the lusuku)"; (sarcastic answer) better first stop your appetite for matooke!
entries.meaning: If you want to stop cultivating, you must first stop hunger, as you will have nothing to eat.

entries.luganda: Okwegaana mulanga : endiga ndege, ente kide, embwa kyuma, embuzi mujugo.
entries.english: To refuse a request absolutely : as the sheep refuses the neck-bells, the cow its bell, the dog the iron(bell) and the goat its neck-pieces (i.e.

entries.luganda: Okwegendereza ng'eyafumbirwa wa mayuuga : bw'alaba ekkonkomi, ng'aga-mba nti anaaba ssezaaIa wange.
entries.english: You are careful, like a woman married to a man with broad jaws : if she sees a large lizard, she says: that will be my father-in-law (i.e.

entries.luganda: Okweggala si magezi : emirembe giva e mbuga.
entries.english: To shut oneself up is not wisdom : peace comes from the chief's place.
entries.meaning: To bury grief is not wise : peace comes from the heart.

entries.english: Buying is better than stealing.

entries.luganda: Okwekobereza : ng'afumbye gonja, nti lyako abiriridde.
entries.english: To make excuses : as the woman does, when she has cooked gonja (instead of matooke, saying) eat, it is soft.
entries.meaning: Gonja is not appreciated, because it only becomes soft when soaked in water.

entries.english: To relish one's idleness : like a slave-girl who has been given disposal of the whole house (in the absence of her mistress).
To rumble ominously : like the rain clouds in the dry season.

entries.luganda: Okwerinda si buti : ensanafu etambula egaludde (= eteze).
entries.english: Caution is not fear : the red ant travels with the mandibles raised.
entries.meaning: Engl. "Discretion is the better part of valour". Ital. "Chi va piano, va sano e va lontano". Germ. "Vorsicht ist besser denn Nachsicht".

entries.english: To play straightforwards as in playing a flute : a hornblower blows sidewards.
To keep at a distance : like the little toe of a dog.
To exert oneself uselessly : like an underdone potato.
entries.meaning: Further cooking will not make it soft.

entries.english: To worry oneself to death about something that does not worry about you : as the storm does on a rock.
entries.meaning: It does not make the slightest impression. - Engl. "Water on a duck's back".

entries.english: To listen attentively : as one does when tuning a harp (turning the pegs).
entries.meaning: M.737, 57.12. 3855 Okweyagaagula : ng'ow'ensimbu atabaala. (cf. Weeyagaagula: 5342) To take a risk : as when an epileptic goes to war.

entries.luganda: Okweyisaako : ng'omwavu agamba, nti kiki ekinnuma?
entries.english: To avoid the point : as the beggar does, when he says: what is biting me?
entries.meaning: Reply: Perhaps the fleas in your rags!

entries.luganda: Okwezza ennyuma ng'ensama : yenkana nte, esuula nkiringi.
entries.english: To have broad hindquarters like an ensama (water-buck) : they are as broad as a cow's, but produce only goats' dung.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus" (Horace).

entries.luganda: Okwogera endibattiriro ey'omuyizzi : nti mala okunaaza omusu ojje onkulu-buute ku bigere; nti omusu gwe mba nnaaza, ggwe baze gwe mba nkulubuuta.
entries.english: To talk in a muddle like a hunter (who says to his wife) : first wash the edible rat (I have brought); then come and rub my feet; (the wife answers laughingly) oh, it is the musu I am to wash carefully and you, my husband, I am to rub only?

entries.luganda: Okwogera nnyo si kulya bwami : singa ennyonza erina obwami.
entries.english: Much talking does not mean receiving a chieftainship : otherwise the robin-chat (bird) would have one.

entries.luganda: Okwogerera waggulu si kitiibwa : singa eŋŋaaŋa ye kabaka w'ennyonyi.
entries.english: To shout is not to receive honour : otherwise the hornbill would be the king of birds.
That is selfconsciousness : as a bearded man is selfconscious about the spittle dried up in his beard.
entries.meaning: He remains sitting in the hope that it won't be noticed.

entries.english: That is now a really good laugh : the nose has done it to me.
entries.meaning: The laughter (of mine) was so great that (only) my nose saved me. - The nose prevented the mouth from stretching to the forehead.

entries.english: You are irritating when visiting : like a beerfly.
entries.meaning: It comes back so often as to be unwelcome.

entries.luganda: Olaba eyagenze n'ebyayi ng'adda n'olutala : ng'akatale keetuuze.
entries.english: If you see one who went (to the market) with plantain-fibres (for sale) going away with a load of salt : then the market(ing) is upset.
entries.meaning: He has probably stolen the salt, because the proceeds from the fibre could not have paid for the salt.

entries.luganda: Olaba lulema yalukedde : nga ggwe atandise mu ttuntu onoolukola otya?
entries.english: If you see that the lubimbi (piece of one-day's cultivation) is too much for one who started early : how will you, who has started only at midday, manage it?

entries.luganda: Olaba nnasswi akulembedde : nti Obuganda mirembe?
entries.english: If you see the little finger in front (on the spearshaft) : will Buganda be at peace?
entries.meaning: Brandishing the spear one holds the little finger foremost on the shaft; when that finger leads there is trouble (war) on. The little finger is called "mukulu".

entries.luganda: Olaba omugenge nga yeeyuna ettu : ng'engalo kw'asigalako ensajja.
entries.english: When you see a leper eagerly opening up a foodparcel : you know he has still a thumb on his hand.
entries.meaning: If he hadn't, he could not do it. Rub.C.466. 3873 Olaba omukulu afungiza (= adduka) : nga ky'agoba kiriibwa. (cf. Bw'olaba: 1094) M.739, Ssal.p.39.

entries.english: You are careless (thoughtless) : like one who spears what cannot be eaten (e.g.

entries.luganda: Olejjalejja : nga baakwaluza mukalo gwa ndegeya.
entries.english: You are talking incessantly : as if, at your "name-giving ceremony", they had used dried endegeya-meat (instead of enkejje).
entries.meaning: The weaver-birds make a great noise; but fishes are silent. Duta 250. 3879 Olekeredde afuluuta n'osoya enju. (cf. Otabaala ng'alekerera: 4568) Rub.C.798.

entries.luganda: Oleese mawano : ng'atadde emmindi ku kamwa.
entries.english: You have brought evil forebodings : like a person putting his pipe into his mouth (to blow smoke in the direction of somebody, to harm him).
(also: Olidde ka bulanga : omwana wa boowo k'alya ewaa-bwe.) You have eaten (you are in possession of) something you received straight-forwardly (i.e.
entries.meaning: it was not stolen; you came by it in an honest way).

entries.luganda: "Olijja ddi ewaffe?" : lye bbanja ery'omugenyi (= omugezi).
entries.english: "When will you come to our home?" : is the debt of the wise visitor.
entries.meaning: He understands at once that there is a present waiting for him. He will not wait long to recover that "bbanja".

entries.luganda: Oh kasobeza ng'omuweesi : akugamba okufukuta n'afukamu amazzi.
entries.english: You are a puzzle (to me) like a smith : he tells you to blow the fire and then he pours water on it.
You are a fist : that beats one who is near.
entries.meaning: You pretend to be helpful, when I am talking to you, but do nothing, when I have gone away.

entries.english: (He who says) "You will see" : does not tell you what you will see.
You are courageous : like the army of Kasujju (ssaza chief - Busujju).
Your loud voice is a pest (mulogo or mutemu).
entries.meaning: Offensive expression, addressed to an accused witness.

entries.english: Cultivate a small piece : and it will be clean.
entries.meaning: French "Peu mail bien". Lat. "Non multa, sed multum" (Pliny).

entries.english: You are telling lies to the visitors (saying that there are beautiful people in the village) : the beautiful ones went with the chief.

entries.luganda: Oli mpaiakitaie : ekaabira ku nsozi essatu.
entries.english: You are a difficult (stubborn) character (like a cooking pot) that requires three hills (cooking stones) to broil upon.
entries.meaning: When there are only two, it refuses to stand.

entries.luganda: Oli mugabi nga jjenje : olulikwatako nga likulekera kugulu.
entries.english: You are generous like a cricket : when you get hold of it, it leaves a (whole) foot in your hands.

entries.luganda: Oli mu ga bulago : nti wano we gattira Omuyima.
entries.english: You are in the water up to the neck : here (the water) killed the Muyima.
entries.meaning: You are in great danger : here another came to grief.

entries.luganda: Oli mugayaavu nga kyannyanja : kisula mu mazzi ne kitanaaba kutukula.
entries.english: You are as lazy as a fish : it lives in the water and needs not wash itself to be clean.

entries.luganda: Oli mugezi nga Munnabusiro omubbi : nti "ndi ku Bbira awo".
entries.english: You are clever like the thief in Busiro : (saying) I am living there at Bbira.
entries.meaning: Bbira is a village in Busiro. Clever play upon words: "Ndi ku Bbira awo" and "Ndikubbirawo" (I shall steal there from you).

entries.luganda: Oli mukaba nga nsiko : etuyana kiro.
entries.english: You are shameless like the grass in the wilds : it sweats at night only (application to drunkards, fornicators etc.).

entries.luganda: Oli mukalabakalaba ng'omumwi w'ekirevu : awatali linnyo, awangawo You are clever like one who shaves his beard : where there is no longer any tooth, he puts his tongue between (to flatten out the skin).
entries.english: You know how to help yourself.

entries.luganda: Oli mukubi wa mpi mu kigongo.
entries.english: You are one who beats the hand on the back.
entries.meaning: Said of one who mocks mercilessly a prisoner who is being stripped and beaten.

entries.luganda: Oli mu kulya : nga Katonga ajjula?
entries.english: You are going on eating : whilst the (river) Katonga is flowing over the banks!?
entries.meaning: Irresponsible carelessness; there will soon be no opportunity to ferry over.

entries.luganda: Oli mukuusa nga jjembe : liva ku kikondo; nti nva Buvuma.
entries.english: You are a cheat like a charm : it comes from the pole (where it was hanging) and it says: I come from Buvuma.
You are free (unhampered) like the neck of a rat (not caught).
entries.meaning: If it is caught, a banana fibre is tied round its neck, to take it home for the dog.

entries.english: You will light a torch in the clan.
entries.meaning: You will spread bad news among the people.

entries.english: You are like a night wizard : he cannot look at a bananary from afar (without desiring to dance therein).

entries.luganda: Olina akajanja : akannamukazi-omu; nti omwandu tunaagukisa wa?; nti ggw'oli-na?
entries.english: You are overbearing (you boast) : like one who has only one wife (and says) where shall we hide all the plunder?; (reply) have you got any?
entries.meaning: "Omwandu" means war-booty and generally consists of women.

entries.luganda: Olina akambayaaya : akasengusa ennyonyi ekiro, ng'ewa musolo.
entries.english: The imagination you have is as far fetched as that of the bird that migrated at night, imagining it had to pay tax.

entries.luganda: Olina akasattizo (= amampaati) : akambaliza ekkovu ekita, nga ligenda kusenge-jja.
entries.english: You are full of pretensions : that put a calabash on the snail, as if it were going to filter beer.
entries.meaning: The calabash is the shell of the snail.

entries.luganda: Olina enfubitizi : ekusuza n'omulamu ng'agenda okufa ali wall.
entries.english: You are spiteful : sleeping with a woman who is healthy, whilst somebody over there is dying.

entries.luganda: Olina kasiikuuzi : akakubya emmomboze eyajja n'ebigere byayo.
entries.english: You have mad ideas (in your head) : which make you beat a vagabond who has come to you of his own free will (and you have taken him on and you have given him work).
entries.meaning: He will leave you again.

entries.english: You are anticipating the fun : like one who laughs at his own jokes (before the others laugh) (spoiling thereby the fun for others).

entries.luganda: Olina obukabakaba obwa wamumwa : nti tulye entanda.
entries.english: You have the impertinence of the mouth : (the mouth says) let us eat the food (for the journey).
entries.meaning: The mouth always interferes in matters concerning others. It wants to eat with-out doing work.

entries.english: You are like the eye-lash : it winks to one who gives it nothing.
entries.meaning: Expression for: I refuse your request, you ask me in vain.

entries.english: You are an "eŋŋaŋala" : like a tobacco pipe that survives being blocked up.
entries.meaning: The ŋŋaŋala is an otter-like animal (kaneene). It has a half choked cry and feeds on small fish. The cry of the animal resembles that of a half choked pipe being smoked.

entries.english: You are like a bee : that fetches (sugar from the) dregs of mubisi.
You are (like) a chicken : you are ungovernable.
entries.meaning: A hen will lay her eggs, where she chooses. - Said to an unruly person.

entries.english: You are a slut (a sloven) : drinking the water at the well (like eating the food (you bought) at the market).

entries.luganda: Oh nnasajja : ng'omugomo ogutta ensonzi n'obuyamba.
entries.english: You are a clever fellow : comparable to a mugomo (fish trap), whose narrow meshes catch nsonzi and even buyamba (both small fish).
You have climbed up to where the water comes from (and that means that) you have to drink dirty water.
entries.meaning: Application: You have offended your superior and you have to make recom-pense.

entries.luganda: Oliraana wa butwa (omuwa-butwa) : n'otoliraana wa kyokoola.
entries.english: It is better for you to be neighbour to a poisoner : than to one who casts a spell over you.
entries.meaning: You can guard yourself against the former; but the latter makes your goats etc. perish.

entries.english: You are like Ssekadde (the old man) : who made himself chief of Mukono (Ssekiboobo).
entries.meaning: Said of people who assume positions which are not theirs. - "Ssekadde" is a personal name of the mmamba-clan.

entries.luganda: Oli wa kyejo : bwe nnaakusimbako enjala, omukka onoosiza mu byayi nga tabs.
entries.english: You are insolent : when I get my claws into you, you will breathe (as a man would when) tied up like tobacco.
entries.meaning: Tobacco is wrapped up tightly to preserve its aroma.

entries.luganda: Oli wa mukisa : ng'anyaga embwa ekuzizza.
entries.english: You are lucky : like a person who steals a dog that is near bringing forth.
entries.meaning: He has hardly reached home, when he gets a litter of puppies as well.

entries.luganda: Oli wa mukisa : ng'omunafu gwe baagala.
entries.english: You have luck : like a lazy person whom they love.
entries.meaning: As a rule a lazy woman is not loved. Such a woman, if she is a favourite, might be lucky to find a bunch of good matooke in uncultivated land and is praised for the food she brings; a diligent woman who mixed some overripe bananas into the matooke, is scolded by her husband.

entries.luganda: Oli wa mugoonyo : bw'otta enkoko, ofumba kasooli.
entries.english: You are a spiteful person (towards guests) : when you kill a chicken, you cook kasooli (maize).
entries.meaning: The two don't go together.

entries.luganda: "Oli wa nnyomba mbi" : ng'alima emmere ye ku kkubo.
entries.english: "You are a very quarrelsome person" (so they say to) one who plants his food along the road.
entries.meaning: You get yourself into trouble (you ask for trouble), e.g. through other people's goats, through thieves etc.

entries.english: You are of Ssambwe (village near Nnandere in Bulemeezi) : like Nnabugwamu (whose family estate was Ssambwe).
entries.meaning: Nnabugwamu stands for "intruder". Therefore: You are an intruder, a meddler in things not concerning you.

entries.english: You are denouncing a favourite in the darkness (as if nobody had seen or heard it).
entries.meaning: Nobody takes notice of evil talk.

entries.english: You exchange a basket without a bottom for a good one.
entries.meaning: Applied to people who take somebody else's thing (cow or goat) and bring back an animal of inferior value.

entries.luganda: Olubuto kyoto : alutyabira (= alusombera, = akisennyera) enku y'akoowa.
entries.english: The stomach is like a fireplace : the one who has to collect firewood for it, gets tired.
entries.meaning: Engl. "He that gapes until he be fed : well may gape until he be dead". Germ. "Die gebratenen Tauben fliegen einem nicht ins Maul".

entries.english: The stomach must be fed.
entries.meaning: Otherwise the body cannot work.

entries.english: A rebellious stomach : makes you confess what you have eaten.
entries.meaning: Engl. "Open confession is good for the soul". Germ. "Die Schuld will heraus".

entries.english: A miserable old civet-cat is wrestling with death (that is the end).

entries.luganda: Olufumbe olukulu bw'olaba nga lulwanya embwa : ng'essanja basala.
entries.english: When they see the old civet-cat fighting with a dog, they cut the dry banana leaves (for its grave).
entries.meaning: They used to cover the grave of the dead with dry banana leaves. Meaning: That civet-cat can't run any longer. It is doomed.

entries.english: Relationship goes with the eating : if the related person goes away hungry, he (she) won't come back.
entries.meaning: The sacred duty of hospitality.

entries.english: Relationship comes from meeting on the road.
entries.meaning: It often happens that far relations get to know each other as relations only by meeting one another on the road.

entries.english: Relationship improves by friendship.
entries.meaning: Being related without liking each other is not much use.

entries.luganda: Oluganda nkovu : teggwa (= teruggwa) ku mubiri (or: sirunaabibwa).
entries.english: Kinship is like a mole (on the body) : it never disappears.
entries.meaning: But friendship might come to an end.

entries.english: Hesitation (in adding water) scorches the "nnumbu" (kind of yam) in the cooking pot.
entries.meaning: Too much water makes it sloppy and tasteless; too little water scorches it.

entries.english: The miserable hungry leopard that prowls on strange territory : does not respect a sacrificial goat (destined for the lubaale).
entries.meaning: Disrespect for other people's claims.

entries.luganda: Olukadde olwa Nnyenga : w'otolulaba mu katale, ng'ogamba nti yafa.
entries.english: If you don't see that little old man on the market at Nnyenga, you say: he is dead.
entries.meaning: Otherwise he would surely be there.

entries.english: When a father beats his child : he is likely to beat also its mother (who wants to protect the child).
entries.meaning: Or: Death that strikes the child : is inclined also to strike the mother.

entries.english: Striking the nose leaves the eye in tears.
(olumyu) An old hare gets suckled by his (her) own children.
entries.meaning: What the parents have done for the children, the children must do for their parents. Duta 708, Kag.16. 3968 Olulimi katebulanya : lwe ky'ayogedde enkya, kaakano lukyegaanyi. The tongue is a treacherous little thing : what it has asserted in the morning, it denies now (in the evening).

entries.english: (The woman says) The stolon (stem of the vegetable-marrow-plant) of the hated woman does not dry up (her troubles never come to an end) : mine has produced fruit again (new trouble has cropped up again).
Silliness (useless endeavours) make(s) a barren woman miss her dinner.
entries.meaning: She pretends to have to go and help another woman in childbirth, (although she has had no personal experience).

entries.luganda: Olumbe kijjolooto : olaba lutta Kagulu atafa.
entries.english: Death is a strange thing : you see how it kills Kagulu who can't die.
entries.meaning: King Kagulu Tebutwereke, an extremely cruel ruler, was killed by his sister Ndege and thrown into the lake. Therefore he has no grave in Busiro.

entries.english: (A man who says) Sickness has finished off all our chickens : throws (a chicken) on the roost.
entries.meaning: He complains that he has nothing to eat any longer; but he is too stingy to eat that one or to offer it to a guest.

entries.luganda: Olumbe lw'omugagga tiwabula alutuukamu : wakasanke atuuka mu lwa mpanga.
entries.english: At the death of a rich man mourners are sure to be present : the small red finch comes at the death of the cock (for feathers).
entries.meaning: They all hope to get something.

entries.luganda: Olumbe musolo : teruddukwa; gye lukusangira gy'oweera (= gye gukusangira gy'oguweera).
entries.english: Death is like poll-tax : it is unescapable; where you meet it, there you pay.
Death does not kill in one way only.
Death is not given a hand.
entries.meaning: Nobody encourages it to come. All flee from it.

entries.english: One single day : does not make the meat rot.
entries.meaning: Engl. "Rome was not built in one day". Said to somebody who hurries up others unduly.

entries.english: If there is deadly danger (from a wild animal) : the little forest (where you could climb up a tree) moves away from you.

entries.luganda: Olunaakutta : 1) lukuggya enunere mu kamwa; 2) lukuggya we bajjula.
entries.english: Sickness that will kill you : 1) takes the food away from your mouth.
entries.meaning: Omufu talya. The evil of hunger that will kill you : 2) drives you away from where they serve food. You hope to get food elsewhere and find they have finished eating.

entries.english: The evil that will kill you : sneezes twice.
entries.meaning: Somebody's sneeze was considered as a bad omen for a planned action. So if one says: I am going to X., and somebody sneezes, he will change his plans; but when that somebody sneezes again, his not-going is wrong as well.

entries.english: The death that will kill the dog : blocks up his nose.

entries.luganda: Olunderebu olwambaliza ekkovu ekita : nga ligenda kusengejja.
entries.english: It is stupidity that puts a beer calabash on a snail : as if it were going to draw beer.
entries.meaning: Ridiculing the shell of a snail (something useless, silly).

entries.luganda: Olunkulu lwayokesa Ssekiboobo Mbuula embuga ye.
entries.english: Arrogance caused the enclosure of Ssekiboobo Mbuula to be burnt down.
entries.meaning: He had driven away a certain Mugogo from his home at Nnamiryango and built his embuga there, without heeding King Muteesa's warning. "Therefore" light-ning struck his place and burnt it down.

entries.luganda: Olunkulu lw'emisota : emito n'emikulu gyonna girya gigalamidde.
entries.english: Arrogance of the snakes : all of them, the young ones and the old ones, eat lying on the ground.
entries.meaning: If children of men do that, they are strongly reprimanded by their elders.

entries.english: A hill (place) of thieves is where the Mugema (Ssaza chief of Busiro) lives, (because anybody who lives there, says) "I live at Bbira" (but, written together, it can be understood as: "I shall steal from you there").
The hill of workers is (there where one says) : I also have to be counted (as worker).
entries.meaning: Play of words: Mbalwa is a village in Kyaddondo, near Nnamugongo.

entries.luganda: Olusozi lw'abammi : ndeke okulya, mpe ggwe?
entries.english: The hill (place) of misers : (is where one says) shall I leave off eating and give the food to you?
The stalk of the gourd-vine that drives shoots : gives you the idea of building up the trellis.
entries.meaning: With the help of good advice one can achieve things.

entries.english: The (sausage shaped) calabash for the hated person is filled with lung (instead of mikalo = dried meat).
entries.meaning: Such calabashes are used for storing meat.

entries.english: When you are on a journey (you think longingly) : now the boys (at home) are dipping the mmere into the nva.
Childish talk (voice) like that of the brown kite (high pitch).
When death takes the one who supports you : it finishes your strength.
entries.meaning: Loss of a father or benefactor etc.

entries.english: The killing of the cow makes the dog travel (to get meat, bones).

entries.luganda: Oluva e Mukono lwe lulissa Abakunja entubiro.
entries.english: The bad news that comes from Mukono will kill the Bakunja by drowning.
entries.meaning: The king had ordered his Ssekiboobo (ssaza chief of Kyaggwe) to round up the Bakunja (Nkokonjeru district) for human sacrifices. They fled to the lake and were drowned.

entries.luganda: Oluvulunguti : abasajja lwe balya mu magi.
entries.english: A mix-up : as the men eat it in eggs (an egg contains head, feet, feathers etc.
The anvil (stone) that helps to forge the needle : helps to forge also the knife.
entries.meaning: "The hand that rocks the cradle : rules the world". The position of the mother in the world.

entries.luganda: Olwali wa gundi : lwali ku njovu Kavumba.
entries.english: (lumbe) The "kwabya-olumbe" (finishing of the funeral rites) at So and So's : was like the elephant hunt at Kavumba (village in Busiro).
entries.meaning: The king had killed an elephant at Kavumba and an immense crowd gathered there to partake of the spoils.

entries.english: The burial of a good man : does not pass without praise.

entries.luganda: Olwatika olunatta entamu : lugifuluma mu ntobo.
entries.english: The crack that will finish the cooking pot : is the one at the bottom.
entries.meaning: An evil (or sickriess) which attacks the vital parts, is disastrous.

entries.english: "Will the quarrel about the meat not come to an end?" : (so asks one) who has eaten the hump (the best part).

entries.luganda: Olwa kulya : lusuula emmese mu kita.
entries.english: Greed for food : throws the rat into the calabash (where it is caught).
entries.meaning: Passion blinds the intellect.

entries.english: Greed for food : throws away the needle.
entries.meaning: A person busy with needlework forgets all about it, when hearing that the food is ready.

entries.luganda: Olwokya enju : lwe lulaga nnamunye ekkubo.
entries.english: (Death) which burns the house, shows the pied wagtail the way.
entries.meaning: Death in the house also brings other troubles.

entries.english: If a hair is tickling you in your nose : you remove it yourself.
entries.meaning: Because you can judge best yourself, if it hurts. 2.30. 4029 Olya akatono : nga ke kako. (cf. "Kange" kakira "kaffe": 2149) You might possess little : but what you possess is yours.

entries.english: You eat a few ants : (and you enjoy them better than when you eat many of them), because they are not mixed with soil.
(akamere) You are eating at somebody else's : without having worked for your food.
entries.meaning: You are a parasite. Germ. "Sich mit fremden Federn schmacken".

entries.luganda: Olya kizze : nga muwooza wa katale.
entries.english: You are eating (taking) what comes to you (what they bring to you) : like the tax collector on the market.
entries.meaning: Much easier work than collecting other taxes.

entries.english: Better to eat little than to die.
entries.meaning: Be satisfied with the little you have and don't steal. If they catch you stealing they will beat you to death.

entries.english: (katiko) You are looking round : like a man who got only one mushroom.

entries.luganda: Omala okuyombera ku buko : nti "alinnyimba ndimutta".
entries.english: (= Omala okukola obubi - -) You behaved badly, when you were with your marriage-relations : (saying) I shall kill the one who talks badly about me.
You have given me strength : (as) hunger gives it to the head.
entries.meaning: Energy to look for food.

entries.luganda: Ompiseeko kkuutwe : embwa ly'eyita ku mubumbi, ng'egenda eri omuwazi w'amaliba.
entries.english: You have passed me by in a hurry : like a dog when he passes a potter and runs to a dresser of hides.
entries.meaning: There is something to be had there.

entries.luganda: Ompise Ssekibotta akubira enva engalabi : ezange leka wano.
entries.english: You call me a "Ssekibotta" (a fellow who buys nothing and still wants his food) that drums a dance for the vegetables, saying: put mine down here!
entries.meaning: So says the impatient husband to his wife who brings the food. - Bad mannered, impatient husband.

entries.english: You pass me by : (as if indicating) I shall come back and greet you!
entries.meaning: You have refused to greet me.

entries.english: A thief is stealing from you : a scandal-monger does not remain sitting with you (but goes and tells others what you have told him in confidence).
entries.meaning: A visitor staying long and listening to what you tell him, goes and broadcasts what he has heard (another kind of stealing).

entries.english: A thief is like a rat : he is trapped with a bait.
A thieving child will not be taken (readily) into custody.
entries.meaning: Nobody wants to take a thief into his house.

entries.luganda: Omubi abijja n'ebibye : mpokya abijja n'eggobe lye.
entries.english: A dirty person is despicable with all his property (food, beer, etc.) : the bean becomes disfigured through its withered leaves.
entries.meaning: Expression of disgust and contempt: "I don't want anything from a dirty person like you".

entries.english: An ugly person is better than nobody at all (wife, child, friend etc.).
(also: Omubi eyeenyumiza - - ) An ugly man who chats (makes himself pleasant) : is preferable to a nice one who does not greet (who is haughty, snubs you).

entries.luganda: Omubi atavaawo : olwaddaaki anaaza omulungi emabega.
entries.english: The ugly person who faithfully remains : will one day wash the beautiful person's back.
entries.meaning: When the favourite helper is not there, the ugly one comes in handy. - "Any port in a storm". - Don't despise less-gifted people!

entries.english: When your body shrinks on you (i.e.
entries.meaning: becomes mere skin and bone) : the one who did not know you before despises you. It is easy to underestimate a person.

entries.english: The body (of man) is like a thicket : what comes out of it, can devour you.
entries.meaning: In the thicket there might be an animal; out of the body comes sickness, murderous attacks etc.

entries.english: The body is like a barkcloth-tree : if you don't protect it, you cannot keep it healthy.

entries.luganda: Omubumbi akaza : ye yeetenda, nti ezange nsinziira ku kibanyi ne nsuula wansi.
entries.english: A potter drying (his pots) : is bragging (when he says) I stand here on the drying shelves and throw (my wares) down (and they won't break).
entries.meaning: He won't risk to do what he says.

entries.english: One who has been told (only), seems to know more (about it) than one who has seen it himself.
entries.meaning: The former is inclined to exaggerate.

entries.english: A slave who becomes a member of the clan : becomes a father of twins (title of honour).
entries.meaning: He is treated and esteemed like other clan-people.

entries.luganda: Omuddu lw'abaaga : lw'afuna kitaawe ne nnyina.
entries.english: If a slave skins an animal : he gets father and mother.
entries.meaning: They say to him: "Mwana wange, leeta nkufumbire!"

entries.english: A dead person provides food for a living one.
entries.meaning: The child of the deceased is taken into the family of a brother or sister and cooks for them.

entries.english: The news of a person's death spreads quicker than the summons of a drum.
The inheritance of a dead man is taken by his feet (because they say: the son has "stepped into the footsteps of his father" (yadda mu bigere bya kitaawe)).

entries.luganda: Omufumbo bw'atagenda mu ffumbiro : abagenyi tibakkuta.
entries.english: If a married person does not go to the kitchen : the guests won't be satisfied.
A married man is not "devouring" the food (even when he eats much) (because then his wife will only say: to-day my husband is enjoying his food (nti leero gamuwoomedde)).
A dead man does not complain.
entries.meaning: He takes meekly everything given to him. - Also said of helpless old people.

entries.luganda: Omugabi teyeeseera : bwe yeeseera, nga wa ntondo.
entries.english: A distributor does not cheat himself : if he does, he is dissatisfied.
"A rich man lets his riches rot" (so one says, when refusing financial help) : but when he has a festering wound, he presses out the pus.
A rich man fills his pipe with tobacco on top of the dottle (without cleaning the pipe first).
entries.meaning: Heaping new riches on the old ones.

entries.luganda: Omugagga tabaamu mwoyo : ennyanja tezza mpiso ng'eguddemu.
entries.english: A rich man knows no generosity (grabbing, cheating and keeping all to himself) : the lake does not give back even a needle which has fallen in.
A rich man's name does not die (is not forgotten).
Where a rich man eats : there are always leavings (crumbs).

entries.luganda: Omugagga w'emmere : enjala ettira ku kkubo.
entries.english: A man who has plenty of food (at home) : famine kills (him) when travelling.
entries.meaning: He does not think, that elsewhere there might be no food.

entries.english: A witchdoctor does not cure himself (he goes to another one).
entries.meaning: Engl. "Physician cure thyself!" Lat. "Medice, cura teipsum!" Ug.Journ.

entries.luganda: Omugano gw'enswa : tiguleka mukadde mu kyalo.
entries.english: A swarm of flying ants leaves no old person at home.
entries.meaning: Said of things which attract general interest.

entries.english: A favourite gives presents of stolen things.
entries.meaning: If a chicken has disappeared, he (she) says: an animal has taken it.

entries.english: A well-beloved person : does not fall into the baskets.
entries.meaning: If he finds people at meals even if he is not expected, he is welcome; he quietly washes his hands, because he is sure to get his share.

entries.english: A favourite : can't do wrong.
A visitor shows his appreciation according to the food (matooke) eaten.
A guest who has had a good meal : sees the intestines of his host.
entries.meaning: He says: "Bye ndabye, mbirabye" (expression of satisfaction), which can be understood: "Byenda bye mbirabye".

entries.english: A visitor who has had enough food : makes the food speak The food says: you have not finished me yet.
A visitor throws you into debt.
entries.meaning: If you have nothing to offer him, you go to your neighbour to ask for the loan of a chicken.

entries.english: A guest visits where it is peaceful.
entries.meaning: If there is trouble in the place he visits, he cannot expect presents, because he has to commiserate or to help.

entries.english: A visitor who announces his visit : does not eat a chicken that is freshly killed.
entries.meaning: It is softer and tastier, if it is killed the day before the cooking.

entries.english: A visitor who stays long (overstays his welcome) : becomes insipid (is no longer interesting).
A visitor who stays long : is made to tread out the beer (in the lyato) (a job not usually done by visitors).
A visitor who comes first : calls those following "spongers".
entries.meaning: He is afraid that he won't get sufficient attention paid to him.

entries.luganda: Omugenyi atagalamira : nga gy'ava eriyo omusango.
entries.english: A visitor who does not lie down to sleep : gets into trouble from where he came.
entries.meaning: He says: I shall lie down after my journey.

entries.english: A visitor who overstays his welcome : causes trouble.
A visitor who does not talk much : sees much.
A visitor who has not announced his visit to you : finds you in the place cur-tained off (in bed).
A visitor who does not intend to stay : you put him on the road when it is still daylight (in good time).
A visitor who does not leave in time : has words with his host.
A visitor who arrives during a family quarrel : does not get enough to eat.
entries.meaning: Being preoccupied with their quarrel, they will not pay sufficient attention to him.

entries.english: A visitor pleases on the day he arrives.
entries.meaning: French "Je vous adore jusqu'd l'aurore".

entries.luganda: Omugenyi nkuba : by'esanga mu luggya by'etobya.
entries.english: A visitor is like the rain : what it finds outside the courtyard, it makes wet.
entries.meaning: Said of an unexpected visitor; he threw the household into turmoil.

entries.luganda: Omugenyi omulungi : akusanga na ga lwayi.
entries.english: A welcome visitor : comes when you have nothing to cook (no fat in the byayi containers).

entries.luganda: Omugenyi omusulize : y'agoba Ssebwana ku ntebe.
entries.english: The visitor who was given hospitality : drove Ssebwana from the throne.
entries.meaning: King Kimera, the son of Kalemeera and born in Bunyoro, was thrown into a loam-pit; but he was saved by the owner of the pit, became a great hunter and, going to Buganda, occupied the throne of his father by expelling Ssebwana the Katikkiro, who had made himself king.

entries.luganda: Omugenyi omuyite : ajja avunja; Lukongwa yavunja Bbira.
entries.english: A guest who has been asked to come : comes with pleasure; Lukongwa came readily to Bbira.
entries.meaning: Prince Lukongwa was called by chief Nnatiigo of Magala (Ssingo) to help him to suppress a rebellion. Lukongwa came, settled down at Bbira and remained there for ever.

entries.english: A shy visitor spills the sauce with his eyes open.
entries.meaning: Shyness makes him awkward and clumsy.

entries.english: A guest who overstays his welcome : uses the barkcloths he has beaten out as court-fees.
entries.meaning: He will get into trouble (court cases) (women) and has to use his income for paying fines. - A guest used to work and was given money for it.

entries.english: A visitor from near-by : dies of hunger.
entries.meaning: They don't reckon that he will stay and don't cook for him.

entries.luganda: "Omugenyi tamala zenkana awo" : nga ze yalaga zituuse.
entries.english: "A guest should not stay so long (so many days)" : (says a visitor) when he has stayed the indicated number of days.
entries.meaning: It is only pretence, because he would like to stay longer.

entries.english: A visitor does not treat himself : it is the host who treats him.

entries.luganda: Omugerengetanya alya ga musumba (= ku g'omusumba).
entries.english: A resourceful man eats the matooke (steamed in the skin) of the herdsman.
entries.meaning: Not being satisfied with his own portion, he also takes from what is reserved for the herdsman who will come later. He says: they can steam other matooke for him.

entries.english: A clever man sells you a forest.
entries.meaning: He is able to make you buy a thing which is no use to you (formerly forests were not considered valuable); or he sells you things which you can easily make yourself without any expense, e.g. hoe-handles.

entries.english: A clever man finds a thing which has been lost (forgotten) long ago.
A wise man is like a traveller : where he feels tired, there he rests.
The stick belongs to the one (who can say) "I have cut it" : not to the one (who says) "I have found it".
entries.meaning: Cutting a stick involves more work than finding it. - One who has simply found a thing, cannot claim it as his property. Munno 1912, M.762, 35.72. 4122 Omuggo oguli ewa munno : tegugoba ngo mu nju. The stick which is in your neighbour's house : does not drive the leopard out of yours. Things which are not at hand, are of no use in case of an emergency.

entries.luganda: Omugoba amagamaga : y'agobya eryato ku mayinja.
entries.english: A steersman whose gaze wanders : steers the canoe on to the rocks.

entries.luganda: Omugwa gw'omwana w'obuwala : gubeera ku kisasi.
entries.english: The rope of a woman : is always ready on the porch.
entries.meaning: A girl not allowed to marry according to her own choice, or a woman offended by her husband, is soon ready to say: I am going to hang myself.

entries.luganda: Omukabakaba asanga bbambe : nil wabuze kugololawo bw'oti.
entries.english: A clever man finds the skin pegged out : (and he criticises) you failed to stretch it properly here (like this).
entries.meaning: He always manages to arrive, when the work is done; but that does not prevent him from criticising the work.

entries.luganda: Omukabakaba kalabakalaba or omukalukalu) : bamusiima azzizza pnoma.
entries.english: They congratulate a clever fellow, when he has been given a promising post.
entries.meaning: Some people might be difficult at home, but develop great faculties, when they are given responsibility.

entries.luganda: Omukabakaba tabula kimulema : amatu tigawulira vvumbe.
entries.english: Even a clever person is sure to fail sometimes; the ear is not able to perceive a fine smell.

entries.luganda: Omukaba taggya busera : bwe bumwokya, nti bunjokezza we njagala.
