entries.english: A brazen-faced man does not scald himself with (hot) porridge : if it scalds his mouth, he says: I like it hot like this (to save himself from being laughed at on account of his greediness).
An old man dies of cold and hunger (clothing and lacking food).
An old man (in the house) is better than a deserted house.
entries.meaning: You will find better hospitality in an old man's house than in an empty place. Engl. "Half a loaf is better than no bread".

entries.english: The old man gets hold (of his disobedient grandson) at his meal.
entries.meaning: The boy has run away to escape punishment; as the old man cannot run after him, he gets hold of him, when he comes back for food.

entries.english: An old man goes hunting : but to go to war he simply refuses.
entries.meaning: On the hunt he forgets his age and runs with speed; but when they call him to war, he remembers his years.

entries.english: An old person is like an "enkomangwa" (tree) : when it breaks, it cannot be joined again.

entries.luganda: Omukadde wa muno tayomba : ng'obuziina bwe we yabulese w'abusanze.
entries.english: Our grandfather (grandmother) does not grumble : if he (she) finds his (her) rags where he (she) left them.
entries.meaning: Old people do not like having their habits upset.

entries.english: A woman runs away from you : but she does not defame you.
entries.meaning: In Buganda it would be a breach of the accepted code.

entries.english: Your wife might run away from you : but she does not die.
entries.meaning: As long as he considers her as his wife, he is her husband. After her death he is called "widower".

entries.english: A woman is like the legs (ends) of a hide : if you don't rub (crumple) them, they won't become soft (yielding).

entries.luganda: Omukazi ky'atalya : kye kiwunya olwendo lwe.
entries.english: What is taboo for a woman (eating) : her ladle smells of it.
entries.meaning: Her children who have eaten such food, drink water, after eating, out of mother's calabash. The mother notices it and abhors the very smell of it.

entries.luganda: Omukazi mmese : ne bw'ekulira mu nju ekubba.
entries.english: A woman is like a rat : even if it has grown up in the home, it will steal from you.
entries.meaning: She is not to be trusted; even after being married a long time, she might run away with somebody else.

entries.english: A woman is like a shield : if you have not tried it on yet, you call it light (handy, manageable).
A woman with withered breasts : drinks beer like a man.
A woman (wife) is like an old cooking pot : you do not give it to your friend to keep it for you.
A barren woman : brings forth visitors.
entries.meaning: She calls her guests: "Baana bange".

entries.luganda: Omukazi omugumba : mbuzi ya nkunku; bw'esowola omugwa togoberera.
entries.english: A barren woman is like a hornless goat : if it slips its halter, you no longer have a hold on it.
entries.meaning: If she leaves her husband, she won't come back to him.

entries.luganda: Omukazi omulima : azaala emmere; omunafu azaala omuddo.
entries.english: A diligent woman brings forth food; a lazy one brings weeds.

entries.luganda: Omukazi omulima : akuliisa (= aliisa bba) n'engabo ku mmere.
entries.english: A wife who is a good worker : makes you eat with the shield over the food.
entries.meaning: When you have eaten enough and she wants to dish up more food, you hold the hand in form of a shield over the food: nti lekera awo!

entries.english: A woman who is diligent in the garden : sees the chicken dancing (rejoicing).
entries.meaning: Plenty of insects from the freshly cultivated ground, remnants of matooke etc. are ever there.

entries.luganda: Omukazi omunafu : akuweeseza olukato, nti agawooma ge gafumita gannaago.
entries.english: A lazy woman forges an awl for you : the last tasty bit of matooke becomes a kind of pike to pick up the remnants.
entries.meaning: Picking up the remnants is a sign that the guest has not had enough and that the woman has been lazy in preparing sufficient matooke.

entries.english: A lazy woman feels resentment if it rains.
entries.meaning: Because she will have to start working in the field.

entries.luganda: Omukazi omunafu : alwala ekigere, talwala ngalo.
entries.english: A lazy woman has a sore foot, but not sore hands.
entries.meaning: When she is supposed to cultivate, she is afraid that soil and gravel might hurt her sore foot; but for cooking and eating she is quite well.

entries.luganda: Omukazi omuzadde : kinnanga kya lumonde (= lumonge).
entries.english: A woman who has borne children : is like a used potato plot.
entries.meaning: From time to time one can dig up some potatoes.

entries.luganda: Omukazi talema kulimba : azze enjuba ewanze, ng'agamba "nkedde bukeezi".
entries.english: A woman can't help telling lies : she comes at 9 or 10 o'clock in the morning and says: I have started off very early.
Luck is with the brave.

entries.luganda: Omukisa gwa munno : tegukukwata; embuzi etebba gye basiba, embwa ebba gye bats.
entries.english: The luck of your companion does not accompany you : the goat which does not steal is tied up; the dog that steals is let free.
entries.meaning: If another had good luck, do not reckon with the same luck for yourself.

entries.english: Good luck is like a flea : even when you sit on it, you don't kill it.
entries.meaning: If one has a "luck star", he can risk anything.

entries.english: Good luck is like a flea : it finds the bed spread.
entries.meaning: A lucky fellow finds everything favourable.

entries.english: Good luck is like a flea : it does not get burnt in the house.
entries.meaning: The flea will jump out and escape. The lucky fellow always escapes.

entries.luganda: Omukisa omubi bwe guba : embwa w'eyita n'eddembe (mu musiri gw'emmere); embuzi bw'eyitawo bagikubira nduulu, songa embwa y'enzibi.
entries.english: As bad luck will have it : the dog walks with impunity through a plot of planted food; but if the goat walks through it, they raise the alarm over it, although the dog is the real thief.
entries.meaning: The dog is usually running free, but a goat is always tied up.

entries.luganda: Omukodo kikere : abaana kibikkira ku mazzi.
entries.english: A miser is like a frog : it hides its young in the water.
entries.meaning: A stingy man does not show his treasures.

entries.luganda: "Omukono gwantandawala (= gwantendewererwa)" : nga awaata ku mangi.
entries.english: (The woman peeling matooke says) "My arm is getting tired" : if she is peeling a big heap.
entries.meaning: A form of bragging: I have so much matooke in my lusuku, that it makes me tired to kuwaata. Like a rich man saying "I have so much money that I get tired counting it". Dutch 't komt op een turfje niet aan, als men in't veep is". - Okutandawala is an old form for kutendewerera. Rub.C.608. 4177 Omukono ogumu : gwe gunaaza gunnaagwo. One hand washes the other. Lat. "Manus manum lavat" (Petronius). Gteek "Ha de heir tan heira nizei".

entries.english: If you don't put your hand down into the pocket (to get out money for buying meat, fish etc.), you won't have any additional dishes.
A shy hand : does not let its people eat enough.
entries.meaning: If the father or mother are too timid to get the necessities of life, the children will suffer want.

entries.english: As far as the arm reaches : it scratches.
entries.meaning: Said of reliable friends, to whom one can say everything.

entries.luganda: Omuko omwavu : y'amera amayembe; nti abadde antomedde.
entries.english: A poor son-in-law : grows horns (because they say) "he has charged into me".
entries.meaning: His "bako" feel attacked, because he never brings anything when he comes.

entries.luganda: Omuko ow'akasitukira : talya nkoko wa mwavu.
entries.english: A father (or brother)-in-law who leaves quickly after arriving on his visit : will not eat a chicken at a poor man's home.
entries.meaning: As he has no chicken of his own, he must first go and look for one.

entries.english: A peasant who refuses (obedience) : rolls a pad for the head (to carry loads).
entries.meaning: The chief will make him work unmercifully.

entries.english: A peasant rests : when he is dead.
entries.meaning: Until then he must work.

entries.english: The tenant quarrels (about the public work) when he is in the forest.
entries.meaning: When the chief comes to him to call him up for work, he does not dare to object; but when the chief has gone, the tenant gets courage and grouses.

entries.english: A master who is absent from his home : loses his influence.
entries.meaning: His power is greatest at hoMe.

entries.luganda: Omukulu ali awawe : tabula ky'alowooza; amazina g'ekirevu gajjira ku mmere.
entries.english: The old man who sits at home : has always something to think about; his beard starts dancing, when he eats (or smokes).

entries.luganda: Omukulu atakwata mu kisibo : zifa nnaganga.
entries.english: If the master does not take care of the goat pen, the goats will die of disease.
entries.meaning: Supervision and control will ensure cleanliness and order. - Duties of parents and superiors. - "Nnaganga"-disease comes from not cleaning the pen properly. The children will not take sufficient care of themselves, if not supervised. Dutch "Het oog van den meester maakt het paard vet".

entries.luganda: Omukulu atakwata mu kyoto : alya lyesitula.
entries.english: (eggye) If the master does not take care of the fireplace (cooking) : he eats, when the army is moving away.
entries.meaning: He has to move with them, before the food is done.

entries.english: A parent who does not use little tricks (kulimbalimba) : won't be successful with his children.
entries.meaning: He promises the children to bring some meat or 'nva', if they watch the house well during his absence etc.

entries.english: Respect is due to the master.

entries.luganda: Omukulu atava (= atadduka, = ateewala nte) ku nte : y'aziza abaana ennyama.
entries.english: The father who does not keep away from a (an angry) cow : bars his children from her meat.
entries.meaning: If he is mortally wounded by the cow, his last will will be: Don't eat its meat! Taboo! Or: A father who does not hand over, till he dies, gives his son no chance.

entries.english: When the father puts something (e.g.
entries.meaning: nnyama) aside : there the child puts its eyes (remembers the fact and hopes to get it later).

entries.luganda: Omukulu mpagi : bw'eva mu kika, nga kimenyese.
entries.english: The master is like a pillar : if it is removed from the clan, its power is broken.
A grown-up person does not brandish the needle : without using it.
entries.meaning: A strong character speaks and acts according to principles.

entries.english: 3438) A master cannot rule two horn French "11 n'y a qu'un pape M.771, Gram.258.
entries.meaning: (cf. Mukulu takulira: 2874; cf. Obukulu ndege: esteads. Rome". Interference in somebody else's domain.

entries.luganda: Omukulu tava nnyuma : nga waliwo ekyamukanga.
entries.english: The master does not move from the rear position : if there is frightening danger from behind.
entries.meaning: There he can protect those in front. Duta 515. 4206 Omukulu tebamusikira kuvuga : bamusikira kubalira. An old man is not put into the boat to row : but to give advice. He cannot row any longer; but he can tell the young men how to row.

entries.luganda: Omukulu w'alaga olunwe : ekizimba we kyabikira.
entries.english: Where an old man points with his finger : there the boil will burst.
entries.meaning: He knows where the trouble lies.

entries.luganda: Omukulu w'essimbo kibbo : oluggyamu emmere, nga kidda emabega, -okutuula ku bukulu.
entries.english: A dignified master is like a food-basket : when they take the ttooke out of it, it goes to sit in dignity.
entries.meaning: He does not tackle the food greedily. - Dignified and calm patience.

entries.english: Friendship also rules a strong man.

entries.luganda: Omukwano gusala mu kabu : enswa nnene.
entries.english: (True) friendship shares even (smallest things like) kabu (tiny fly hovering over ripe bananas or beer) : a flying ant is something big (for friends).
entries.meaning: Dict.72. 4213a Omukwano gusala (= gwala) mukaabu. Friendship thrives on beer.

entries.luganda: Omukwano gutta bingi : enkukunyi emegga embwa.
entries.english: Friendship kills many things : a flea forces a dog down on the ground.
entries.meaning: The flea seems to be very affectionate and friendly with the dog. The dog sits down to scratch itself. Real friendship bears (condones) a lot.

entries.english: Friendship comes from a fight (quarrel).
entries.meaning: A storm clears the atmosphere. Lat. "Amantium irae : amoris integratio" (Terence).

entries.english: Friendship between children : is broken up by laughing.
entries.meaning: If one falls down, the others laugh at him. - Friends should be magnanimous.

entries.luganda: Omukwano gw'ennyanja : gukyalagana nga gwetisse tigufa.
entries.english: Friendship with one who lives across the bay : does not die, if they still visit each other and carry presents.
entries.meaning: Germ. "Der Weg zum Herzen geht durch den Magen".

entries.english: Friendship is like fat : you eat it, while it is still hot.
entries.meaning: When friendship is still young, it provides the greatest pleasure.

entries.english: Friendship is like the body : you do not scratch, where it does not itch.

entries.luganda: Omukwano omunene : 1) gukuloopesa ow'ekika; 2) gumegga, enkukunyi emegga embwa.
entries.english: Close friendship : 1) makes you talk evil even about a relation of yours; 2) lowers (one's feelings), as the flea makes the dog sit down (for scratching).
entries.meaning: Evil can result from it.

entries.luganda: Omukwano omutono : gukwegayiriza akuwerekera, nti ntuusako wall.
entries.english: A weak friendship : makes you ask the host who is seeing you off, accompany me up to there (a little further).
entries.meaning: The visitor loves the host more than the host the visitor, otherwise the petition would not be necessary.

entries.english: A visitor does not exhaust the knowledge of his host.
entries.meaning: The host does not tell him everything.

entries.english: The one who has been ordered (to commit a crime) is not punished with death.
entries.meaning: He who ordered the crime to be committed is responsible.

entries.english: If a madman gives you something : take it there and then.
entries.meaning: To-morrow he will have changed his mind.

entries.english: A prince is like fire : you warm yourself at it, but you keep at a distance.
entries.meaning: Out of reverence one should not become too familiar with royalty.

entries.english: (= Kabaka nvubu - - ) A prince is (feared) like an envubu (hippopotamus) : you don't wait for it in the deep.
A lame fellow : knows himself how to get ahead.

entries.luganda: Omulemeezi bw'omuwa ekintu : yeebaza lusozi, nti "Abalemeezi Kkalwe".
entries.english: If you give something to a Mulemeezi : he thanks you with a hill, namely "Abalemeezi Kkalwe".
entries.meaning: Kkalwe is a hill in Bulemeezi on which traditional worship was practised. It was therefore used as in our "Katonda yeebale".

entries.english: The Mulemeezi does not inquire about the child (home, relations etc.), but about beer.
entries.meaning: He is considered a drinker, whose first question is: "Tunaanywera wa?"

entries.english: The Mulemeezi does not fall : he gathers flying ants.
entries.meaning: He does not own up to have fallen; he says: I only stooped down catching ants.

entries.luganda: Omulenzi omuto ow'ekyejo : bw'alikula alizaala eminene.
entries.english: A young boy who is insolent : on growing up will cause big trouble.
A liar finds a believer.
entries.meaning: There will always be people who give credence to lies or calumnies. - Said when hearing a bird, whose cry is like "twase enswa, twase enswa" (we have killed flying ants).

entries.english: A bad tiller : blames the hoe.
entries.meaning: The fault is always somebody else's. Ssal.p.75. 4236 "Omuliraano gwokya bbiri" : nga mwagalana. (cf. Olukuba Waliiso: 3965) "Neighbourliness burns two houses" (so you say to your neighbour in trouble) : if you love each other. Lat. "Nam tua res agitur, panes cum proximus ardet" (Horace).

entries.english: Neighbourliness that gets on well : is better than mere relationship.

entries.luganda: Omuli w'omu kyalo : tasinda lubuto, asinda nzikiza.
entries.english: A husband who eats in the village (instead of in his home) : does not complain about his hungry stomach, but about the darkness.
entries.meaning: He comes home late; but he does not like to tell his wife that he has eaten else-where; so darkness has to serve as an excuse.

entries.english: A guest who turns up late in the evening : makes the children go to bed hungry.
entries.meaning: For hospitality's sake he is given what the children would have had.

entries.english: A person who has found (a thing) : will not be killed (like a thief).

entries.luganda: Omulungi aleka emisango : nga Lava mu kyalo.
entries.english: A beautiful woman leaves trouble behind : if she does not stop visiting in the village.
A beautiful woman is like a well-polished drum : it finishes off the leaders.
entries.meaning: They all try to get it by fighting and die over it. - Applied to a number of wooers (suitors), all trying to win the same beautiful lady.

entries.luganda: Omulungi tabulako kamogo : embwa tekala nnyindo.
entries.english: Even the beautiful one has a bad point : a dog's nose is always wet.
entries.meaning: The dog may be a good hunter, of noble ancestry, reliable and does not steal. Lat. "Nil perfecti sub sole". Dutch "Niets is er volmaakt op het ondermundsche". French "Chaque tableau a son ombre".

entries.english: A beautiful woman is the sister of many.
entries.meaning: They like to claim relationship with her. - "A fair face is half a portion". A pretty face is a good recommendation.

entries.luganda: Omuluvu mpaawo kimulema : empisi terya menvu.
entries.english: Even a glutton can't eat everything : the hyena does not eat ripe bananas.

entries.luganda: "Omulwadde taggya mutwe wansi" : nga tewannajja (= nga tannalaba) gw'aya-gala.
entries.english: "The sick person cannot raise his (her) head from the pillow" : (so says the nurse) if a welcome visitor has not arrived yet.
entries.meaning: The patient should not be disturbed!

entries.english: A sick person does not forget to sigh.
entries.meaning: His pain will remind him. A person asking for a favour brings strong motives to arouse pity.

entries.english: "The sick person has given me a lot of trouble" : (says the doctor or the nurse) if he (she) is still alive (but I got him through!).
entries.meaning: He would not speak about him, if he had died.

entries.english: A traitor (a dishonest fellow) makes a blood-brotherhood with his calf (with his legs).
entries.meaning: He trusts his legs; when he ought to pay a debt, he runs away.

entries.luganda: Omulyazaamaanyi alya gw'asinze : ensega tegwa ku mulamu.
entries.english: A cheat gets the better of one whom he surpasses in slyness : a vulture does not come down on a healthy (living) man.
From the way he takes the pad (load) off your head : you know, whether you can stay long (on your visit).
If an acquaintance of yours does not offer his hands (for greeting) : you know that he has forgotten you.
One who is accustomed to (getting) a big calabash (full of beer) : is annoyed, if you give him only a small endeku full.

entries.luganda: Omumizi agambwako : nga si mwana wo.
entries.english: The immoderate eater is reprimanded : unless it is your child.
entries.meaning: One's own children "can't" do wrong.

entries.english: Is it the glutton who is the master at table?
entries.meaning: Of course not! The greatest and best bits are reserved for the mwami.

entries.english: A short fellow does not grow old : he does not stoop.
entries.meaning: You don't notice so soon that he is ageing.

entries.english: A short fellow does not see the locusts approaching.
entries.meaning: Application: An unimportant person won't be listened to, if he warns people.

entries.english: One who says nothing (mute like a log) : like a thief who belongs to the household.
entries.meaning: They punish the child for the theft and he keeps quiet.

entries.english: A weak person cultivating a small piece every day : does more than one who cultivates only occasionally a big plot.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Nulla dies sine linea" (Pliny). "Gutta cavat lapidem, non vi, sed saepe cadendo" (Ovid).

entries.english: A lazy person talks his tongue dry.
entries.meaning: By excessive (incessant) talking he tries to get what others get by working.

entries.english: A lazy person is extremely quarrelsome.

entries.luganda: Omunafu gy'ayaya : gye yeeyunira (= wa wowowo, waboobwe).
entries.english: Where a lazy man (or a weakling) finds food (without work) : there he helps himself frequently.

entries.luganda: Omunafu ow'entatankiriza : y'aliisa bba ku mwaka amangu.
entries.english: A weak woman who sows at once (whilst cultivating other parts) : feeds her husband quickly (with new vegetables) in the rainy season.
A lazy woman who is touchy (quarrelsome) : does not feed her husband well.
It is fitting for a poor man to bring a little present.
entries.meaning: His gift can not be very great; but he should show good will.

entries.english: A poor fellow needs introduction.
entries.meaning: A rich one is known to all.

entries.english: A poor fellow who buys food for himself : eats his fill.
entries.meaning: When he has a little money, he buys (meat, fish etc.) and makes a feast of it.

entries.english: A person in trouble is like the yam-plant : it climbs upwards by its own efforts.
When a poor man thinks he has found something (nnyama, engabi, ensunu) : he finds a jackal (uneatable).

entries.luganda: Omunaku y'amala ebibamba : abaana b'emmese be bakuza ab'embwa.
entries.english: A poor man provides the means of meeting the needs of the rich : the young of the mouse make the young dogs grow.
entries.meaning: Peasants make the chiefs rich.

entries.luganda: Omunnyu mulungi : ekisula mu nju kye kisinga obulungi.
entries.english: (Foreign) salt (which you have not got) may be good : but native salt (which you have in your house) is better.
entries.meaning: Engl. "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush". Germ. "Ein Sperling in der Hand ist besser als eine Taube auf dem Dach".

entries.english: (If you hear of) a woman who eats her child : she is a Muganda.
entries.meaning: If the Muganda husband is looking after a baby that will not stop crying, he calls his wife and says "Jjangu olye omwana" or "ondiira omwana" (stop the child crying - by intimidating it).

entries.luganda: Omuntu awatira ku munne : omubiri ku magumba kwe guba.
entries.english: A person who is kept (fed, clothed etc.) by his friend : is like the body (flesh) that is sustained by the bones.

entries.luganda: Omuntu gy'ayagala gy'agenda : evvu ligenda mabega ng'olifuse mu lusuku.
entries.english: Man goes where he wants to go : the ashes go back (towards the kitchen) when you throw them out into the bananary.
entries.meaning: The wind carries them back.

entries.english: A parent dies in the body : but not in the minds (of the children).
(= Okyemanyi : Omunyolo wa Luwalira.) A Munyoro-chief is overbearing at Luwalira's place.
entries.meaning: Luwalira is the proper name of the former hereditary chief of Kabula and equivalent to the present "Lumaama". During the Banyoro domination the hereditary chief had nothing to say and the Munyoro chief was hated.

entries.luganda: Omunyolo omukalukalu (= omukaba) alisalira Abaganda ennyama.
entries.english: A sharp Munyoro will cut meat for the Baganda.
A story-teller does not tell dreams (but what he has seen or heard).
A story-teller does not keep quiet, if somebody interrupts him.
A beggar goes about in day-time : a thief at night.
A man makes an effort : even when he is tired.
The man suckles (his child) like a buffalo (namely standing, not sitting like a woman).
entries.meaning: He provides the food for the child by going to his work.

entries.luganda: Omusajja bw'abeera n'omukazi omu, oil n'amala alwala akogga nnyo.
entries.english: If a man has only one wife and she falls sick : he gets very thin.
entries.meaning: All the work is on him and nobody cooks for him. Rub.C.1025. 4296 Omusajja gy'agenda : gy'asanga banne. Where a man goes there he finds his friends. One can find company everywhere. Engl. "Like will to like". Germ. "Gleich and gleich gesellt sich gern".

entries.english: An angry man : is as poisonous as a viper.
The forerunner of thieving : is lying.
One who actually treads the beer-bananas is better than one who refuses (although he might know it better).

entries.luganda: Omusana ogwase : guzuukusa Kaweekwa e Ggangu.
entries.english: The heat we have today : could raise the dead Kaweekwa of Ggangu.
entries.meaning: Kaweekwa was a legendary rich man at Ggangu in Busiro; when he was very sick, he sent word to another man asking for two cupping horns (biwuubiro) for blood letting. But Kaweekwa died and after his death the man claimed that he had given a cow to Kaweekwa (two horns!) and took the daughter of Kaweekwa instead. The widow of Kaweekwa, whose name was "Gwase", cried so much, that the dead Kaweekwa rose from his grave and put the unjust claimant to shame. Then he returned again to his grave. From that legend the saying: Omusana ogwase - - developed.

entries.luganda: Omusango gukwata yagussa : enjoka tekwata mutwe.
entries.english: The one who has committed an offence, is responsible for it : gonorrhoea does not attack the head.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Quo quis peccat, in eo punietur". Germ. "Womit man sundigt, damit wird man bestraft".

entries.luganda: Omusango oguzzanga ku busenze : n'otoguzza gye bakuzaala.
entries.english: You might risk a court case, where you are a tenant : but not where your home is.
entries.meaning: Because where you are a stranger, your relations and clan-people will redeem you; but if you fall out with people at your own home, you will find no help elsewhere.

entries.english: A case (a misdeed) does not know the difference between a poor and a rich house.
entries.meaning: Poor and rich become involved in cases.

entries.english: A court-case does not come to an end (by lapse of time) : it is the complainant that finishes it (by not sueing the evildoer).

entries.luganda: Omusango twaguwoleza e Lubaga : ebiwalaata ne bijjula entuuyo.
entries.english: We pleaded our case at Rubaga (old residence of king Muteesa) : whilst our bald heads perspired (sitting a long time in the burning sun).
One who works for food tries to get a big 'enkota' (bunch of bananas) for his work.
entries.meaning: Looking after one's own interest.

entries.english: A poor hungry man eats his fill on the day he works for food.
entries.meaning: "Make hay whilst the sun shines".

entries.luganda: Omusasi tattiza lusuku : amala matooke gokka.
entries.english: A man who works for food (foraging), does not clean the lusuku properly : he does the food only.

entries.luganda: Omusazi w'omunnyu : aliira ku kambe ke.
entries.english: A man who cuts grass (eggugu, enseera) for making salt : eats (lives) by his knife.
entries.meaning: The knife is his source of income.

entries.english: A poor soldier (7th army) goes to war without saying goodbye.
entries.meaning: He has nothing to leave his friends.

entries.english: A prisoner does not refuse the stocks.
entries.meaning: It would not help him if he did.

entries.luganda: Omusibira-wala : agenda okumanya nga yaggwa dda ku magumba.
entries.english: A person who has his relations far away, hears of the death of one of them, when the flesh has long since fallen from the bones.
The representative of a peasant : is a derelict house (empty, with sooty cob-webs) (i.e.
When a fool looks for friendship : he forgets his own clan.
entries.meaning: Only a fool neglects his clan; because if he does so, he and his children will find no help, when in need.

entries.english: You have taken him by surprise : just as a person with a squint, takes by surprise someone who has hidden himself.
entries.meaning: The one in hiding thinks that his pursuer is looking somewhere else.

entries.english: The tax of the termite is : you feed on it.

entries.luganda: Omusomesa apanka, nti anywa omwenge alifa; so ng'anywa pnunda bbiri.
entries.english: A catechist preaches loud : one who drinks beer, will die; but he himself takes two big calabashes (in one sitting).
A catechist does not commit fornication : if there is no woman who wants him.
A catechist does not quarrel : if there is nobody to annoy him.
The trader does not kill the (life of a) village : the head-chief kills it.
entries.meaning: The trader comes and goes; but the chief can make life impossible by unjust decisions and by driving innocent people away.

entries.luganda: Omusumba w'embuzi bw'akugamba nti zimbuze : ng'anoonyeza abuliddwa n'alinnya ku bifunvu.
entries.english: If a shepherd tells you: "I have lost my goats" and looks for them and does not find them : he will also climb up the mounds (to look for them from there).

entries.luganda: Omusu omuzadde : tigufa mbwa (= tiguliibwa mbwa).
entries.english: The edible rat with young : is not killed by the dog.
entries.meaning: Whilst the dog attacks the young ones, the mother can escape. - A father, by sending his sons, escapes the fine for not doing his "luwalo".

entries.english: If one is an acquaintance : the warrior hits him on the shield.
entries.meaning: He can risk it with a friend (sham-attack etc.); but one who does not know him, might take it amiss.

entries.english: A warrior does not "find" things : all that he gets hold of he robs.
A landowner is like a millipede : when you touch it, it rolls itself up (remains inactive).
entries.meaning: Passive resistance. - The mutaka considers himself independent, self-sufficient.

entries.english: The owner of the land is leading you on the way : (and you say) can I get lost?
entries.meaning: No danger! He knows his land. - An experienced leader is safe.

entries.english: A drunken fellow understands (and remembers), if they tell him: come early to-morrow!
entries.meaning: The beer will be early to-morrow morning.

entries.english: Even a drunkard does not slaughter his dog (mistaking it for cattle).
entries.meaning: Drunkenness does not excuse every bad deed.

entries.luganda: Omutego olaba gukwasa eggi : ng'akalina obulago tikaayite.
entries.english: If you see that a trap catches an egg (a small thing with no hold on it) : (you are sure) that something which has a neck, will not escape.
entries.meaning: If a small offence is punished, a crime will not be pardoned.

entries.luganda: Omutengu talya kiyiiyize (= A disobedient child will not receive a favour which has been thought over.
entries.english: It is considered unworthy of it.
One with a load on his head does not wait (for the other porters).

entries.luganda: Omutima gukuli mu nteeko : ng'omunafu omubikire.
entries.english: Your heart is in its proper place (socket) (quiet, undisturbed) (your mind is at ease) : like that of a lazy woman who has just been informed about the death of a relation.
entries.meaning: Meaning that she need not go hoeing to-morrow.

entries.luganda: Omuti oguliko ebibowabowa ebigukutte : kibuyaga bw'aguzunzazunza tigutera kugwa.
entries.english: If a twee- has climbers round it holding it : it probably will not fall, when a storm sways it.
A youngster smells of what he has eaten : if he has eaten "mmale" (lungfish).
entries.meaning: Youngsters often don't wash after eating!

entries.english: A child is like a goat : it (the goat) is herded by one with an authoritative voice.

entries.luganda: Omuto ne muto munne : nga kwa njala.
entries.english: If one child eats together with another child : (it is a sign) that there is lack of food Eating together with the adults they would not get enough food.
A free-man is recognised by his token (an ivory ring round his neck).
A free citizen lets himself be fined : and then he pleads in a higher court.
A free citizen (farmer) produces (plenty of) ttooke : if he has plenty of land.
A free man is like the necks of goats : they don't mind the rope.
entries.meaning: Submission to the lawful authority.

entries.luganda: Omutongole kagumba ka morale : tekanyigirwa mu ttooke.
entries.english: An independent citizen is like a bone of the lungfish : it is not squeezed to-gether with ttooke.
entries.meaning: If you do squeeze, you won't eat the ttooke. A mutongole has "protection". If you hurt him, you will lose the court case.

entries.luganda: Omutongole mpagi ya "nnaggomola" : egwa ku kkubo.
entries.english: An independent citizen is like the "nnaggomola"(tree)-post : it falls along the road-.
entries.meaning: A mutongole is not called to work in the lubiri; he works outside, as the nnaggomola-tree is not used for the buildings in the lubiri.

entries.english: A small chief is like an edible rat : it loves the wilds.
entries.meaning: Tenants who have been sent away by him, call him "musu", because their places will grow wild.

entries.english: A free farmer is like seed : it is sown and spreads.
entries.meaning: He attracts other tenants and the village grows.

entries.english: A free man (tenant) cannot be deprived of a part of his lusuku (kibanja).
entries.meaning: His possessions are respected by the chief.

entries.english: If a person with a thin body is ill : he (she) makes you anxious.
entries.meaning: He has not much power of resistance.

entries.luganda: Omuto omutengu : omukulu akombye mu kibya.
entries.english: A disobedient child (gets no tasty bits) : because the father himself scrapes out (lit.
entries.meaning: "licks") the bowl. The father finishes all the nva himself and leaves nothing for such a child.

entries.english: A child doing wrong is not at fault : it is the parent who is at fault.
entries.meaning: The child must be taught and warned before it is punished.

entries.english: The high flight of the pigeon : does not go to the end of the village.
entries.meaning: Pigeons fly high, but not far. - A high-handed chief does not keep his chieftain-ship long.

entries.luganda: Omutunzi lw'amaza : abaana lwe bafa enjala.
entries.english: When an (itinerant) trader has sold his wares : (he says: let me go home) my children (at home) die of hunger.
A salesman must not get angry.
entries.meaning: "A man without a smiling face must not open a shop".

entries.english: A trader does not refuse to open (his bag, box, parcels etc.).
entries.meaning: Other-wise he won't sell much.

entries.english: You notice that one is a dwarf : when he is standing.
entries.meaning: Usually his legs are too short. - One's drawbacks are discovered when one is put in responsible position.

entries.luganda: Omuti w'amaluma : y'ayita n'entanda ng'eriko n'ettu ly'eggobe.
entries.english: One who is afraid of eating without vegetables : travels with his food for the road together with a parcel of ggobe-leaves.
A debtor who is afraid : promises to pay back in a few days.
entries.meaning: He has a better chance of receiving the loan, if he does so.

entries.luganda: Omuvubuka afiiridde mu maanyi : ebintu abirese kivuvu.
entries.english: A young man who has died in the strength (of his youth) : leaves his plans (hopes, undertakings) unfulfilled.

entries.luganda: Omuvubuka atanyumya : mbuzi ya zigeye; bw'egwa mu mazzi, ekala iwa ggulo.
entries.english: A young man who does not talk (quiet character) : is like a goat with stripes and long hair; even when it falls into the water, in the evening it is dry again.
entries.meaning: He does not change easily.

entries.english: The accuser will not leave you unharmed.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Semper aliquid haeret". French "Mentez, mentez! it en reste toujours quelque chose" (Voltaire).

entries.luganda: Omuwa-butwa alina emmere ye : tabuiwa (= tabula) gw'atta.
entries.english: A poisoner has his own food : there is always somebody whom he can kill.
entries.meaning: Said of a rich man, who can always get what he wants.

entries.english: A poisoner cannot hide himself.
entries.meaning: He will be discovered sooner or later.

entries.luganda: Muwa-butwa wa kyejo : amagumba g'ayita eridege; ekiwanga ky'ayita eŋŋoma; essanja ly'ayita embugo; mu ntungo mw'akiiba endiri.
entries.english: A poisoner is a queer (insolent) person : bones he calls ankle-bells; a skull he calls a drum; dry banana-leaves he calls his bark-cloth; his sleeping place is the semsem field.

entries.luganda: Omuwuulu anaasula omwa munne : enkowe atanuza wansi.
entries.english: A bachelor who hopes to sleep at his married friend's home : keeps his eyes downcast.
entries.meaning: If he is too free with his looks, he won't have a chance of a night's rest.

entries.english: An unmarried fellow who smokes : does not go hungry.
entries.meaning: In exchange for tobacco he can easily get food, especially from women who smoke.

entries.luganda: Omuwuulu ow'ekinyumu : y'aba nnannyini nju (= akulira enju).
entries.english: A bachelor who has arranged a dance : is the owner of the house.
entries.meaning: Because they say: "tugende wa gundi" (as if he owned the house).

entries.english: You don't tell a hungry man that the matooke are ripening in such and such a place.
entries.meaning: He would not believe you.

entries.luganda: Omuyima omukyawa bulungi : n'otomuwaayiriza kulya nkejje.
entries.english: If you despise a Muyima, do it fairly : and don't accuse him of eating nkejje (little fish).
A hunter who refuses (to give you part of the meat) tells you about the hunt (and pleases you that way).
A hunter who does not get lost (sometime) in the bush : won't get meat.
entries.meaning: French "Rien sans fatigue". Engl. "No pains - no gains".

entries.english: The hunter does not die : it is the animal that dies.
entries.meaning: Even if the animal escapes, the hunter says: "We will get it to-morrow" or "We will get another one".

entries.luganda: Omuyonjo omufunda (= omutono) : gukyamya enkoko ebyoya (= eky'ensuti).
entries.english: A narrow basket : bends the feathers (tail-feathers) of the chicken.
entries.meaning: Being restricted (in need) leads to many an evil. Poverty leads to theft. Too high a dowry leads to immorality etc.

entries.english: A mother begs things for her child.
entries.meaning: She would be ashamed to beg for herself.

entries.english: A parent finds the dead again.
entries.meaning: Namely in the children. Physical resemblance between grand-children and grand-parents.

entries.english: A mother is not bought.
entries.meaning: A good mother is a gift of God.

entries.english: Where the mother sends (her children) : the childless goes herself.
entries.meaning: She has no child to send.

entries.english: A slave girl who is known (as a slave) : works whilst the sun still shines.
entries.meaning: If the work were not finished, she might be punished.

entries.english: A bad habit (passion) : dies at the death of one who has no children.
entries.meaning: No children to receive the bad inheritance.

entries.english: A bad habit which you are aware of (before getting married) : does not kill the marriage.
entries.meaning: The partner reckons with it.

entries.luganda: Omuzira afiira watono : amazzi gafiira mu ntamu.
entries.english: A mighty warrior dies in a narrow place : the water (which is mighty in the ocean, lake, river) dies in the cooking pot.

entries.luganda: Omuzira kigere kya mbogo : okyegezaamu nga teriiwo.
entries.english: The valiant (courageous) is like the footprint of a buffalo : you step into it, when the animal is far away.
entries.meaning: Those who are superior in body or mind are not attacked in an open fight (but by treacherous means).

entries.luganda: Omuzira mwana gwa ngo : guyimba okuluma n'okutaagula.
entries.english: A courageous man is the son of a leopard : it both hurts and tears to pieces.
entries.meaning: Also used for: "Misfortunes seldom come alone". Germ. "Ein UnglUck kommt selten allein".

entries.english: The one whom you love at the time of the maize-season : (you will) overwhelm with maize-cobs.
entries.meaning: Fresh maize-cobs are very much appreciated. The empty cobs are stored and used as toothbrushes.

entries.luganda: Omwaka gwa nswa : bagutendera ku mulala.
entries.english: You praise the year that brings many termites (flying ants), when the next one comes.
entries.meaning: Good things are appreciated, when they are no longer there.

entries.english: One must work for the chieftain.
entries.meaning: Otherwise there will be trouble.

entries.luganda: "Omwami ankyaye" : empagi aleeta ya lutege (= bitege).
entries.english: (One who complains) "The chief does not like me", brings a crooked pole.
entries.meaning: He causes the dislike of the chief by negligence in his work.

entries.english: Where there is no ruler : a case will not be settled.
entries.meaning: There must be authority in human society.

entries.english: A chief is like a hunting net : he kills also where there is no animal track (kisinde).
entries.meaning: He insists upon levies, taxes etc. wherever he finds you, not only in the mbuga.

entries.english: A generous chief : makes you give thanks as soon as you have touched the gift.
entries.meaning: His generosity allows you to consider it as a gift, before he has actually given it to you.

entries.english: A chief is not brought to the brewing place (to receive his share).
entries.meaning: They take his share of the beer to his embuga.

entries.luganda: Omwami wa lwazo : w'obeera w'ali toyagala.
entries.english: If you are under an exacting chief : you don't like it.
entries.meaning: But you might praise him, if you are not his subject.

entries.english: A child acquires habits, when it is still in the "ngozi" (cloth for carrying the child on the back of the mother).

entries.luganda: Omwana akulema mu buto : nti "ndimuzaalamu bukadde".
entries.english: If you can't bring forth a child in your young years : (you say in vain) I shall bring forth in old age.
entries.meaning: Important things must be started in time.

entries.english: A child who is with its mother : is "impossible" on a visit.
entries.meaning: The child will ask for anything and shames the mother. On account of the mother they don't want to refuse.

entries.english: The girl will collect firewood for me in which there are insects.
entries.meaning: So complains the father of a girl who intends to run away from her husband, so that he has to pay back the dowry. - Carrying that firewood on his head, the insects will sting him.

entries.english: If a child is not looked after : it will even eat mucous from the eyes.
entries.meaning: It eats before washing its face and hands.

entries.english: A child who is not yours : you do not let lick your bowl (you do not give it the last tasty bits).
entries.meaning: That is a favour for one's own obedient children.

entries.english: If a child reviles its clan : it has brought shame upon it.
If you pamper your child : you will have to carry it in a bag.
entries.meaning: It will not be able to look after itself.

entries.english: A place which the child knows : is the place where it rains.
entries.meaning: The child imagines all good things to be there.

entries.english: The death of the child : saves you the trouble of cleaning up.
entries.meaning: "It is an ill wind that blows nobody any good".

entries.luganda: Omwana omukyawe akuza ow'omuganzi : ow'emmese y'akuza w'embwa.
entries.english: The despised child makes the favourite one fat : the young of the rat fattens the young of the dog.
A small child always wants what does not belong to it.
entries.meaning: It is folly to desire things which are not for us. - Living above one's standard.

entries.luganda: Omwana muwala ow'amalala : bw'alikula alizaala emisango.
entries.english: A girl who is boastful : will cause trouble when grown up.

entries.luganda: Omwana omuwere tasookera ku mmere : asookera ku mazzi.
entries.english: A newly born child does not start with food : but with water.
entries.meaning: Same as "Kwata mpola" or "genda mpola" (in the beginning!). Dutch "Lang-saam aan, dan brekt het lijntje niet".

entries.luganda: "Omwana omuwanga, takuba nnimi" : ng'abireetedde ye; ate bw'aba abiggye ku ye, agamba "omwana oyo wa lugambo".
entries.english: "Give a child (often) food etc.
entries.meaning: and it will not talk evil" : (so the master of the house says) if the child brings stories (about other people) to him; but if it talks to others about him, he says: "that child is a slanderer".

entries.luganda: Omwana takkuta watali nnyina eri kitaawe).
entries.english: A child does not get enough food, if the mother is not there.
A child is not thrown away (not even an ugly one).

entries.luganda: "Omwana wange oyo annimu eggwiiso" : nga mugagga.
entries.english: "That child of mine is good luck for me" (says the father-in-law of the son-in-law) : if he is rich.
entries.meaning: Every time the father meets him, he gets something from him.

entries.english: The child of a barren woman does not die a natural death.
entries.meaning: Not only a woman who had no children is called a "mugumba", but also one whose children die soon after birth. She is constantly afraid that her child is being bewitched.

entries.english: The child of a dishonest father is like a cricket that is busy at night.
entries.meaning: The cricket sings at night.

entries.english: The child of a dishonest father does not drop from exhaustion.
entries.meaning: It will always manage to escape.

entries.english: The child of a fisherman always hopes that the father will come back (although the lake might have taken him already).
entries.meaning: "Hope against hope". Lat. "Spes non confundit".

entries.luganda: Omwana w'omunafu eba mbwa : ow'omulima mulangira.
entries.english: The child of a lazy parent is a dog : that of a worker is a prince.
entries.meaning: The lazy man's child has to look for food like a dog; the worker's has plenty.

entries.english: They kill the child of a witchdoctor, before it has taken medicine (when the ceremonies which were to protect it were not yet performed).
The child of a landowner (ancestor) looks after the (father's) grave.
entries.meaning: The relationship is seen by the care the child takes about the father's grave.

entries.english: The child of a land-owner is like a little kiyirikiti-tree.
entries.meaning: It is unsightly in the dry season; but when the rains come, it is a glorious sight in its fiery bloom. So the son of a simple mukopi can become a big chief.

entries.luganda: Omwana w'omutaka : nnyenje; tefiira ku kibanyi.
entries.english: The child of a land-owner is like a cockroach : it does not die on the store-rack.
entries.meaning: It will always find something to eat. Friends, relations.

entries.english: An insolent child has only a mother (and no father).
entries.meaning: The father would punish it.

entries.english: One who is quick at swallowing : leaves his cheeks in shame.
entries.meaning: They all look at him as he chews with full cheeks.

entries.english: "The quick man gets the flying ants" (says the braggart) : who just by chance found them swarming.
entries.meaning: Bragging! Huntsman's slang! Ssal.p.49. 4462 Omwavu afikka ky'okulya : tafikka mulimo. A poor man is overlooked, when they divide food : but he is not overlooked, when they give out work.

entries.english: The poor man makes his neck pay the fine (ransom).
entries.meaning: If he cannot pay, they put a rope round his neck.

entries.english: When a poor man goes visiting : he looks up all his clan-members (goes to each one).
entries.meaning: But when a rich man visits, the others come to see him, where he stays.

entries.luganda: Omwavu bw'atunda, talaba agula : bw'agula talaba atunda.
entries.english: If a poor man sells, he does not find a buyer : if he buys, he does not see a seller.
entries.meaning: When he sells, his price is called too high; when he buys, he has not enough money. He always has bad luck.

entries.luganda: Omwavu ky'afuna : kye yeetuuma (nti nze nsimbi, oba nze mwenge).
entries.english: A poor man boastingly gives himself the name of the thing he receives (I am money, I am beer) (i.e.
entries.meaning: I have plenty of money, beer in galore). If a poor man gets (occasionally) funds, he becomes boisterous.

entries.english: A pauper does not go to hide himself.
entries.meaning: He need not be afraid that somebody calls him aside to ask for money, or to get his assistance.

entries.english: A poor man has no friends.
entries.meaning: Nobody considers it profitable to be his friend. Selfishness of men!

entries.luganda: Omwavu ye mulalu : alya bya kuzaayisa.
entries.english: A poor man is like a madman : he eats food which he never returns (he can't pay back).

entries.luganda: Omwavu ye mulalu : omugagga ne bw'alaluka, taba mulalu mu bantu.
entries.english: It is only a poor man who is called "mad" : if rich man becomes mad, he is not called mad among men.
A marauder is not (necessarily) a devourer (gobbler).
entries.meaning: One who helps himself to a lot of food, often gives to others who have nothing.

entries.english: He who arranges an entertainment : does not quarrel about a few banana-stems broken down.
entries.meaning: Invited guests are pardoned many a thing.

entries.english: When the beer is plentiful : they decorate it with banana-fringes.
entries.meaning: Said of celebrated people; all want to be related to them.

entries.english: You should not refuse your friend (neighbour) a drink of beer (from a kita that has already been drunk from).

entries.luganda: Omwenkanonkano ogwa wakayaayu : omusajja nkoko n'omukazi nkoko.
entries.english: It is all the same for the wild cat : the cock is fowl and the hen is fowl.
entries.meaning: In regulated society there must be authority and law. In allusion to the emanci-pation of women! Nkoko: taboo for women! Ssal.p.47. 4479 Omweyagalire teguba mubi : omutunzi y'erumya enjala yekka. (cf. Kyeyagalire: 2538) Voluntary work (mulimo) is not an evil (is not resented) : the trader inflicts restrictions on himself. He has plenty of eatables in his shop; but he wants to sell them.

entries.english: A cajoler (empty talker) does not make you throw away your little cricket (locust).
entries.meaning: You cannot please everybody. Do not listen to every criticism (crickets are dainties for children).

entries.english: A man who speaks rudely : carries the bag on his own shoulders.
entries.meaning: Nobody is inclined to help him.

entries.english: A talker is like a walker : when he is tired, he rests.

entries.luganda: Omwogezi tatenda bibye : atenda bya banne.
entries.english: A talker (gossiper) does not talk about his own faults : but the faults of others.
The home of a mweso-player is not an eating place (seems not to be a hospitable home).
entries.meaning: Because the winner jestingly tells the loser after a kyeso: "genda olye ewa-mmwe" (you have lost).

entries.luganda: Omwoyo guntintimirira : ng'akanyonyi akakwate mu ngalo.
entries.english: My heart is trembling (beating) : like (that of) a little bird you hold in your hand.

entries.luganda: Omwoyo gw'omuntu kinywa ky'amaggwa : akisiba y'amanya gy'akyetikkira.
entries.english: The spirit of man is like a bundle of thorns : the one who ties it up, knows how to put it on his head.
entries.meaning: Everyone has his own ways.

entries.english: A small (careless) mind : has made you eat the "kasanjasanja"-mushroom (a mushroom of inferior quality).
A shallow mind : has made me love a soldier (7th army).
The soul does not get old : it does not grow gray hair.
Where the spirit reaches : the feet do not reach.
entries.meaning: Good wishes, prayer, telepathy etc.

entries.english: You are in no hurry : like one who has only a few teeth left to brush.
You are in no hurry : like a bald man fetching his razor.
You have looked at me as an "endabi" (small, quick, ever-watchful animal) looks at an approaching danger : which is unescapable hunger.
entries.meaning: Also said of one who does not give you a chance to explain.

entries.luganda: Onigguuka ng'ayogera : nti Omuzungu yankwatira e Ntebe.
entries.english: You are boasting like one saying: "The White man got hold of me at Entebe".
entries.meaning: The others purposely misunderstand: The White man offered me a chair.

entries.luganda: Onigguuka ng'empagi y'ennongo : bannannyinimu balya enkolo nga yo esa butta.
entries.english: You are haughty like an (old) "nnongo"-pole (in the house) : the inhabitants of the house eat the root stocks of the banana-plant (famine food) and the pole grinds flour (the pole is worm-eaten and the dust (mpumbu) drops from it).

entries.luganda: Onigguuka ng'ow'ekiwalaata afiiriddwa : nti ekyandyako abaana sildmanyi.
entries.english: You are haughty like one with a bald head, who has lost all his children, and says: I don't know what has robbed me of the children.
entries.meaning: Reply: Do you know what has robbed you of your hair?

entries.english: You have helped me : as Sunday helps the lazy woman.
entries.meaning: On that day she need not "kulima".

entries.english: You have despised me in the bush : like a hunter (who needed my help on the hunt and gave me hardly any meat).
You have fought for me (helped me) : as God helps the weak man in search of food.
You have helped me : darkness helps the devourer of food.

entries.luganda: Ono alya n'ono alya : ye mmere egenda (= ewooma).
entries.english: This one eats and the other one eats : and so the food goes.
entries.meaning: In company one has better appetite than when eating alone. - Also used for "Fair play!"

entries.luganda: Ono atoola n'ono atoola : ye mmere ewooma.
entries.english: This one takes and the other one takes : (that shows that) the food is tasty.
entries.meaning: Seeing others eating gives one appetite.

entries.luganda: Onoggwa ekkuuka : omusezi ly'aggwa mu lutabaalo.
entries.english: You will get enough of it : as the night-sorcerer gets enough in war.
entries.meaning: Plenty of dead, with which to practise his witch-craft.

entries.luganda: Ono mulungi n'ono mulungi : mpaawo gw'osinza musango.
entries.english: "This one is all right and the other one is all right" : if you (the chief) say so, you make nobody win the court case.
entries.meaning: Both have brought good bribes.

entries.luganda: Ono wa mugoonyo : bba okutta enkoko n'afumba kasooli.
entries.english: This is a spiteful woman : the husband kills a chicken and she cooks maize.
entries.meaning: The woman can't partake of the chicken meat. Muzizo! Maize and chicken don't go together.

entries.english: You ask me for money : have I to kill a Muziba to get it?
entries.meaning: The Baziba were traders and supposed to have money. Meaning: I have no money!

entries.english: You have given me the advice of the mongoose (clever advice).
entries.meaning: The advice of the mongoose saved the lives of the other mongooses. Ap. Eng. 12, Rowl.Tales p.16. 4520 Onsalidde kanywa : okukuloopya ky'okoze. You have cut the sinew of my foot (you have spoilt my reputation) : (saying) that I have given away the secret of what you have done.

entries.english: You have found me (prepared) : as the cheeks are prepared for potatoes.
entries.meaning: I am ready for your attacks.

entries.english: You are a puzzle to me : like little banana-food.
entries.meaning: Too little for two, too much for one. - Said of a person who is never satisfied, whether you do right or wrong.

entries.luganda: Onsobezza ng'entumbwe zange : gye nnassa emabega gye zassa olubuto.
entries.english: You puzzle me like my calves : to where I turn my back, they turn their front.
I fail to understand your ways (as I don't understand my mother) who has brought me up : she pinches you (when you are crying) and (when you are crying on account of that) she tries to pacify you.
You have thrown me a little papyrus-stalk : just at the moment when the river Mayanja was going to sweep me away.
entries.meaning: Engl. "A drowning man will catch at a straw". Salvation in the nick of time.

entries.luganda: Onsuulidde omwoyo : nga nnakyeyombekedde akufumbira embaala.
entries.english: You have thought of me (helped me) : as an independent (unmarried) woman who cooks embaala (tasty flying ants) for you.

entries.luganda: Onsuulidde omwoyo : 1) ng'ow'omu nju akuwandiikira; 2) ng'olukuttira ata-kwagala (= akuloga).
entries.english: You have thought of me : 1) as one living in the same house writing a letter to you.
entries.meaning: You have helped me : 2) as death does, when it kills for you a person who hated (or: bewitched) you. Ssal.p.19, Kag.166. 4529 Ontuuse : Nnalunga yatuuka Jjuuko. You have been heart and soul with me : as Nnalunga was with Jjuuko. Nnalunga was king Jjuuko's wife. She protected him with her faithful counsel against the murderous intentions of Jjuuko's son Kayemba. But when she became blind, she could no longer warn him and he was killed.

entries.english: You have helped me : darkness helps the fast eater.
entries.meaning: "Night covers many a deed".

entries.luganda: Onyiikira ng'akagobera mbuga : bwe kanaalya abaana ab'omwami, tibaaku-kwate?
entries.english: You do your utmost like one who is following a wild animal into the chief's compound : if it should eat the children of the chief, will people not get hold of you?
You are talking praisingly about the scrapings (from a fresh hide), saying that they encourage the appetite.
entries.meaning: But what about the meat itself which was next to it? That will not only make the matooke disappear, but the people as well.

entries.english: You praise the big mushroom : (whose name is) "the chief's calabash".
entries.meaning: The "endeku y'omukungu" is very big and very tasty. - Expression used to praise the beauty of a woman or the good qualities of a chief etc.

entries.english: You have increased my share (of food) : the lazy woman increases the chances of the wild cat.
entries.meaning: Weeds near the house give a better chance to the wild cat to get at the chicken.

entries.luganda: Onzise kabiri nga manda : okuva mu muliro ate okudda mu muliro.
entries.english: You have killed me twice, as is the case with charcoal : coming out of the fire and returning into the fire.
entries.meaning: The charcoal-burner makes coal through fire and for the fire.

entries.english: You are working : like one who brews poison (for the hunters).
If a man asks you for a single banana (and you refuse to give it), you ask for (have to look forward to) a refusal.
entries.meaning: "Ndikulaba" means "I shall pay back to you". So when you will ask him for something, he will refuse it too.

entries.english: You are mad with joy : like a despised woman coming from the burial of the favourite woman.
entries.meaning: Perhaps she is expecting too much.

entries.english: You are fidgeting about (feeling uneasy) : like one who has sat down in the place of the master of the house.
(kifi) "Cut small pieces!" (says one) who already has received a big piece.
(bifi) "Cut small pieces" (says the one) who has already received his share.
entries.meaning: He would not say so, if he had still to get it.

entries.english: (ekiswa) You are drumming on a deserted anthill : because there is nothing in.
entries.meaning: You waste your efforts. Oteganira bwereere!

entries.luganda: Osapnanga mukulu amalawo : n'otosanga muto wa leero.
entries.english: You find an old man (who has little food left) leaving off eating and giving the rest to a guest who has just arrived : but you don't find a youngster of to-day doing so.
(eddiba) You have arrived, when the skin was already stolen by the dog.
entries.meaning: The meat is no longer there or, you have come when the food is finished.

entries.english: You are talking nonsense : like one who visits the place where he was sold (his home) and asks to be redeemed.
entries.meaning: They will not be willing, because they wanted to get rid of him.

entries.english: You grin like a kikutuzi (insect), seeing somebody spreading his bed (to go to sleep).
entries.meaning: The kikutuzi is a small insect living in old grass that is spread on the floor of living houses; it bites the sleepers. - Looking forward to a good meal!

entries.english: You visit incessantly : like one who has his "love" in the neighbourhood.
You are everywhere : like the "ngalabi" (long drum) in the season of plenty.
entries.meaning: You are to be seen at all parties.

entries.english: You are left with the remnants of the meal : like the kabangala (small variety of the edible rat).
entries.meaning: When the misu (the bigger kind of the edible rat) have left their eating place, the small kind comes and finishes off what is left. - To arrive "after the feast"!

entries.english: You have pushed one who was wavering (who was going to fall).
entries.meaning: Also used in the moral sense.

entries.english: You have sent the child to his grandfather (grandmother).
entries.meaning: There they fulfil all the wishes of the child, even if the chief sends his son there to bring in the poll-tax.

entries.english: You are restless like a guest who has a dog with him.
entries.meaning: If the dog goes out of the house, the guest also goes out to see, whether the dog does any mischief.

entries.luganda: Ositunkana ng'omugenyi atakkuse : nti "bagundi ka nnende mbalabire ddala".
entries.english: You are fidgeting about like a visitor who has not had enough to eat : (saying) I must go and see So and So properly.
entries.meaning: He hopes to get more food there.

entries.luganda: Osse aga n'aga : ng'agula omugumba omunafu.
entries.english: You have failed both ways : like one who buys (marries) a barren woman who is lazy.

entries.luganda: Osuddeyo gwa Nnaggamba : 1) eyaleka omugole ku kkubo n'agenda mu ntujjo; 2) ng'eyasibira endiga ye e Mbaale.
entries.english: You have lost your memory as Nnaggamba did : 1) when he left his bride on the road (or mu lusuku) and went to the dance; 2) like the fellow who tied up his sheep at Mbaale (Mawokota) and left it there.
entries.meaning: Mbaale is supposed to be the cradle land of the "endiga" clan. Therefore, a Muganda reckons that all the people there are relations of his, who won't steal, as they do not eat "ndiga". The proverbial forgetful person! Thoughtless like Nnaggamba!

entries.english: (He who asks you) "Where do you live?" : wants to find out things about you and tells your enemies.
You are fighting like one who spares the man snoring in the but and pokes (with his spear) the (grass of the) hut.
entries.meaning: He does not dare to attack properly.

entries.luganda: Otawaana ng'envi : gwe zaasooka tizinnamutta, nga zikwata omulala.
entries.english: You are fussy like grey hair : when the one on whom it started is not dead yet, it gets hold of another one.

entries.luganda: Oteeka mu nnyindo ne weerabira akamwa?
entries.english: Do you put (food) to your nose : and forget your mouth?
entries.meaning: "Nnyindo" stands for "yourself" and "kamwa" stands for "your children"; can one refuse to help one's own children (relations)?

entries.luganda: "Oteranga n'oggulawo" : nga gw'ayagala y'ali ku luggi.
entries.english: "You open the door soon" : (says one) if one whom he likes is at the door.

entries.luganda: Oteera nnaku ng'amaaso : ne ky'otoofune gatunuulira.
entries.english: You are making fun of my misfortune like the eyes (do with a man) : they also look at things which you cannot get.

entries.luganda: Oteese nga ga Lubigi : bw'olaba gasikuuse, nga mwayiseemu Bannabusiro.
entries.english: You are at peace like the waters of the Lubigi (river in Busiro): when you see that they are disturbed (stirred up), you know that the people of Busiro have gone through (to sell sugar cane at Kampala).
entries.meaning: If you are worried, it shows that something has come across you.

entries.english: You are fidgety : like the little men in Bulemeezi.
You are stricken with grief (beyond help) : like menvu that have perished.
entries.meaning: As rotten bananas prevent a successful brew of beer, so also a grief-stricken mind is uncapable of joyful conversation.

entries.luganda: Otontomereza : ng'eyanyaga ente emu; nti "Kabaka y'ankongoola"; nti "yaku-temeddeko omukira?" You are complaining incessantly like one who brought only one cow from the raid; (saying) the king despises me; (ironical reply) has he cut off your tail?
entries.english: Play of words: "okukongoola" means to bully, to be hard, to fleece; but "oku-kongola" means to pick off stalks, pediuncles, fruits, vegetables.
entries.meaning: Deliberately misunderstanding the word "y'ankongoola".

entries.luganda: Otudde olubuti : ng'omubi atudde mu balungi.
entries.english: You sit tight (without moving) like an ugly man sitting amongst beautiful ones.
entries.meaning: Or: like a bad man among righteous people; he is ashamed and feels uneasy.

entries.luganda: Otudde tovaayo nga toliko gy'ogenda okukola, sso nga bakugambye.
entries.english: You sit there and don't move and you are not willing to do anything although they have told you.

entries.luganda: Otuula buli kafo : ng'enkejje erimu munnyu.
entries.english: You move about from place to place : like a salted sprat (tasty little fish used for "kukoza mmere").
Sleep does not make an exception even for one who laments his mother.
entries.meaning: It makes one forget even the greatest sorrow.

entries.english: You look with burning desire : like a goat (on a rope) crying for potato-leaves (which it can't reach).

entries.luganda: Otunula enkakaba (= enkaliriza) : 1) ng'alagirira omusota; 2) ng'ejjanzi eriruma ekitooke.
entries.english: You stare with fixed eyes : 1) like one who points at a disappearing snake; 2) like a locust with its big eyes, attacking the banana plant.

entries.luganda: Otunula gadibe ngalye : ng'embwa etunda omuzigo.
entries.english: You look like a person wishing that things should be left over for eating : like a dog that sells butter.
entries.meaning: You have a hungry look.

entries.english: You look with flashing eyes : like a married man who swallows hot matooke.
entries.meaning: Old Kiganda "table manners" required that the husband should wash his fingers as the last one and that he waited till the matooke dished up for him had cooled down a little.

entries.luganda: Otunula kaliisoliiso : ng'enkoko ebiika awali embwa.
entries.english: You are staring suspiciously : like a hen sitting on eggs, when a dog is near.
entries.meaning: She is afraid of remaining on the eggs and she does not want to leave the eggs to the dog.

entries.luganda: Otunula kirungube : 1) ng'embuzi eyali ekulabye tejja kukulamusa; 2) ng'e-sswera ekkulu.
entries.english: You are staring (with wide-open eyes) : 1) like a goat that has seen you and refuses to greet you; 2) like a big fly (with huge eyes).
You gaze into empty space : like the (empty) shell of a snail.
You look cold and gloomy (in helpless anger) : like a dog who walks with the raiders.
You are staring with two empty eyes : like a dog that looks after a sick com-panion.
entries.meaning: It cannot help him (give him medicine). Useless impotent stare.

entries.luganda: Otunula mpulunkanya : ng'ow'ettulu alamusa abangi (or: all mu kitimba).
entries.english: You are looking cock-eyed (squinting) : like a one-eyed fellow greeting many (or: who is behing a curtain).

entries.luganda: Otunula mpwangali (= mbebere, = nnamulanda) : 1) ng'akaabira gw'atalabako; 2) ng'omukulu ateetimba; 3) ng'omukondeere amazeewo emyungu; 4) ng'e-mbwa esudde ekyuma.
entries.english: You are looking helpless (as if at a loss) : 1) like a child crying for the absent mother; 2) like an old man who has no curtain in front of his bed (he is sur-prised at the light in the morning); 3) like the hornblower who has eaten the gourds (so that he cannot make any more trumpets); 4) as a dog looks, when he has lost his bell.
You are despising us (the owners of the girl say) : when others take their girl (without considering the legitimate customary ways).
You are taking a risk : like a chicken swallowing biting ants.

entries.luganda: Otuwewula mukonga : ng'embwa egenda ku mulambo.
entries.english: You devour us with your eyes : like a dog passing a corpse.
Take the little (I can give you) with kind words.

entries.luganda: Ovudde mu muwumbo : n'odda ku kitole.
entries.english: You went away from plenty of matooke : and go to a little mouthful.
entries.meaning: You are a fool to leave a promising situation (work, marriage) and turn to a hopeless one.

entries.luganda: Ow'akagaali y'afuuka nkima : nti olinkima ku ggaali yo.
entries.english: The cyclist becomes a monkey : (because they say to him) "oli-nkima" (you will fetch me) (teasingly: you are a monkey).
One who possesses his own property (kantu, kamere, kanyama), may use it : a refusal to give others does not do away with relationship (as it would do with friendship).
He who possesses his own millet : does with it as he likes.
Wherever the vendor on the market chooses to be, there he puts his wares.
entries.meaning: Formerly there were no fixed places (masa) to be rented by the vendors; but each one tried to come early, to get the most promising place. - "First come, first served". Germ. "Wer zuerst kommt, mahlt zuerst".

entries.english: A glutton : cannot be told about hospitality (received).
entries.meaning: If he is told about the food which they could not finish, he cannot believe it.

entries.english: (He who is brewing beer) does not let a passionate drinker taste his half-fermented beer.
entries.meaning: Because he would never stop, when he has once put his luseke into the beer vat.

entries.english: A glutton is a carpenter (cuts boards).
entries.meaning: Because when you tell him of a luscious meal, he says "mbaawo" (if I had been there), I should have eaten like a king!

entries.luganda: Ow'amagezi amangi gamuba ku mwoyo : ow'amatono ku mumwa.
entries.english: He who possesses much wisdom, has it in his heart : he who has little, has it on his lips.
A strong man beats you with the stick which you had in your own hands.
entries.meaning: He beats you with your own weapons.

entries.luganda: Ow'amaanyi amatono : mu lumbe anyagamu nnyina.
entries.english: One of little strength : wins a mother at the funeral (of the father).

entries.luganda: Ow'amaanyi amatono : y'agagera; wakasanke atwala bya mu nkwawa, ebiwe-wuka bye kayinza.
entries.english: One of little strength : measures it wisely; the kasanke (wax-bill-bird) carries away the soft feathers from under the wings (of the chickens), the soft ones (light ones) it can carry to its nest.

entries.luganda: Owampanya ng'atatte mukago : 1) nti omukazi taliiwo; 2) nti osanze mmaze okulya.
entries.english: You are making excuses like one who is not willing to make blood-brotherhood : 1) (saying) my wife is not at home (I cannot give you any food); 2) (saying) you have come after I have finished eating (the rubrics prescribe eating only after the ceremony!).

entries.luganda: Ow'amatama amangi : si y'aba omwami; waŋŋaaŋa si y'alarnula ewa wakasanke.
entries.english: It is not cheekiness that makes one a chief : the hornbill does not rule in the sphere of the small red finch.
An obstinate person does not get the meat, but only the broth.
entries.meaning: He offends the host and is no longer welcome.

entries.english: If you don't tell a hunchback the truth to his face : you will not cover yourself.
entries.meaning: Sleeping on the same bed, he will require the greater part of the kikunta (blanket). - Selfishness. - Inconsiderate people must be told.

entries.luganda: Ow'ebbango olaba yeebaka obugazi : nga ekitanda mulimu ekinnya.
entries.english: If you see a hunchback lying on his back : in that bed there is a hollow.
One who has a debt : promises to pay back in a few days.

entries.luganda: Ow'ebigere mwami : ne Diisi amufuyira eŋŋombe.
entries.english: A pedestrian is a chief (superior person) : even the D.C.
entries.meaning: (District Commissioner) blows the trumpet for him. Give way for my car!

entries.english: (amatu) Your conversation is empty (shallow) : like the packets in which butter was wrapped up.
entries.meaning: You are talking uncharitably. - The butter wrapped up in the packets of byayi has melted away.

entries.english: A townsman likes to see porters.

entries.luganda: Ow'ekikye talemererwa : enjovu teremererwa masanga gaayo.
entries.english: What is given to one (by God, by nature), is not beyond his strength : the elephant can carry his tusks.

entries.luganda: Ow'ekikye tiyeerabira (= takyerabira) : Walumbe tiyeerabira mukadde.
entries.english: The owner of a thing does not forget it : death does not forget (to fetch) the old.
As a visitor (who comes to you) at night calls you : so you answer him.- If he calls you with a loud voice, you answer loudly; if he speaks softly, you answer softly.
(= Omugenyi w'ekitiibwa - - ) A visitor of high standing makes you serve up underdone meat.
entries.meaning: You are afraid to let him wait long.

entries.luganda: Ow'ekitiibwa n'ekikye : mu nnyindo temugenda nnwe bbiri.
entries.english: Let a person of respect have the honour due to him : you can't put two fingers into one nostril.
entries.meaning: Mwami - mukopi, mugabe - mutabaazi.

entries.english: A bald fellow lets his courtyard grow wild : and hoes his head.
entries.meaning: What grows on his head, he combs out. - Said of people who do useless work and neglect their duties.

entries.luganda: Ow'e Kiwaama atuuse mu lumbe : asinga wa Maziga mangi eyalira e Ssingo.
entries.english: A mourner from Kiwaama who comes to a burial, is worth more than one who has plenty of tears and sheds them in Ssingo.
entries.meaning: "Wa Kiwaama" is one who cannot shed tears. - Silent grief is worth more than loud wailing.

entries.english: A bad butcher : makes you get hold of the meat yourself.
entries.meaning: Said of any bad workmanship, also in cooking etc. Also of laziness.

entries.english: (= Ow'embugubugu - - ) One who is overhasty : starts eating when the king is not yet resting.
The goatherd tells tales about the shepherd.
entries.meaning: The pantry boy about the cook.

entries.english: The shepherd does not look in a friendly manner at the cowherd.
A man with a timid heart : does not sell on the market.
entries.meaning: Anyone who comes with a spear would frighten him. - "Faint heart never won fair lady" (Shakespeare).

entries.english: You behave(d) shamefully : like one who won't go back to Buganda.
entries.meaning: Shaming one's own tribe, living abroad.

entries.english: He who postpones sowing in time : eats begged vegetables.
entries.meaning: The industrious (prudent) woman sows the vegetables immediately after the first rain; the subsequent rains will make them grow abundantly. The lazy woman postpones the sowing for a better time which might never come. - Lazy at work and dissatisfied afterwards.

entries.english: (= Ow'envumula mbi - - ) A bad doctor : gets only the fee paid in advance.
entries.meaning: "Kikuba-nsiko" is the fee the medicine-man demands, before he goes in search for medicine. If he can't heal the sick person, he gets nothing else.

entries.english: A selfish eater : does not eat the mucus of his nose.
entries.meaning: Because he keeps all good things for himself. - Bukodo, meanness.

entries.english: He who has an offensive way of talking : is not asked questions.

entries.luganda: Ow'enkaaba mbi : agoba omwami mu lumbe (nti "eya kuno ngiguze"; ko omwami, nti "nze mmusse?").
entries.english: A woman who exaggerates her wailing (at the burial of her husband) : drives the chief away from the burial (she cries: "I have paid for the food" (wailing expression); and the chief retorts: "Have I perhaps killed him!?").
An idle talker : is preferable to a brewer.
entries.meaning: The brewer does not tell you that he has beer; but the talker finds out the beer places and tells you.

entries.english: A slanderer observes (watches) things (some of his judgement is correct, some wrong) : but what finally breaks him, is calumny.
A scandalmonger does not wash the mubisi off his feet (after treading the bika-mulo; he is so keen to take the news to other people, that he has no time to wash).
A man who sings bad songs : sings them amongst his friends.
entries.meaning: The friends are as bad as he is.

entries.luganda: Ow'ensala mbi : akwasa omwami mu nnyama.
entries.english: He who cuts the meat badly (distributes unfairly) : makes the master get hold of it.
entries.meaning: Bad workmanship makes the master do the work over again.

entries.luganda: Ow'ensala mbi : asalira mu mbuga ye.
entries.english: One who administers judgement badly : does it in his own place.
entries.meaning: Answer of a chief who has been told that his decision is not fair: "I have decided so; if you are not pleased, go somewhere else!" Ssal.p.34:

entries.english: A man who treats his tenants badly : his superior chief puts tenants on the land.
entries.meaning: The inexperienced little chief does not get any tenants of his own. All are afraid of him.

entries.luganda: Ow'ensumika mbi : akyala ewa muganda we (= asumikira mu babe); ssemukuto wa nnamunyenye.
entries.english: One who is badly dressed : visits at his brother's (at his relations) (or: dresses amongst his equals); the tree-cricket visits the glow-worm.
entries.meaning: Both have ridiculously short wings.

entries.english: An inconsiderate talker : does not keep back his words on the teeth.
A man who has got a wide-open cooking pot.
entries.meaning: Compliment for a hospitable person, a good host.

entries.english: He who has only little food for the road : is the first to open the parcel.
He who has no manners in seating himself : easily finds a place.
entries.meaning: The others shun him. He elbows his way through the crowd.

entries.luganda: Ow'entuula mbi : y'atuula mbogo mu maaso.
entries.english: He who sits in a wrong place : sits down in front of a buffalo (king, big chief).
entries.meaning: He will be punished: degradation, jail, death.

entries.luganda: Ow'ewange awulira nga mbwa : bw'alaba abagenyi, ng'addira kibbo kukola.
entries.english: My wife at home is obedient to the dog : (the dog announces visitors) and she seeing them gets hold of the basket to get food to cook for them (as if the dog were her husband).
An unmarried girl is like a bushbuck : also one who will not spear it, stalks it.
entries.meaning: A desirable girl has many suitors.

entries.english: An unmarried person (boy) is like a crow : where it sees a skin, it comes down.
One of petty-quarrels : always raises them at home.
entries.meaning: Because at somebody else's home he has nothing to say.

entries.english: (muliro) One who has a fire which burns well : does not look at one who has got only a smouldering one.
entries.meaning: Despising those not so well-situated.

entries.english: An angry man does not cut off all of the ears.
entries.meaning: In his hurry he lets pieces stand. - Anger (rashness, precipitation) performs no proper work.

entries.english: A scandalmonger is like the pest : when it destroys homes, it does not leave off (talking scandal).
A tale-bearer is like one with a new pipe : wherever he sits down, he lights it (to be seen).
He who possesses a fish trap : will not eat without nva (fish).
The owner of a fish-trap : does not die of hunger.
A blood brother is like a kibalangulo (piece of very smooth wood - ssettaala or musasa - on which the razor is stropped) : a piece of barkcloth is placed upon the kibalangulo and then cut straight.
entries.meaning: As the stropping block is covered, so the blood brother has to cover (protect, defend) his friend against any harm.
