entries.english: A man with one wife : is chief among the unmarried.
entries.meaning: One with more wives has always somebody to work for him. But when one's only wife has gone away, he has to cook, fetch water etc. himself.

entries.luganda: Ow'omulimo teyeetereka : omubazzi w'enseke ku biwondowondo.
entries.english: A working man does not do his job in hiding : the maker of beer-tubes (for sucking beer) is seen at the biwondowondo (twigs used for making the tubes).

entries.luganda: Ow'omulimo teyeetereka : nnabbubi ayita n'ebitimba bye; kasennya-nku n'enku ze.
entries.english: A working man does not do his job in hiding : the spider walks with its web; the kasennya-nku (ingect) with its firewood.

entries.luganda: Ow'omuliraano bw'olaba ayita mu ntungo : nga bwe litaabe ddalu, kinaaba kizindo.
entries.english: If you see your neighbour passing through your semsem-field : if it is not madness, it is plundering.
A cock is not eaten without your neighbour being invited.
The neighbour does not love his child (as much as) he loves its ears.
entries.meaning: Because when he hears a strange noise outside (at night), he tells his children: amatu musuuza bweru (listen!). In case of a raid they would flee themselves, not let the ears be thrown outside. Play upon words!

entries.english: A glutton is like a chief : (he eats first and) when he has had enough, he lets others partake.
A man with a bad temper who buys a dog : makes it bark (because he beats it).
He who is harsh with (beats) his wife : understands (his foolishness), when he is a bachelor again (when his wife has left him).
A woman who has a (small) child : does not become mad (although she talks a lot to the child without getting an answer, the people don't call her silly).
entries.meaning: One without a child and doing so is considered mad.

entries.english: A man who has got his own will (taste) : buys what he fancies.
entries.meaning: Engl. "There is no accounting for tastes". Germ. "Des Menschen Wine ist sein Himmelreich".

entries.english: It is easier to cure one of a wound : than of hunger.
entries.meaning: Hunger always comes back. Hunger is an incurable sickness.

entries.luganda: Owoza kandolindoli : ng'omusajja agamba, nti omusota gusse ente yange.
entries.english: You are pleading (complaining) incessantly : like a man who says: "A snake has killed my cow".
entries.meaning: Would it have been better, if it had killed the herdsman? - It could have been worse.

entries.luganda: Owoza ng'omusibe alwadde : nti mbikka bbiri mbugume.
entries.english: You are pleading like a prisoner who is sick : (saying) "Cover me with two blankets, that I may get warm".
entries.meaning: As if he had made the blankets (bark-cloths) himself!

entries.luganda: Owoza olujerengu : Bannasingo lwe bawoza; baali enkumi bbiri, nti tunaasula mu Kiyonjo.
entries.english: You plead (talk) nonsensically : as the men of Ssingo did; (when they pleaded their case), they were 2000 in number, and they said: we shall sleep at Kiyonjo (kyalo).
entries.meaning: Sarcastic reply: Will there be room for all of you in a kiyonjo (hen-coop)? Play on words!

entries.english: You have heard the whistle : but you have not seen the seller of salt.
entries.meaning: Meaning: Laughing at somebody who is disappointed. - In former times Banyoro went round selling lumps of salt and announced their presence by blowing a whistle. - Engl. "The early bird catches the worm". "Procrastination is the thief of time". "Make hay whilst the sun shines". Germ. "Was du heute kannst besorgen, das verschiebe nicht auf morgen".

entries.english: "You are in a great hurry" : (so you say to one) who goes to a place he knows (expecting something pleasant there).

entries.luganda: Oyanza amagalo : ng'omuwa-butwa asigadde awali omulwadde.
entries.english: You feel about with your hands : like a poisoner who remains with the sick person (till he gets a chance to poison him).

entries.luganda: Oyigganga otta : omwabukira busa si muyiggo.
entries.english: When you hunt, there should be results : if you get nothing, it is no hunt.

entries.luganda: Oyogedde bikuliko : ng'ow'amalibu, nti tunaakeera mu lubungubungu.
entries.english: You talk of things concerning yourself : like the toothless man who said: we start off at dawn.
entries.meaning: The word "bungu" indicates also "with missing teeth". Duta 141. Other similar sayings will be found under "Okekkera", "Weekiina", "Weeyoge-za" or "Weenyumiikiriza".

entries.english: You are saying contradictory things : like the fingers (of the hands).
entries.meaning: They all have different lengths.

entries.luganda: Oyogedde kirabika ng'omukadde nti nvudde emmanga, ng'omubiri gunjii-kaylika; nti tulabye ensalosalo mwe guyiikidde.
entries.english: You are saying what is obvious like the old man : (who said) I come from down there and my body is trembling and weak (literally: the strength of my body has flown out); (reply) we see the channels (i.e.
entries.meaning: the wrinkles) through which it has flown out. Play on words: "okuyiikayiika" means "pour out in continuous stream" and "be flabby".

entries.luganda: Oyogedde kirabika ng'omusale w'amatu akwekweta : nti tuzze katwe kasa; nti garneredde mu kikwekweto?
entries.english: You are talking about what is evident, like one whose ears have been cut off and who says (coming home from a raid) : we came back with nothing on our heads (no booty); (sarcastic reply) did your ears grow again during the raid?
entries.meaning: We knew that you had no ears on your head. Rub.C.937. 4726 Oyogedde kirabika ng'ow'ekiwalaata alabye engo : nti "enviiri zinvudde ku mutwe". You are talking of what is obvious, like the man with a bald head, who had seen a leopard (saying) "All my hair came off my head".

entries.luganda: Oyogedde kirabika ng'ow'entumbi : nti nnasuze olubuto lundi eyo.
entries.english: You are talking of what is evident, like a man sick of dropsy : (saying) I have spent the night with a troublesome stomach.
entries.meaning: Of course, such a stomach will cause trouble!

entries.luganda: Oyogedde kirungi nga kya kudda Buganda : n'ataanyaga alanga.
entries.english: You are speaking of cheerful things like talking about returning to Buganda : even one who has no booty (from the raid) rejoices.

entries.luganda: Oyogedde kituufu : nga ddiba lya nte.
entries.english: What you are saying is sufficient : like the hide of a cow.
entries.meaning: One cow-hide is big enough for a garment.

entries.english: You talk loudly (about somebody) : like a favourite trying to accuse somebody in the chief's place.
entries.meaning: He likes to draw the attention of the master, although he does not address the chief directly.

entries.luganda: Oyogera kuno na kuno : nga mukono ogw'omusasi.
entries.english: You talk about this and that : you are like the hand of a man who works for food.
entries.meaning: He came for matooke; but seeing other things (vegetables etc.) he asks for them as well. - Not easily satisfied.

entries.luganda: Oyogera tolototto : nga kamwa kanaku (= ng'ow'omumwa atakuba).
entries.english: You are complaining (criticising) constantly : like a man who is harsh with his wife (or: like one who has not the courage to beat her).

entries.luganda: Oyomba olutulumuko : nga gwe babbira omuzigo.
entries.english: You are quarrelling incessantly : like one from whom they stole butter (to rub on the body).
entries.meaning: Always complaining about the same thing. Rub.C.391. 4737 Oyota gwa vvu : nti nnina abaana. You are warming yourself at a fire which is more ashes than fire : (and you say) "I have children!" Don't you tell them to clean out the ashes from the kyoto? P. 4738 Ozaala abakulu : nga bbumbuzzi? Are you bringing forth grown-ups : like the bbumbuzzi (mason-wasp)? Used as an answer to "Mwana wange", if employed by people of equal age.

entries.english: You report missing, but not dead.
entries.meaning: Rather be missing than dead. Used by people far from home, or talking about experiences in foreign lands.

entries.english: You might send your body abroad : but you won't forget your mother-tongue.

entries.luganda: Ozeesennyedde za kukwokya : kijja-na-nnenge ku kkubo.
entries.english: You have gathered firewood to burn yourself : like a person walking with a lubugo (garment) hanging to the ground on the road.
entries.meaning: It gets dirty and torn. - You have caused trouble for yourself! Your own fault!

entries.english: (ekibibi) You put on airs like one who managed to heap up just one potato-hill.

entries.luganda: Ozinuka nga w'eriiso limu ng'agamba : tunaatambula obudde ne bukya.
entries.english: You are bragging (put on airs) like a one-eyed person saying : we shall walk all night till dawn.
entries.meaning: He can scarcely see the way! - Lat. "Parturiunt montes - nascetur ridiculus mus" (Horace).

entries.english: You walk with airs : like a .fat goat that has broken a cooking pot.
You have refused to take a meal at a bachelor's home.
entries.meaning: Your refusal is acceptable to him, as he has no wife to cook the food.

entries.english: (okwawa = okunoga) You are eating with one who can pluck (plenty of) vegetables in her garden.
entries.meaning: A woman saying so, is pleased with your appetite - and will give you another helping.

entries.english: It is easier to prevent somebody from entering (your home) than from leaving it.
entries.meaning: Unwelcome guests, drunkards etc.

entries.luganda: Ozze gawanye nga bisesemye : okwata mumwa biyuza ngalo.
entries.english: You come suddenly like vomit : you might try to hold your mouth shut, but it will pull your fingers apart.

entries.luganda: Ozze katwe kasa : onoddayo katwe kasa.
entries.english: You have come with nothing on your head (no presents) : you shall return with nothing on your head.

entries.luganda: Ozze oyambalidde mu ntumbwe : nga nkoko.
entries.english: You have dressed above the calves : like a hen.
entries.meaning: Feathers half-way down the legs - "Knickerbockers".

entries.english: Azzizza gwa: 0765) Ap.Eng.No.29.
You have committed a crime like the chief who cheated Nnaggomola of his burial.
entries.meaning: Not fulfilling promises made. - A debt which is never paid.

entries.english: I don't want to be spied upon in my ddiiro (eating place).
(A man who says) "I don't want to start a quarrel" : begins to be awkward.

entries.luganda: "Sala ku kino, owe kayombera" : nga y'alidde ekikira.
entries.english: "Cut from this and give it to the grouser" : (says) the one who has already eaten a bigger piece (of meat).
entries.meaning: Ostentatious magnanimity. Rub.C.1298. 4761 "Sala ku yange, owe kalwanira". (cf. Sala ku kino: 4760) Rub.C.1955.

entries.english: I have not bought a cow : I have bought a heap of trouble.
entries.meaning: So says a man who has hired or bought a cow and cannot pay for it, although the creditor comes day after day to collect his debt.

entries.luganda: Sazza musango : nnazza olubanja lwa Nnamunkululu (= Nnamunkukulu) oluta-ggwa mu nju.
entries.english: I have not committed a crime : but I have contracted a huge debt, the debt of Nnamunkululu (namely a tremendous affair), which does not come to an end in my house.
entries.meaning: "Nnamunkululu" is a voracious monster, never satisfied and like the "lubuto".

entries.english: (mukka) I do not desire a long nose (considered a sign of beauty) : I only want to breathe.
entries.meaning: Not aesthetic, but practical considerations.

entries.luganda: "Segulira, emmandwa etuule" : nga bye yamulagula byatuukirira (= byalaka).
entries.english: "Make room for the soothsayer to sit" : (so says one) to whom the soothsayer has prophesied what became truth.
entries.meaning: Expression of praise for a wise man whose prediction came true.

entries.english: "I have nothing to do with (your) row about hunger" : (so says the man) when his favourite woman has taken the food (of the others).
entries.meaning: He would speak differently, if it had been the "mukyawe".

entries.luganda: "Siba nze ne ntuula" : asula ku miggo.
entries.english: "If I were you, I would not stay" (with such a husband, so says a woman to her friend who is often beaten) : but she herself suffers under the sticks (and does not go away).
If I had not come, this food would not have been finished.
entries.meaning: So says one who first pretends not to be willing to eat, but then changes his mind.

entries.luganda: "Siibisobole" : ng'agenze; amannyo ag'engulu ogasanga ku kiwanga enviiri n'a-matu ebyajjirako nga bigenze.
entries.english: "Those things beat me" (I cannot understand them) : as it is with a dead person; the upper teeth you find still in the skull, whilst the hair and the ears which were born on it, are gone.
entries.meaning: Allusion to replacement of old things (persons) by new ones. The old don't want to retire!

entries.luganda: "Sibula kambe mu kibira" : nga yaluma ku kibowabowa ekikaawa.
entries.english: "I am not without a knife in the forest" : (so says one) who has bitten off a bitter climber (liane).
entries.meaning: That taught him to use a knife instead of his teeth. Lat. "Experientia docet".

entries.english: "I am not asked for medicine" : (says the woman) who has children who suck lustily.
entries.meaning: The children are never sick; so the mother has no experience with medicine.

entries.english: "I never lose anything" : (one who says so) is a poor man.
entries.meaning: Because nobody comes to him for a loan.

entries.english: The man whci says "I shall not be ruled" dies a vagabond (a pauper).
The man who says "I am not going to be ruled by a chief", becomes a tenant of the king's mother.
entries.meaning: He will be ruled by her chiefs and is then ruled by a woman. Germ. "Yom Regen in die Traufe kommen". Engl. "From bad to worse". - "From the frying-pan into the fire".

entries.english: One who says "I am not going to kneel to a chief" : don't give a chicken to him to keep for you!
entries.meaning: It won't be safe there, because he will get into trouble with the chief, who will requisition it for disobedience.

entries.luganda: Sigaba bikunta : nga sinnaggyamu kya kwebikka.
entries.english: I do not give away (distribute) bedding : without first taking from it what might be useful for my bed.
entries.meaning: Engl. "Charity begins at home". Lat. "Proximus sum egomet mihi" (Horace).

entries.english: The man who says "I don't say that there is anything in the jungle" (a wild animal or a snake) : is giving a warning.
entries.meaning: Phrase used to indicate that there is some danger (thief, robber) inside the hut.

entries.luganda: "Sigatta mugugu na mmandwa" : bw'esamira terwa kugukutikka.
entries.english: You say "I don't want to carry a load with a musamize" : when the spirit comes over him (on the road), he will soon put it on your head (and you will have to carry two loads).
"I do not remind a rich man" : (says one) who has enough to eat (namely to remind him of something he has promised me).
"Not even for the sake of the children" : (says the one) who is left in the wilderness.
entries.meaning: He does not dare to take the risk of travelling through the danger. The lesser evil is to stay put.

entries.english: (kalulu) (A man confronted with the necessity of submitting to an ordeal says) "I am not shunning it" : and it bums him (he loses the court case).
entries.meaning: Such ordeals were used to settle cases between two litigants who did not find satisfaction with the chiefs (judges). They had to drink the "akasera" (made from poisonous maduudu seeds). When the potation worked and the men were overpowered by the strong drink, they were ordered to get up and step over a lusanja tied low between two banana-stems and to come to the mixer of the maduudu drink "okweyanza" (magunda). The one who was able to do it, won the court case.

entries.luganda: "Sikirabanga" : 1) bamukubira ku buko; 2) y'amala n'akiraba; omukazi tayita njala kujja.
entries.english: (One who says) "I never saw such a thing" : 1) is being beaten at his wife's home (a son-in-law is never beaten by his "mukoddomi"; not even his dog may be beaten); 2) sees it there and then; if the woman complains about famine, she does not want it to come.
"I shall not desert you in your work of cutting grass (for thatching)" : (so one says) if he has seen beer (at your home).
entries.meaning: He helps you a while in the hope of being rewarded with a drink.

entries.english: This is not killing : but finding (i.e.
entries.meaning: easy to get). Hunting and killing the animal means effort.

entries.english: I have not a mere piece of wood in my hands : but an axe.
entries.meaning: So look out, if you don't want to be hurt.

entries.english: "I don't care about them (the children) any longer, I shall beget others" : (so speaks the father) when the children intend to kill him.
entries.meaning: Expression about a hopeless situation.

entries.english: (He who says) "I shall not do it again" : 1) has his hands on the back (his hands are tied on the back and that makes him say so); 2) does not give up his evil inclination (sorrow does not always mean betterment).

entries.luganda: "Sikyaliko bye ntenda (= gwe mbitendera)" : nga takyaliko gw'abibuulira (or: nga takyalina gw'ayogera naye).
entries.english: I have nothing more to tell : (says the talkative person) if there is nobody left to listen to him.
(The man who protests) "I am not going to make blood-brotherhood again" lives already with a blood-brother.

entries.luganda: Simala kulya : ne ndyoka njogera kindeese.
entries.english: I don't want to eat first and then to speak about what has brought me here.
entries.meaning: First duty, then pleasure; first work, then relaxation.

entries.english: "Choose the one (lubugo, lugoye) you like" : (says the) husband to his favourite woman.
entries.meaning: He has brought several garments; but his favourite is given the first choice.

entries.luganda: "Sinywa mwenge" : bw'atuuka awali enguuli, ng'atereera; nti ogwa kabula gwe gusinga enguuli obuka.
entries.english: "I never drink beer" (says the man) : but when he comes to a place where there is waragi (spirits), he settles down; we might ask: is the beer made of kabula-mbidde perhaps stronger than waragi?

entries.luganda: "Siriiko kye nkukisa" : bw'akyama gy'oli akubayo mabega.
entries.english: "I hide nothing from you" (he says); but when he goes aside, he turns his back to you.
"I shall not desert you in trouble (in an evil place)" : one saying so may desert you, because you offer him food without vegetables (or meat).
entries.meaning: He may desert you, only because he is not satisfied with the food. - Lat. "Donec ens felix, multos habebis amicos" (Ovid).

entries.luganda: Sirina gawemukira Bunyolo kulya nvubu : ng'atalidda Buganda.
entries.english: I have no mind to do despicable things in.
entries.meaning: Bunyoro (= abroad) e.g. to eat hippo meat : as one might do who does not intend to go back to Buganda.

entries.luganda: "Sirina kye nkukisa" : bw'aba yeesiba, akukuba mabega.
entries.english: "I have nothing to hide from you" : (she says) but when she dresses, she turns away from you.
If the money does not suffice (to pay for a thing) : the carrier does not roll up his head-pad (to take it away).
entries.meaning: It is no use starting a thing which is beyond your means.

entries.luganda: "Siringi zaabula" : asiiba waka; nti sings ze zijja nga zikunoonya?
entries.english: "I have lost my money" (he says) : and stays at home; why don't you go and look for it?
entries.meaning: Do you think the money will come and look for you?

entries.luganda: "Siringi ze nfuna, simanyi gye zidda" : awasa banobye.
entries.english: "I can't understand where all my money goes to!" : (says one) who married women who have run away from their husbands.
entries.meaning: He does not remember the fines of the law-suits!

entries.english: "I shall never leave here" (a mother might protest) : but sickness of her child will move her.
"I shall not move from here (I shall always remain with you)" (so one assures you) : but trouble with the dog (musango gwa mbwa) gets him away.
entries.meaning: Owners of dogs are very sensitive about their pets; a man might send away his wife, if she has not fed the dog.

entries.english: (He who maintains) "I do not dream what does not happen" : drives the whole village away.
entries.meaning: He predicts evil (raiders falling over the village etc.) and frightens the people away.

entries.english: (One who says) "I don't eat (I have nothing to eat)" : shows his emaciated body (to make people believe that he is hungry).
He who says "I don't eat little" : has foul breath (remains hungry).
entries.meaning: One who asks for too much, goes away emptyhanded.

entries.english: "I don't let go the knife" (says the stubborn child), as long as it has not cut him yet.
entries.meaning: People often will go on playing with danger or doing evil, until harm comes to them. Engl. "The pitcher goes so often to the well, that it is broken at last'.

entries.english: "I don't give up what belongs to me" : (says) the banana plant of Katente (which does not shed the bracts of the kiwago).
entries.meaning: "Sita-kange" is the name of a species of banana. - Alluding to miserly behaviour!

entries.english: "I do not kill a young Munyoro (in battle)" (I prefer to keep him as my slave) : (but) when he grows up, he will make you lose your market wares (they are good businessmen).
entries.meaning: Or, if he becomes chief, he will kill your children.

entries.english: I do not kill (an animal for meat) in the morning and wait (with eating) till evening (i.e.
entries.meaning: I prefer to tackle it at once). It might be stolen by men or animals. Engl. "Make hay whilst the sun shines".

entries.luganda: "Siva nnyuma" : nga waliwo ekyamukanga (= ng'alina ekyamutiisa).
entries.english: "I am not moving from the back" : (says one) who is threatened (or: frightened) by something in front.
entries.meaning: He wants protection from the front.

entries.luganda: "Siva (= siive) we boogera" : 1) y'abuuka n'akabalangulo mu mutwe; 2) ze mbale.
entries.english: "I am not going away from where they.
entries.meaning: discuss things" (he thinks or says) : 1) but he flies away with the axe-handle on his head (they beat the intruder); 2) that means bumps on his head (he who mixes himself in other people's business receives a hard lesson).

entries.english: "I am not going from here, let them talk" : (one saying so) goes from there with bumps and wounds.

entries.luganda: "Sivaawo ne bangeya" : 1) olubugo asigaza nsawo; 2) olubugo yeesiba lwa nkundulu.
entries.english: (He who says) "I am not going away from here, although they speak evil of me" : 1) leaves his barkcloth (dress) looking like a bag; 2) wraps his barkcloth round him like a bag of banana fibre (from the long sitting).
(Although he says) "I am not going to leave this place" : hunger moves him.

entries.luganda: "Siwakana zituula" : ng'alabye gw'amegga; naye obanga tamumegga ng'agamba "sizibaako".
entries.english: (mpaka) (The man who says) "I am not going to argue whilst sitting down" : has seen somebody he is able to throw (in wrestling) (meaning: get up, fight!); but if he sees that he will not manage him, he says: "I have nothing to do with the affair".

entries.luganda: "Siwa muto lugero" : nga talumanyi (= nga lumbuze).
entries.english: "I do not speak in proverbs to a child" : (he says so) because he does not understand (remember) them himself.
entries.meaning: Used for reasons which are only pretence. Like "Sour grapes".

entries.english: "I am not crying for mercy" (so one pretends) : as long as he is not caught.
(He who says) "I shall not be put to shame" (I shall not act shamelessly) : dies with the chief.
I am not joining the dog in its speed.
entries.meaning: Expression of one who does not want to exert himself.

entries.luganda: "Siiyimbe mwana na ttooke" : nga gy'ava akkuta.
entries.english: "I am not going to carry the child and the ttooke (nkota)" : (says the lazy woman), if she has eaten enough at home.

entries.luganda: "Siyita mu kyoto" : 1) nga tumuli ky'ayokyamu; 2) nga tofumbiddwa wa mumwa (luwazo).
entries.english: "I am not going to pass through the fireplace" (she says) : 1) when there is nothing to be roasted; 2) if she is not married to a man who is a hard master (and beats her) (in this case she tries to escape even through the fire).
"I do not want to go alone" (you say to your younger sister), if there is one.

entries.luganda: "Siyombera bya mu lumbe" : bw'atuuka mu kkubo ng'abala mu ngalo.
entries.english: "I do not quarrel about things (which are divided) when somebody has died" (one who says so) can only count his fingers, when he goes away (empty-handed).

entries.luganda: "Siyombera mukwano" : nga gwe yakwana emitala gukaze.
entries.english: "I am not vexed (jealous) about my (girl) friend" (one might say so) : if the love, he had on the other hill, has cooled down.
"Dip your morsel first into the sauce" : (so one says) who measures carefully your "nnoga" (morsel, what you take).
entries.meaning: Also said of a woman who plays her husband into the hands of another woman (her sister), in order to have a reason later to sin with another man.

entries.luganda: Ssajjabbi : liwoomera mu ngabo (or: liwoomera mirimu).
entries.english: An ugly man looks charming, when he is in battle-dress (when he works).

entries.luganda: Ssajjabbi : tiribulwa kye lisiimwako (= tabulwa ky'asiimibwako).
entries.english: A bad man does not lack qualities which are pleasing in him.
entries.meaning: Even bad characters have their good points.

entries.english: Fat : is an attraction for buyers (of meat).
entries.meaning: Good looks are a recommendation.

entries.english: The man who is nearest to the enemy in pursuit : is the real leader.
Those who come back from fishing 'nsonze don't pass straight (openly) through the courtyard.
entries.meaning: They don't want to be seen with their catch, lest they should have to give to others.

entries.luganda: Ssebaddusa enteme : baleka emisala mu kyalo.
entries.english: They run away with the cuttings of the mutuba tree : but the good bark on the old tree they leave behind in the village (where they lived).
entries.meaning: The valuable things they leave behind and apparently useless things they take along. Said jokingly of people who have to leave their home and take along what they can. Twigs of the good old mutuba tree are taken along to be planted in the new home.

entries.english: Those who let the corncockle grow (do not weed out the maize field in time) : will next pull out the maize plants (with the roots of the cockle).

entries.luganda: Ssebagayaaza muddo : nti tugende tukoole entungo.
entries.english: Those who let the weeds grow (let them in peace) : (say) let's go and weed out the semsem!
entries.meaning: And they will pull out the semsem plants with the weeds. Belated remedy!

entries.english: A liar (swaggerer) : a single banana he calls "beer".
entries.meaning: He tells a person: go to gundi, he has beer, although gundi has only a few "mbi-dde".

entries.english: Those who do not want to get children : forget their old age.
entries.meaning: They will be sorry, when they have nobody to help them.

entries.english: They close the doorways and forget the gaps (between door and wall).
entries.meaning: To prevent evil one must consider more than one source of it. Baggala-miryango is a proper name.

entries.luganda: Ssebakiina jjenje : nti lino ssaabi; nti omuzigo liguggya (= lisaabira) mu ttaka?
entries.english: They make fun with the cricket : (saying) this is well smeared in; (reply) does the cricket get the fat out of the soil (or: smear itself in the soil)?

entries.luganda: Ssebakiina luwombo : nti lukira ekibya; olumalamu enva ng'asuula.
entries.english: They make fun of the banana leaf (in which food is cooked) : (saying) it is handier than a bowl; when one has finished the food, one can throw it away.

entries.luganda: Ssebakiina musibe : omukiina akukibia; ng'omugamba "omusango gukulumya omwoyo gwa kukutta"; naye ng'addamu "ppenda okugulekera nga ggwe wagu-zza".
entries.english: People are nasty with a prisoner : you sneer at him and he sneers at you; you say to him: "Your evil deed is worrying you, because you will have to die for it"; but he gives back: "I am going to bequeath it to you, as if you had com-mitted it yourself'.
entries.meaning: What has that to do with you? That is my own business.

entries.english: He who hides the fire (which he was to fetch) : is waiting to be abused.
entries.meaning: He has brought the fire, but hides it behind his back, until they call him names; then he produces it and has a good laugh at them.

entries.luganda: Ssebakisa mulwadde : 1) okukuba kulimuloopa; 2) owulirira ku nkoko.
entries.english: When they hide a sick person (the sickness of a person) : 1) beating about with a stick will reveal him; 2) from the cackle of the hens you can hear (that some-body is there).
One who hides his mallet (i.e.
entries.meaning: a cunning, fraudulent person). When he does not actually use it (in beating barkcloth), he hides it wrapped up in the corner behind the entrance (ezzizi), so that nobody can ask for the loan of it. Still he will be seen using it next morning. Duta 848. 4879 Ssebalamu tebeesigwa. The living are not to be trusted.

entries.english: Those who kill themselves (say) : the spirit kills us.
entries.meaning: Blaming somebody else for one's own evil deed.

entries.english: Somebody with many children : one of them will certainly receive a chieftain-ship.

entries.luganda: Ssebanaku beekiina : nti embuga ndiddeyo omukono gw'embuzi (= essunsa).
entries.english: The beggars are exaggerating : (one says) I ate at the chief's place a whole leg of a goat (or: vegetable leaves).
They blame the person who has stayed out long on a visit : (saying) he has brought sickness into our home.

entries.luganda: "Ssebayita baayita bokka" : kwavanga ku ddagala lya biswa.
entries.english: (The musawo says) "The sick call me on their own account (for their own good)" : as it is with the medicine blown into the termite hill (to make the termites come out).
entries.meaning: Meaning: the patients have to pay if they want my services. Rub.C.1292. 4887 Ssebayita-mbwa : 1) nga mu ngalo ataddemu eijinja; 2) ng'omuggo agukisa. (cf. Nkwegaanyi: 3154n) He is like a man calling the dog (that has stolen something) : 1) in his hand he holds a stone (to punish the dog); 2) whilst he hides a stick (behind his back). Treacherous allurement!

entries.luganda: Ssebeevumya nsogobe : eriiso teriva mu kyoto.
entries.english: (The balaalo) speak contemptuously about the still-born calf (not much good for eating) : but the eye does not leave the meat over the fire place.
entries.meaning: Application: People often belittle things, which they covet much.

entries.luganda: Ssebingi bwe bikwalira : ogamba nti tebirimbula.
entries.english: If your riches multiply : you say: "I won't lose them".

entries.luganda: Ssebugenyi bwa nsanafu : bwe bukukyalira tiweebaka (= gwe zizinda teyeebaka).
entries.english: When red ants pay you a visit (or: surround you), you won't sleep.
entries.meaning: Said of people whom you cannot trust. Lat. "Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes" (Vire).

entries.english: The tiny legs of the nnyomo (small ants) : make the path smooth.
entries.meaning: "Many hands make the work easy".

entries.english: The successful sale of an ox : must not pass without a "bakshish" (given by the seller).

entries.luganda: Ssebuko bunaafa : olabira ku nsugga (sso nga edda walyanga enkoko).
entries.english: If relationship (love) is going to die : you can judge it by the nsugga (vegetable).
entries.meaning: The man is not supposed to be offered nsugga at his wife's home. So if they offer him nsugga, it means that the family ties are broken. If he is welcome, they treat him with an enkoko or with butiko!

entries.luganda: Ssebukulu bwa nte : buli efuluma yeetuukira (= buli evaayo yeesitukira).
entries.english: Old cows : each single one going out of the kraal gets up herself.
entries.meaning: The young ones do not help her or bring food to her. Men also often treat old people like this. - Other explanation: There are some things everyone must do himself.

entries.english: The holes in which a snake lives : may not be pointed at with the finger.
entries.meaning: "Ssebunnya bwa musota" is a title of the Baganda kings expressing the deadly danger of their presence (i.e. busungu bwe busagwa).

entries.english: The bride in her silliness and inexperience : calls marriage "love".
entries.meaning: Many see their mistake soon.

entries.luganda: Ssebusiru bwa njoka : zitta ziruma) nnyinizo; nti mmwe munaalarnira wa?
entries.english: The folly of a stomach-ache : lies in the fact that it is a self-inflicted evil (pain, death); how can you fare well (remain healthy), doing such a thing?
entries.meaning: Engl. "As you brew so you must drink". French "On est puni par oil roil a pechr. Germ. "Was man sich eingebrockt hat, muss man auch ausessen". Rub. C.169, Duta 592, 83.92. 4900 Ssebusiru bwa nkoko : 1) bukunga kye bunaalya; 2) ku kyalo kw'ekulidde amazzi enywa manaabemu. (cf. Ssebukoko: 4894) The silly little chicks : 1) are looking wonderingly at what they are going to eat; 2) in the village where they grew up, they drink the water in which they bathed. Inexperience. Innocence abroad! Germ. "Die Unschuld vom Lande!" M.853, Ssal.

entries.luganda: Ssebuwufu bwa ngo : tebuyitibwamu mbwa (= nnantayitibwa mbwa).
entries.english: The tracks of a leopard : are not trodden by a dog.
entries.meaning: The king's honour is frightening; he kills those who are crossing his ways.

entries.luganda: Ssebwavu bwali dda : abejjereza (= awaayiriza) omunyago.
entries.english: His poverty is an old fact : he only slanders people (relations) saying that they have robbed him.
entries.meaning: He wants to give the impression that he was once rich (nti baanyaga edda).

entries.english: A big male dog : is no present for visitors.
entries.meaning: Visitors receive a goat or a chicken; but such a dog is no use to them.

entries.english: As the baby-girl treats (sucks) the breasts (of her mother) : so they (her children) will treat her own breasts.
If heaven commands it : the sun cannot refuse the clouds obscuring it.
entries.meaning: Vis maior, the higher power!

entries.english: When the cock stops his crowing : his muscles also relax.
entries.meaning: When a proud man stops his overbearing manner, his subjects are at ease.

entries.english: I don't care about the man who covers me.
An obstreperous person lives in the house of a good-natured man.
entries.meaning: He does not care about the just wishes of the one in authority; but the latter bears up with him. 58.17. 4912 Ssekabanja ka mulogo : n'addamu talema kubeera mulogo. If the plot of land formerly belonged to a witchdoctor : then the one who follows him will be a witchdoctor. The spell of the predecessor and his reputation pass on to the successor.

entries.english: Too eager a buyer : the answer (of the seller) frightens him away.
entries.meaning: The seller understands that the customer is so keen and at once raises the price.

entries.luganda: Ssekkadde lya munno : nti "ekkadde lya gundi likulukumba".
entries.english: (Seeing) the old father of your neighbour (walking) you say: "That miserable old fellow (the father of So and So) is strutting along!" If it was your father, you would say: the poor old man has no strength any longer.

entries.luganda: Ssekammira bya tere : ensimbi emu emummya ekyasa.
entries.english: The miser who refuses to give trifles : one cent (he refuses) causes others to refuse him 10 cents (100 kauris) (which they otherwise might have given).

entries.luganda: Ssekamwa : akayita ku kibi ne koogera ekirungi.
entries.english: An evil tongue : (is the one) that passes over its evil qualities and speaks about the good ones.
Grey heron, you are tall : tell us the news of the city!
entries.meaning: Visitors coming from town are greeted like that.

entries.luganda: Ssekibakati (or: Ssekimakati, Ssekimeketi) eyiiza amagezi : ntodde mmese, nsibye ku kugulu.
entries.english: Hunger produces cleverness : I took a (dead) rat and tied it on my leg.
entries.meaning: The shrewd man pretends to have a gangrened leg in order to have good food cooked for him. Song at beer parties. Rub.C.2152. 4922 Ssekibette : ng'omusajja akubira enva engalabi; nti ezange teeka wano! A rude fellow : as when a man beats an "engalabi"-dance for the vegetables. It is considered rude for the husband to drum with the fingers in order to hurry up the wife with the food.

entries.english: On the path that leads away the cow : you can also look for the herdsman.
The flower of the luwoko-bush : is not edible (poison).
The kii-iyorno-ant which takes the flying ants, guards them.
entries.meaning: Name of King Ssuuna I's mulongo. Application: A good king keeps and guards his people.

entries.luganda: Ssekisolo ekibuulira abantu : nti abaana b'empisiiyisi be bambuulira.
entries.english: The animal (kibe) that is telling the people (says) : the children of passers-by have told me.
entries.meaning: The cry of the kibe (jackal) at night is considered a bad omen: announcing the death of somebody.

entries.luganda: Ssekiswa kimpi : kimala kifa enswa empanvu.
entries.english: Although an ant-hill may be small : it still can yield many flying ants.
entries.meaning: Also an inconspicuous giver can give valuable help. Expression of appreciation!

entries.english: The arum-lily (vegetable) that is eaten by the master : does not lack taste.
entries.meaning: The children like to eat it too.

entries.english: The real heir cannot be changed.
entries.meaning: The inheritance always goes to the blood-relations.

entries.luganda: Ssemamwa agaakugeye edda : we gakulabako gasaanyiriza (or: ge gayimba oku-loopa n'okuwolereza).
entries.english: Lips that slandered you before : will pretend friendship when they meet you (or: do both, accusing you and defend you).
entries.meaning: Duplicity of men! Beware of double-dealers!

entries.luganda: Ssemanda : gamenya embazzi ne gayunga (= gayimba okumenya n'okuyunga).
entries.english: Charcoal : breaks the axe and joins it again.
entries.meaning: It breaks the axe when the trees are felled (for charcoal burning); it joins it when the live coal in the smithy welds the pieces together.

entries.luganda: Ssematiko agaggyibwa omuwuulu : omufumbo (= nnyinimu) y'agagaba.
entries.english: Mushrooms (that) are collected by the unmarried : the married one (the master of the household) divides them.

entries.luganda: Ssemiti gya jjuuni : basimba beegekkereza (= beegeketeza).
entries.english: The young shoots of the arum-lily are planted slantingly.
entries.meaning: When they catch roots, they will straighten up. - Bringing up of children.

entries.luganda: Ssemiyagi (= Ssemuyagi) gulambulwa : atagulambula alya amaluma.
entries.english: The "njagi"-plant should be visited (watched) : one who does not watch it, eats without vegetables.
entries.meaning: The "njagi" (= ntula) have to be plucked at the right time, namely when they are not quite ripe; otherwise they are uneatable. - Watch your chance!

entries.english: The one who fights with spears : will be killed with a spear.
Words (opinions) are different.
entries.meaning: Quot capita, tot sensus!

entries.english: He who takes the loan of a male animal (for breeding purposes) : brings back a female one.

entries.luganda: "Ssemukulu akusoose ekibi" : nti abato ba leero tebaasoboke.
entries.english: "The parent has sinned before you" : (is the right answer to the complaint) the children of now-a-days are unmanageable.
entries.meaning: Lat. "Laudator temporis acti". Bad example of parents.

entries.luganda: Ssemusota gusimbye (= guli) mu ntamu : ogutte toolye, oguleke toolye (or: bw'ogutta toolye, bw'oguleka toolye).
entries.english: If a snake rises from the cooking pot : you won't eat, whether you kill it or whether you leave it alone.
entries.meaning: If you kill it, you break the pot and you can't cook; if you leave it, you can't do anything.

entries.english: The trick of the mweso-seeds catches you, whilst you are looking.
entries.meaning: You see it coming and you cannot escape.

entries.luganda: Ssemutego tegulwala mugongo : nga kye bagutuma tegunnakikwata.
entries.english: A hunting trap has no back-ache : when it has not yet caught what it has been set for.
Where the small boy has killed (caught) a big "engege" : there he will again cast his net.

entries.luganda: Ssemutunulo gwa mbwa : tegukugaana kulya kikyo (= tegulayirira alya ekikye).
entries.english: The expectant look of the dog does not prevent you from eating your meat.
entries.meaning: His look tries to move your kindness only.

entries.luganda: Ssemutwe guttidde : omukulu gwe bayita ekiwalaata.
entries.english: A head that is free from weeds : (that is) an old man whom they call "bald-head".
entries.meaning: Applied to a seasoned marriage, with the welfare of the children established.

entries.luganda: Ssemuze gukuwadde balo : ab'ebweru bayima ku lusozi ne balangira; nti eki-gwagwa kya munno, anti weegaana Id?
entries.english: The evil trait of character has given you your husband (i.e.
entries.meaning: you knew his bad qualities, when you married him) : and now the outsiders stand in high places and shout: that monster of a husband is yours! Don't deny it!

entries.english: You cover white pumpkins and they uncover themselves.
entries.meaning: You cover them with leaves; but the leaves dry up and the pumpkins- appear again. - Said of people who are unknown in their youth, but make themselves known in later life.

entries.english: I have come out of it : (and) I fell into it again.
entries.meaning: French "Tomber de Charybde en Scylla". Engl. "From the frying pan into the fire". Germ. "Vom Regen in die Traufe geraten". Grammatical explanation: "Sse-" is the same particle as in the following proverbs: "Ssenkusigulenkusigule", "Ssenkuzaalenkuzaale" etc.; "ga" probably stands for "maziga". (Sse-n-ga-vuddemu : n-ga-zzeemu.) Rub.C.512, Ssal.p.29.

entries.luganda: Ssenkuba ya ggulo : bw'etekuba mubbi, ekuba musezi.
entries.english: If the evening rain does not fall on a thief, it falls on a night-wizard.
entries.meaning: Both start their work, when it is dark and rainy; but ordinary people remain at home.

entries.english: A mutual dependence (reliance) : like the tripod (used for stripping the bark off the mutuba).
entries.meaning: The man supports the tripod and the tripod supports the man. - Mutual help, service.

entries.english: "Let the hurt you" : (says) the bone to the gullet.
entries.meaning: Used On one who does not want to listen. Oli ssenkulume = towulira.

entries.luganda: SseiikusigulenkusiguIe : ogw'engulu gusigula ogw'emmanga, nti tulye (= tuwuu-te) ebyokya; bwe bijja, nga gwo gukikinala.
entries.english: "Let me tempt you" : says the upper lip to the lower, "let us eat the hot food"; when the food comes, the upper lip keeps aloof.
entries.meaning: French "Tirer les marrons du feu". Germ. "Die Kastanien aus dem Feuer holen".

entries.luganda: Ssenkusigulenkusigule : ng'ow'ettulu, nti mutunule nnyo, tunaabukeesa.
entries.english: "Let me encourage you" : like the one-eyed person, who says: keep awake, we carry on till morning!
entries.meaning: He need only keep one eye open; the other is asleep. - Suggesting is one thing -and doing is another.

entries.english: "Let me be your father" : the infant-boy (can say to his aunt, when he inherits his grandfather).
entries.meaning: His aunt becomes thereby his "child" and she says "Ssebo" to him.

entries.english: One does not eat his own flesh (may it be ever so savoury) : except King Ssuuna II.
entries.meaning: did it. He ravished his own children.

entries.luganda: Sseruba lwa mbuzi : sirubula kye lwegaaya.
entries.english: The jaw of the goat : has always something to chew (ruminating!).
A person who opens deserted houses : will (one day) open one in which there is a man (who will deal with him roughly).

entries.luganda: Sserugoye oluli eka : sirubula kye lusiba.
entries.english: A good plantain fibre (ekyayi) which you have at home : won't fail to be used for tying up something.

entries.luganda: Sserukama mayute : olunyiga ku lirye ng'akaaba (= bwe bakama agage ng'akaa-ba, = bwe bakwata ku lirye ng'awoloma).
entries.english: When they touch his own boil, then the one who squeezes other people's boils, cries out.

entries.luganda: Sserukundugga : akunduzza eza banne, ng'czize zigejja.
entries.english: The miser makes thin the goats of his neighbour, whilst his own get fat.
An old dried up person (lusajja, lukazi etc.) at her or his home : is always with something.
entries.meaning: At home there is always work.

entries.english: If there is beer at a mourning : comforters won't be missing.

entries.luganda: Sserulume lubi : luwazisa mu lugo lwalwo.
entries.english: The miserable old bull : attacks the cows in the kraal.
The impudent cricket-eater : leaves the holes (which the crickets made) wide open (after catching the cricket).
entries.meaning: Applied to people who return borrowed things in a bad condition.

entries.english: You walk over the old field of your mother as long as she is alive.
entries.meaning: But when she is dead, a new owner will prosecute you for trespassing.

entries.luganda: Sserwajja okwota : lukira (= lukiza, = asinza) nnyinimu entannama.
entries.english: The (miserable) visitor who came to warm himself claims greater comfort (rights) than the owner of the house.
entries.meaning: Abuse of hospitality (as regards a. place at the fire, food, bed, women).

entries.luganda: Sserwali lundi : omusibe tayita Jjimbo (= Ggimbo).
entries.english: (Remember) the day of old!
entries.meaning: (Since then) no prisoner passes the path to Ggimbo in fetters. When he is led over a certain ditch his ropes are taken away. The name of the ditch is "Sserwali lundi". Explanation: Ssuuna I. challenged a prisoner (Sserwa-li) on the road to Ggimbo (Busiro) to throw him in wrestling. But Sserwali threw the king and the furious king killed Sserwali.

entries.english: If the ssessolye (bulbul) does not die (as long as he is not dead) : he will get to a ripe ppaapaali (or ttooke).
entries.meaning: example of perseverance! Lat. "Dum spiro, spero". As long as there is life, there is hope.

entries.english: A place where formerly cows were kept : you recognize by the (luxuriant growth of the) kalanda-lugo-grass.
entries.meaning: The one-time-riches of now poor people can be concluded from certain remnants (a big house, heir-loom, certain habits etc.).

entries.english: (He invites you) Speak to us about yourself (your family or business) : but when you have gone, he points his finger at you.
entries.meaning: Your contribution to the conversation might politely be asked for, but is not always appreciated.

entries.english: (= Ataabalamule - - ) He who does not intend to separate the fighting parties : (says) give them sticks and they die.
entries.meaning: He wants to have his fun. - Peace making is better and nobler than urging on a fight.

entries.english: The tobacco of a quarrelsome person : dries on one side.
entries.meaning: Nobody wants to help him turning what is laid out for drying, for fear of his suspecting them of stealing.

entries.english: He who has not made the journey : calls it an easy one.
(= Atamukedde - - ) He who did not come as early as the other : speaks about him as "devouring his food".
entries.meaning: If he had been first, he would have had more!

entries.english: A person who has died, will not be sent back.
entries.meaning: Death does not send back his victims.

entries.english: They will not do it again : like one with syphilitic (cracked) feet who has stolen shoes.
entries.meaning: Because he got what he wanted.

entries.english: Men do not all grow up in the same way.
"They have no consideration for me" (i.e.
entries.meaning: these young folks eat up everything) : (this thought) makes the old man devour (what he can get).

entries.english: Heroes do not kill themselves : (others) kill them (in the battle).
"I do not want to lose" (says one who) bites off a piece from his neighbour's chunk of meat and gives the rest to whom he dislikes.
(obwavu) Poverty does not let you know who loves you.
(= Nze tebwaza.) I am barrenness which will not multiply.
(= Enkoko eteefe - - ) The chicken which is not going to die : will bring visitors.
entries.meaning: Expecting visitors, the owner will not kill the chicken for his own meal. - "Live long" draws the visitor. Visitors often save people from harm. If a child is due for punishment and a visitor comes, it escapes the punishment. Or a woman going to be beaten by her husband, is safe if a visitor arrives.

entries.english: The bananas don't bear where they eat them.
entries.meaning: The owner of the bananary speaks despisingly about his gardens, because he does not want people to think that he has much food. Or: pretences of people who minimize their income before others, to avoid taxes.

entries.english: Mistakes are not made by one only (all make them) : even the White Man makes them.
The market does not resound from quarrelling, but from bargaining.
entries.meaning: The great noise on a market day seems to be quarrelling; but it is only haggling.

entries.english: (ekitimba) The animal did not keep outside the hunters' ring : and fell right into the net.
entries.meaning: To run into the trap, into perdition.

entries.luganda: Tekyali kya kumanya : ng'eyakwagala akuyita embwa.
entries.english: There is no more to be heard (said) : as it is with the person who loved you once and calls you now a dog.
entries.meaning: First friendship (love), then lasting enmity. You know now that that person will tell everything she knows about you.

entries.english: Unharmed : like the nose of a cow.
entries.meaning: Although it feeds amongst pointed branches and thorns, the nose does not show wounds.

entries.english: Fitting naturally : like a sturdy dwarf dancing with banana fringes round his waist.
Death does not announce the days of its arrival.

entries.luganda: Terulongoosa : lukuttako gw'oyagala ne lulekawo gw'otoyaga1a.
entries.english: Death is not partial : it kills the one you like and leaves the one you don't like.
Death knows no offerer (knows no bribery; otherwise the rich would never die).
Death has not waited for me.
entries.meaning: Mourning cry (wailing) of one who has lost his parents by death, whilst he was away.

entries.luganda: Tewali ayagaliza ya munne kuzaala nduusi.
entries.english: Nobody wishes his neighbour's cow (or goat) to bring forth a female young.
entries.meaning: A father of many daughters is the object of envy (rich dowry).

entries.english: The one of Nnamataba is not here (namely Mulindwa).
entries.meaning: Mulindwa is a personal name, here taken in its literal meaning ("one who is waited for"). There is none to be waited for, so let us start. Nnamataba is a place on the Jjinja-road (32 km from Kampala) and is the former butaka of the mmamba-clan. Two famous brothers from there became Ssekiboobo, namely Ssebwato and Kibudde. Kibudde had a son called Mulindwa who inherited the riches of Ssebwato and Kibudde. - Instead of saying: "We have not to wait for anybody", they say "Tewali w'e Nnamataba".

entries.english: Do not praise your work in the field, when they (i.e.
entries.meaning: the visitors) see it with their own eyes. Let them praise it, if it is praiseworthy!

entries.english: The prisoner will not fail to get them (ensimbi or rupiya).
entries.meaning: If one is in prison, he will find somebody to pay the ransom money for him.

entries.luganda: "Tezifudde" : ajja na lusoggo (or: adda na kasoggo).
entries.english: They did not swarm (properly) : (one who says so), comes with a lusoggo (banana leaf rolled up as funnel).
entries.meaning: He has only a few flying ants (enswa). The funnel is nearly empty.

entries.english: They are not weeping over the son-in-law (whose wife died), but over their own daughter.
They are not spreading the mat for the son-in-law, but for their own daughter.
They are not afraid of the shield, but of the man behind it (not of the defence, but of the attack).
There is no end to bigambo : they are as plentiful as war-booty.

The feet do not exact payment from their owner (for having to walk) : they do not raise the alarm over a mother nursing her child (because she is supposed to do her best in looking after it, even when the child cries).
The matooke do not bear in one place only : (one who says so) is afraid of work.
entries.meaning: He is told to cultivate a fertile spot overgrown with elephant grass, which he would have to clean.

entries.english: The moon (month) is not shown to one who has a debt.
entries.meaning: He has agreed to pay, when the moon is again full. To draw his attention to the growing moon would worry him.

entries.english: (A man who tells you) "There was never any better brewed than this" : makes you draw unfermented beer.
entries.meaning: You want to drink it before it is ready.

entries.english: "Don't blame the women (c-ooks)" : (so one says), if he has had nothing to eat, where he came from.
entries.meaning: He hopes to get food here; therefore he tries to curry favour with the cooks.

entries.english: (ennaku ennungi) Lucky days do not dawn a second time.
entries.meaning: So says the visitor who has had a good time (eating and drinking).

entries.english: "The drums are not beaten without cause" (says one who has heard that) they have slaughtered on the next hill.
(Where a man tells you) "If it had not been you" : there it is you escape the punishment (for a bad deed).
Don't tackle prematurely a (wounded) kibe (fox), as long as it does not dribble saliva.
entries.meaning: Don't take too great risks!

entries.english: Do not despise the millet grain in the room (it has a hidden power, fermenta-tion).
entries.meaning: Do not minimize (underestimate) others!

entries.english: Do not despise little things : a hen is enough for (several) visitors.
(= Togayanga batono - ) Do not despise little things : you cannot kill a flea with the palm of the hand.

entries.luganda: Togaya kigalamidde : emmanvu etta embaala (or: emmanvu eva wansi n'etta enswa).
entries.english: Don't despise what is on the ground : people put the little trough on the anthill, drum on it and entice the ants to swarm (or: the little trough is on the ground and still it kills the flying ants).
entries.meaning: The "embaala" are considered as particularly tasty termites. Application: Small men may be powerful.

entries.english: Do not condemn the secrets of a child.
entries.meaning: French "La verite sort de la bouche des enfants". Lat. "Maxima debetur puero reverentia" (Juvenal). Germ. "Kinder and Narren reden die Wahrheit".

entries.luganda: Togayira ggyirikiti mu ntooma : bwe likula osanga litikkidde ya mujunga.
entries.english: Don't despise the "kiyirikiti"-tree (Erythrina tomentosa) in the new green grass : when it grows up, you find it crowned with tassels.
entries.meaning: Application: Don't expect too much from a beginner.

entries.english: Do not importune with questions one who has fallen : he will tell you, when he gets up again.

entries.luganda: Tokliya ŋŋonge nto : bw'ekula ogyambalako eddiba (= enkoba) (or: ob'oli awo n'ogyambalako engatto).
entries.english: Do not despise a young otter : when it grows up, you will wear its skin (or: perhaps one day you will wear it as shoes).
entries.meaning: The child is the father of the man.

entries.english: Do not do things negligently : what you do, do well!
"You don't know how well I can produce children" (says the father who is keen to get dowry for his daughters) : and then he offers you a dwarf for marriage.

entries.luganda: Tosala (= towuliriza) gwa kawala : nga tonnawulira gwa kalenzi.
entries.english: Do not give judgement in favour of the girl : before you have heard the pleading of the boy.

entries.luganda: Tota mabi : omutwe gw'ente nga si mukube.
entries.english: Do not utter bad words (magambo - accusations) : when the head of the cow is still over the fire.
entries.meaning: At the ceremony of "kwabya olumbe" a cow is usually killed for the mourners. Its head is reserved for the bajjwa (nephews and nieces etc.) of the deceased; they should not complain prematurely that they have received no meat, as long as the head is still there. - Application: Do not utter suspicions or accusations, before you are sure that you have been wronged (rash judgement).

entries.luganda: Tova mbwa w'eyotera : n'ogenda gonja w'akalira.
entries.english: Don't move away from the place where the dog warms itself, in order to go where the gonja (large sweet banana) is roasted.
entries.meaning: There it will be too hot. Lat. "Qui amat periculum peribit in illo".

entries.luganda: Tovumirira egwa wala : enjala bw'ekuluma osakirawo (or: bw'ezza emmere osakirawo).
entries.english: Do not curse the rain that falls far from your place : perhaps, when you are hungry, you will have to go there for food (or: when it brings food, you will have to fetch it from there).

entries.luganda: Towakanira ebaagwa : nti munda mulimu ento.
entries.english: Do not argue about an animal which is being skinned (obstinately maintaining) : it is with young.
entries.meaning: No use arguing; we shall see soon enough.

entries.luganda: Toyima mu nkondo za mbuzi : n'owakana n'ababaka.
entries.english: Don't stand near the pegs where the goats are tied up (when the men of the chiefs want to take you for work), refusing to follow them.
entries.meaning: Seeing the goats they will requisition one as fine.

entries.luganda: Toyiteko kalambiko : ekibbo kiyita ku mugenyi.
entries.english: Don't pass (without looking at me) : the food basket passes by a guest like that.

(He who says) "Let's take the things" (and encourages the others to go on a thieving campaign with) "May Kiwanuka - a lubaale - accompany you" (does not go with them and is not caught, although he is the main culprit).
Let us ask the old people : the nose asks the shoulder.
entries.meaning: When the nose smells something, it turns to the shoulder: what smells here? -It's wisdom to ask advice from the elders.

entries.luganda: "Tudde eka, tukube abakazi" : akuba muziziko (= bisenge).
entries.english: "Let us go home and beat our wives" : (one who talks like this) beats only the dark empty place behind the door.

entries.luganda: "Tudde ku butaka" : azzaayo kiwanga (= si bulamu).
entries.english: (He who says) "Let us go back to our ancestors' land" : takes his skull there (or: will not be alive long).
"Let us go quickly" : it's only strips of barkcloth with which he dismisses his guest.
entries.meaning: Instead of the big piece of barkcloth which the host promised, the guest receives only odd pieces.

entries.english: Let us get out the one of Luwunga (namely Kagenda).
entries.meaning: Play of words: "Kagenda" was a chief in Mawokota and his place was called "Luwunga". "Kagenda" is taken in its literal meaning:. one who goes, leaves the place; i.e. tuggyeemu olugendo or: tugenze, weeraba!

entries.english: "We have enough" : (this statement) does not hold good for two (persons).
entries.meaning: Perhaps the other man is still hungry.

entries.english: "Let us beat the messengers" : (a man saying so) will not go to the king's place.
entries.meaning: If he is seen there, they will take him to court.

entries.english: (The coward brags) "We are fighting hard" : and returns home with both his spears.
entries.meaning: He has not thrown one!

entries.english: (He who says to you) "We are both weak persons" : overburdens you with work (leaves the hard work to you).
(ejjembe) "We are many" (says the warrior) and omits to suck (strength and courage) out of his fetish.
entries.meaning: Relying upon the multitude of warriors he neglects the usual ceremony (to put the fetish to his lips, before going into the battle, and to draw strength from it) and consequently is killed.

entries.luganda: Tuli bataka n'abataka : embazzi tetema mbwa (kubanga bonna basula mu kyoto).
entries.english: We are both landowners : the axe does not hurt the dog (both are near the fire place at the end of the day and live in peace).
"We shall kill them whilst they are rolled up (asleep)" : as one kills (steps on) a ggongolo (millipede) that wants to pass the doorway.
entries.meaning: The ggongolo rolls itself up when sensing danger.

entries.english: We are gripping each other, pressing against each other, in passing, like the spittle and the Adam's apple.
entries.meaning: The spittle goes down and the Adam's apple goes up.

entries.luganda: Tuli byuma na byuma : akambe tekasala mpiso.
entries.english: We are all tools (so let us have peace) : the knife does not cut the needle.
entries.meaning: "Dog does not bite dog".

entries.english: "We shall die together" : (so a man promises; but when the real danger comes) he holds his hands over his head (i.e.

entries.luganda: "Tuligalya amadda" : bagalya mu kibanja (= basanga Idbanja).
entries.english: "We shall eat (the amatooke), when we come back" : (the visitors say so who want to be off), but they eat on the empty plot (= they find the empty plot).
entries.meaning: Those who have invited them, have left meanwhile. Engl. "Make hay whilst the sun shines".

entries.english: We are like a (brass) bracelet : we are fixed to the arm.
entries.meaning: We are under authority, tuli "bafuge", we are to go where the arm of the master takes us.

entries.luganda: Tuli ppoma : tuvugire amatuine (or: tuvuga amatume).
entries.english: We are like drums : we sound the message which was given to us.
entries.meaning: We are the messengers, but not responsible for the message.

entries.english: (The quack, asked about the price of the treatment, says) "We shall judge that by the sickness" : that's the way the quack cheats you.
entries.meaning: It will be of no use haggling afterwards.

entries.english: a nnyina.
Sleep is courageous (powerful) : it throws down even the strong.
"Let us eat the tasty matooke" (says the guest) : but he offends against good manners and makes you eat with the guest.
entries.meaning: Guests were always treated separately.

entries.luganda: "Tulye ku by'amagulu" : w'alinnya mu busa, asanguliza ku ssubi; nti lya busa bw'olinnyamu.
entries.english: (He says) "Let us eat from the work of our legs (stamping budongo or treading bikamulo) (let us use our gain)" : but when he steps on cowdung, he wipes it off on the grass; (remark) eat the cowdung you stepped on.
(He who says) "Let us try hard" frees the mushroom-anthill of the grass.
entries.meaning: The embaala-termites are considered as a great delicacy. Therefore people don't mind trying hard to clear the ground for the mushrooms which grow on the kibaala.

entries.english: "Let us eat and finish the food" (says the visitor) and makes the neighbour quarrel with your host (because a neighbour coming afterwards gets nothing to eat).
(One who says) "We shall hear the news" : does not run in the direction of the alarm.
entries.meaning: He leaves the duty of helping to others.

entries.english: (He who says) "We shall divide up the things on the other side of the valley (or: on that overgrown bananary)" : cheats you.
entries.meaning: He wants to be alone with you, without witnesses.

entries.luganda: Tunaagenda naawe akalannamo : ettooke ekkulu na mumizi.
entries.english: We shall go together at ease : as the seasoned matooke goes down the throat of a gourmand.
entries.meaning: It is soft and slips down easily.

entries.english: "We shall pass through the chief's place" : (so says one) if he is well dressed.
"Let us be friends" : (so one talks to you) if he has seen you with beer.
"Let us be friends" : (says the boy) if he has seen that you have a sister.
(The man says to his wife) "We shall talk only pleasant things" : if those who came (on a visit) are of the relations-in-law.
entries.meaning: Now we eat humble pie, but later we shall speak differently.

entries.english: Whe shall have a very long conversation : as long as the plaited-barkcloth-wick (lufuuzi) of Ssenkoole.
entries.meaning: Ssenkoole was the title of the King's executioner. He also had to keep the King's fire alright by burning plaited barkcloth-wicks. These always glimmered, except when a King had just died. - Ssenkoole's butaka was at Buwaate.

entries.english: (The visitor says) "Thank you'?
entries.meaning: : (but as soon as he has gone away) he throws the piece of meat down (saying) "that is all he has given me!" Dissatisfaction.

entries.english: We help each other : like the white ants (when they sound the alarm).

entries.luganda: Tutemya bukofu : magi (= enkwale) eraga obudde.
entries.english: We are awake like the guinea fowl : the crested crane (or: the partridge) is announcing the day.
entries.meaning: The guinea fowls are wary birds, even during sleep. The crested cranes start crying at 3 a.m., the partridges at 4 a.m.

entries.english: We have come without driving the flies away (in a hurry) : like the frog (which can not drive them away, because it has no tail).

entries.luganda: Tuzze twetunula ku nnyindo : ng'abagole, We have come looking down our noses : like brides.
entries.english: Joke on beautifully dressed people.
entries.meaning: A bride is supposed to look bashful.

entries.english: "We have dispersed all over the world" : (so say children) whose father is dead.
entries.meaning: They have no longer any meeting place.

entries.english: Even the man who says "We love each other" does not tell you that he is swallowing his spittle.
entries.meaning: Even most intimate friends do not tell each other everything.

entries.english: We used to eat the matooke together, (says the woman) dipping the ennoga alternatively with her husband into the sauce.
entries.meaning: They have only one dish between them, or, they understand each other well.

entries.luganda: "Twagenda Buganda kulya nnyama" : ge maddu agassa enunandwa e Masajja.
entries.english: "We went to Buganda to eat meat" : that is the passion which killed the lubaale-priest at Masajja.
entries.meaning: These priests went to Masajja, a village infected with plague, to break the spell of plague and to eat meat. They were killed by King Kyabaggu.

entries.luganda: "Twakwana masogola": omusambi w'ekikanja akoma ku ndeku (or: omusogozi akoma ku bikanja).
entries.english: "We have been brewing beer together" (so one complains who has been helping to brew beer) : but the one who has been treading the grass (used for making beer) gets only a full calabash (or: gets only the dregs which he can use once more to make weak beer).
"We knew each other formerly" (says the rich man to his former friend) and gives him an old pair of trousers.
entries.meaning: What is not good enough for himself any longer, must be good enough for his poor friend.

entries.english: (or: Twaliraanya mayumba : emmeeme tezaaliraana.) We built our houses next to each other : but our hearts were not neighbourly.

entries.luganda: Twalyanga mbidde : nga nnamukago all ku Buganda.
entries.english: (A man says) We have been eating mbidde (beer bananas) : if he finds nnamu-kago (good eating bananas) in Buganda.
entries.meaning: Application: One married to an ugly woman sees a beautiful one and regrets his misfortune.

entries.english: We have killed our own (kabuzi etc., i.e.
entries.meaning: we don't want to let others partake in the feed) : (a man constantly acting selfishly like this), will have to ask his own wife to bleed him. Nobody else will help him.

entries.english: (He who says) "Let us hide it" (store away the good things for ourselves) : is wiser than (one who says) "we shall refuse" (to give it).
entries.meaning: Concealing things which might arouse the interest or desire of a visitor, is wiser (kinder) than refusing to give them to him.

entries.english: (If the one who said) "Let us cultivate for ourselves" : gets a big crop of maize, he will not give you part of it.

entries.luganda: "Tweriire (= tweriire byaffe)" : akukyawanya n'ow'omuliraano (= ng'akuggya-ko ow'omuliraano).
entries.english: (He who says) "Let us eat our own food (and not give it away)" : causes enmity with your neighbour (or: robs you of a good neighbour).
(If they say) "Let us fight for ourselves" : then certainly a good man will fall.
We have adopted King Kamaanya's method (of fighting sham-battles as prepa-ration for war).
entries.meaning: Kamaanya incessantly called old and young warriors for military manoeuvres. We are practising.

entries.luganda: Va eri engabi (= ku ngabi) : 1) tosimira mbwa lumonde; 2) simira mbwa lumo-nde!
entries.english: Away from the bushbuck!
entries.meaning: : 1) you do not dig potatoes for the dog; 2) first dig potatoes for the dog! You have brought nothing for the hunt.

entries.english: "Get away, I'll pay you!" (those who talk like that) will not come back (to pay the debt).
"Get away from here, that we may talk" : (one who says so) knows your weak-ness (namely that you cannot keep it to yourself).

entries.luganda: Vviivi we livaako enso : omuggo nga bakutemera.
entries.english: (= Evviivi - ) If the knee-cap comes off your knee: then they cut a stick for you (i.e.

entries.luganda: Vvule ekkadde : lye baasomera okwasa (= lyabalobera okwasa).
entries.english: He is like an old muvule tree which they wanted to split, (but couldn't).
entries.meaning: Applied to strong willed people who defy others to influence them.

entries.english: A chief who has many children (relations), does not settle disputes (does not give judgement).
entries.meaning: It would be difficult for him to be impartial.

entries.english: The child of the inside of the house is called "child" : but is the child of the door (outside) also called "mwana"?
entries.meaning: Answer: yes; the child born by father and mother is their child (muzaalire ddala); but the child born by the brothers and sisters of father and mother (kitaawe muto nnyina muto) is also their child.

entries.english: (= Awagenda - - ) Where the shield goes, there also is the spear (ready for the defence and ready for the attack).
If one travels he finds his living place.
entries.meaning: Said of one who leaves his place, settles somewhere, becomes rich and finally a chief.

entries.english: He who has his own home, behaves in his own fashion (makes his own laws).
A braggart (scandalmonger, quarrelsome person) also has his field (where he works, namely his mouth).5.3

entries.luganda: Wakka awunya : nga ggwe omulumbye ku nswa ze.
entries.english: The "wakka" (stinking black ant) stinks, when you have attacked it among its flying ants.
entries.meaning: No wonder you get into trouble, when you interfere with other people's busi-ness. - One who is robbed of his things, fights.

entries.english: When the big (green-red and blue) lizard crouches down, he gets up again.
(= Awakubirwa - ) Where a messenger (of the king etc.) is beaten, there won't be peace.
entries.meaning: The injury done to the messenger, is done to his master. Rub.C.1570. 5203 Wakula buteesagga : ng'omukira gwa munya. You have grown up not (able) to defend yourself : like the tail of a lizard. The tail of a cow drives away the flies; but the tail of a lizard cannot do like-wise.

entries.english: A person acting independently (an odd fellow) like the thumb!
entries.meaning: It always points in a direction different from the other fingers.

entries.english: (= Awalabye - ) Where a man has seen his way of climbing up : there might be no coming down.
entries.meaning: It is easier to do things than to undo them.

entries.english: (If a cross-questioner asks you) What have you seen there (i.e.
entries.meaning: what proofs can you bring forward)? : he makes you lose the court case.

entries.english: Awali - - ) Where there is a little pond, one needs a fishing net.
entries.meaning: A kasambajjo is a kind of shallow sieve made from twigs. It is held under the water in a corner of the pond. The nsonzi are driven above the sieve and then lifted out of the water.

entries.english: Death catches (you) unexpectedly.
entries.meaning: Death takes people who think they have been left and forgotten. Expression taken from the mweso-game. Death has its surprises.

entries.english: Death does not plead in court : he kills you and all (your unavailing) arguments.

entries.luganda: Wamala okulya obwakabaka : tokyalina kye weetaaga.
entries.english: You have become king : there is nothing more that you could desire (i.e.
entries.meaning: you have all that you could wish for).

entries.luganda: Wa maanyi abulwa w'avuba : Nnamalere yabulwa omwalo.
entries.english: Even a powerful man might have no place for fishing : Nnamalere had no har-bour.
entries.meaning: Nnamalere was the lubaale of lightning; therefore he was feared.on water and on land. Being supposed to hover in space, he could not call a harbour his own. Even the power of the mighty has its limits.

entries.english: The owner of goats exaggerates the riches of the owner of sheep.

entries.luganda: Wambwa aludde : n'ebigobero kw'atadde (= we byenkan4 Wambwa alu-dde okulabika : nga n'ebigobero.) Mr.
entries.english: Dog has been absent a long time : meantime he has had plenty of bones (and hidings).
entries.meaning: Also said of persons and their experiences after a long absence.

entries.luganda: Wa mukisa ng'aliibwa ngo : yava munda ate adda munda.
entries.english: It is a blessing for him to have been eaten by a leopard : he came from the womb (eya nnyina) and returned to the womb.
You have put me into an impossible position (you have jeopardized me).
entries.meaning: Like a visitor leaving his stealing dog with his host and going away. The dog gets the host into trouble.

entries.luganda: Waŋŋaaŋa tafa ddogo : ng'era Wammamba bw'atafa ttama.
entries.english: The hornbill does not give up its horrible voice, even when dead : just as the lungfish does not give up its cheek.
entries.meaning: Even when the hornbill is dead and you poke its belly with a stick, it makes a noise almost the same as it did when alive, and the lungfish hurts your fingers with its teeth, even when its head is cut off.

entries.english: What the hen produces : serves as ransom.
entries.meaning: You cannot give away the mother-hen, because that is your capital. - Do not sell your land, sell its produce!

entries.english: (One who tells you) From here I can't reach it (a coveted thing like fruit) puts a mortar there (to stand on it) as soon as you have gone away.
There is nothing useless in a cow.
Where there rises a little smoke, there the hungry man invites himself.
entries.meaning: Name given to one who turns up everywhere, where people are cooking. Un-invited guest, gate crasher.

entries.english: Where something (or somebody) has sunk down (in the grave or in the water) : there is nothing left.
Where a knife fits in : a hoe does not fit.
entries.meaning: Where there is room for a knife, there might be none for a hoe. Use the right instrument; the right man on the right spot. Engl. "A round peg in a square hole".

entries.luganda: Weebale, weebale : akumalira ebibyo (or: amala ebintu).
entries.english: One who often says to you "thank you", finishes off your things.
entries.meaning: Every time he speaks so, you lose something.

entries.luganda: Weebale, weebale : azuukusa mbwa mu kyoto.
entries.english: He who shouts for joy "Well done, well done", rouses up the dog from its place on the hearth.
entries.meaning: Somebody has brought meat and unpacks it: and the others show their appre-ciation and the dog is also attracted.

entries.english: You are excited like a mason-wasp.
entries.meaning: You are fidgeting about, be quiet! Ssal.p.63. 5255a Weebugabuga : ng'omwavu akomera enju. You are taking over much trouble : like a poor man fencing in his house. He has no goats to fence in and no thieves will come.

entries.english: Are you inquiring whether the king has an army?
You have done a silly thing : like the toothless person who refuses (a piece) of liver.
entries.meaning: Having refused something (meat) that is soft, what else will you be able to eat?

entries.english: (He who says to you) "You have changed your character", will disown you (disinherit you) at the burial rites.
You are particular : like a poor man who refuses to eat fat.
You are careful like the wife of one with protruding jaw-bones.
entries.meaning: She will not mention the word "kkonkome" (big lizard), for she fears that it might be taken as referring to her husband.

entries.english: You are walking carefully like one with protruding jaw-bones, walking over a bridge.
entries.meaning: He might lose his equilibrium.

entries.english: You buy yourself a wife who is a wizard (poisoner), whilst seeing her (i.e.
entries.meaning: I warn you not to marry her).

entries.luganda: Weeguluma nga bijanjaalo : enkumbi ebirima esula wansi, byo Walla waggulu ku mpagi.
entries.english: You are overbearing like beans : the hoe that cultivates them, sleeps on the ground but they are high up on a pole.

entries.luganda: "Weekakire" : omugenyi yeekakira taaba mubie (If the host says) "Fill it as much as you like" : the visitor fills his pipe with bad tobacco.
entries.english: If the visitor had been welcome, the host himself would have filled the pipe for the visitor with good tobacco.

entries.luganda: Weekambazza ng'ow'effumu erimu : nti sikukuba manyago.
entries.english: You are bragging like one who has only one spear saying: I am not killing you with spears (shafts).
entries.meaning: He ought to speak in the singular, as he has only one spear.

entries.luganda: Weekannansula nga nnamwandu agaba eddagala; nti olwatta balo lwayita wa?
entries.english: You are bragging (cheating) like a widow who gives out medicine : where did the sickness pass that killed your husband?
entries.meaning: You could not even cure your husband! Lat. "Medice cura teipsum!" P.

entries.luganda: Weekennenkula nga bbugga : balyaye kibbo lidda munda.
entries.english: You are disappointing like "bbugga" (vegetable leaves) : people plucked them by the basketfuls, but the leaves shrink together.

entries.luganda: Weekiina nga Kasuipu, nti: Embuga nnaagikuba mu ggulu.
entries.english: You are exaggerating like the Kasujju (ssaza chief), when he said: I shall put up my headquarters at Ggulu (place in Busujju).
entries.meaning: Reply: Ggulu (heaven) is rather a high place for a ssaza-chief to reach!

entries.english: You act in a careless manner : like a sick person getting the loan of a cow (think-ing: my relations will give it back).
"Smear yourself!" : even a lazy woman smears herself with soil (pretending to have worked well in the garden).
You feign to be very busy : you will not be of any help to your neighbour (who sounded the alarm).
Do you keep hold of the food and the knife?
entries.meaning: You don't give anybody a chance to eat.

entries.english: You are in a scrape : like a woman who has put no food aside for her husband.
You are showing off : like the millipede dressed in a rag.
You are considering it carefully (on the mweso-board) like one who is going to pick an enjaliko (single luwiki) whilst the big heap is still remaining.
entries.meaning: Comparison taken from the mweso-game.

entries.luganda: "We mmala okulya, simalirawo (bigambo) byange" : ng'anaalya ku bbiri (= n'awalala).
entries.english: 'Where I stop eating, I do not stop talking" (says one) who intends to eat in a second place.
entries.meaning: He did not get enough to eat.

entries.english: You are mighty careful : like a syphilitic person after a haircut (being anxious not to show the sickness).
